LEWIS'S IN LIVERPOOL,
AND THE PROVIDING OF THE BEST TEA TO FAMILIES, HOTELS, AND PUBLIC AND PRIVATE INSTITUTIONS THROUGH-

OUT TUE UNITED KINGDOM. Who are Lewis's? Well, Lewis's are as well known in Liver- pool as the Bank of England is known in London. Lewis's began business in Liverpool thirty years ago, and Lewis's have at this present time one of the very largest businesses in Eng- land.

Lewis's have not always sold Tea, but having a very large number of empinyi,,s to provide with an afternoon meal, Lewis's were struck with the difficulty of procuring a good drinkable and refreshing Tea for them at a moderate price. The ordinary Teas were perfectly abominable. Tired of the constant and not unreasonable complaints and of the perpetual changing of their Tea Dealers, Lewis's at last resolved t) buy their Tea for the use of their establishment direct from the shippers, and to en- gage a qualified person to make the purchase. Lewis's could hardly believe there could be such a change for the better in the cost and quality of the tea so bought, but "experience teaches." Lewis's thought what was good enough for the use of all their establishments, public and private, would surely be good enough for the general public. Lewis's then began to sell Teas to their friends, and at last were induced to make thesale public in Lancashire, where they sell 20.000 pounds of Tea per week. Lewis's now feel they have benefited only a small pro- portion of the population; they intend in future to make their Tea known all over the United Kingdom. Lewis's pure, splendid Tea, is one stated price, 2s a pound. Lewis s have no other price Tea, neither higher nor lower, and this Two Shilling Tea is fit for the Queen to drink. Two shil- lings is a favourite price with fewis's, they having been able to supply the public with many excellent things at the price. Not till after much hard work did Lewis's succeed in blending a splendid and most deliciously-flavoured Tea, which they are giving to the public for 2s a pound. Many tea dealers charge the public 3s and 38 6d for a similar quality. Lewis's desire to be the universal suppliers of Tea Tea is drunk in every house- hold in the United Kingdom; it should therefore be sold at a less profit than any other article of consumption, except bread. Lewis's wish particularly to direct the attention of every family and every househo: de r to the great advantage there is in buying Lewis's Two-Shilling Tea. The flavour is so good and the strength eo very great. that one pound goes further than IS ounces of most ether Teas, providing always the water boils thoroughly. The proof that Lewis's do not exaggerate the appreciation in which their Two Shilling Tea is held lies in the fact that they receive thousands of orders every day from all parts of the United Kingdom. Lewis's would like members of the Press all over the United Kingdom to write for a pound of Lewis's Two Shilling Tut ; they are sure to be satisfied ai-d astonished with the result. Every hotel-keeper, and every public and private institution throughout the country, sh iuld write to Lewis's in Liverpool for a pound of Lewis's Two shi ling Tea. The risk is not great; it is only to send 2s in stamps to I ewis's in Liverpool, and in return they will receive a sound of splendid Tea, packed neatly in a box, carriage paid, to any address in the United Kingdom. —Address Lewls's in Liverpool.

7.-esittn. APRIL FOOLS. He who mourneth day by day That his youth doth pass away Like the blossoms on the tree, Sure an April fool must be; For the blossoms fade and die That the tree may fruit supply; So youth fled, we e'er should find Fruitful wisdom left behind. He who lives to garner gold Selling what should ne'er be sold Bartering peace for dross, why he Sure an April-fool must be! Many who'd have mourned his end Will rejoice that they may spend, For the ingots he may save None will bury in his grave. • He who spurns the horny hand Throwing loom or tilling land, Treating labour scornfully— Sure an April fool is he. Were the loom of toil bereft, Spider would weave warp and welt; Earth and labour are allied— Thriftless groom makes thriftless brid He who thinks that Time hath done All for which Time was begun, Nor its onward course doth see, Sure an April fool must be!

The love that lasts—the love of money. Bad seats to occupy—conceit and deceit. "Who is the most finished orator ?" asks a correspondent. Well, Demosthenes has been finished about as long as any
of them. "After all," says an old doctor, "there are only two kinds of disease—the one of which you die, and the other of which.

you don't." "Do you think," asked Mrs. Pepper„" that a temper is a bad thing in a woman ?" "Certainly not, ma'am," replied a gallant philosopher. "It is a good thing, and she ought never to lose it." Foote praising the hospitality of the Irish after one of his trips to the sister island, a gentleman asked him whether he had ever been at Cork. "No, sir," Foote replied, "but I _ _ .

_ • have seen many drawings of it." A little boy was munching a piece of gingerbread. His mother said, "Who gave you that, Tommy ?" '" Miss Johnson," he replied. "And did you thank her for it ?:' said his mother. "Yes, mamma, but I did not tell her so,"

he replied. NO UsE.—Prof. Young, of Princetown College, says "Take a railroad freM the earth to the sun, with a train running 40 miles an hour without stops, and it would take about 265 years and a little over to make the journey." He estimates the fare, at a cent a mile, to be 230 million doLs.

These figures kill the project. Amman-D.—Response of a gilded youth to one of his friends, who has just announced formally his approaching marriage :—" I should like to be able to congratulate you both, but you see, as I do not know the lady I can't con- scientiously congratulate you, while as I do know you I can't conscientiously congratulate the lady." MOTHERS-IN-LAW IN PARIS.—The domestic affections of the ouvrier, where he has not been demoralised by licen- tiousness or vice, are strong, and his sense of duty to his relatives unusual. Thus it would seem not at all uncommon for a workman to snpport his wife's mother, even when she lives far away. An ouvrier who had done this for some time fell, through the state of public affairs, into such dis- tress'as to be obliged to earn his bread by selling journals in the street. After a time he recovered his position; but all through his period of poverty, the mother-in-Jaw was allowed to believe that no change had taken place in his circumstances. Another ouvrier, who had originally been in business as a butcher, partly ruined himself by under- taking the charge of his wife's family. However, he never forsook the mother-in-law, but when he had a numerous family and only the small and precarious wages of a day labourer, she remained as much part of his family as the children.—" Good Words" for April. AN EXTRAORDINARY PREDICTION.—It is recorded of the poet Dryden, by Charles Wilson, in his "Life of Congreve," that having, strange to say, belief in astrology, he was care- ful to ascertain to the second the time at which his son Charles was born. He then calculated the boy's nativity, and was alarnied to discover that evil influences prevailed in the heavens—Jupiter, Venus, and the sun being below the earth, and the lord of his ascendant afflicted with a baleful square of Mars and Saturn. He concluded that in his eighth year, and on the day of birth, his son's life would be seriously endangered, if not lost; and that if he lived the same danger would exist when he attained his twenty-third birthday, and again on his thirty-third or fourth. On the boy's eighth birthday, despite every pre- caution to keep the boy from every possible danger, he was nearly killed by the fall of a wall. On his twenty-third birthday he was seized with giddiness and fell from an old tower belonging to the Vatican at Rome, and he was drowned at Windsor while swimmieg across the Thames in his thirty-third year.—" The World of Wonders." "THE BUTCTIF.R'S LEAP."—On the north side of the Marienplatz stands the new Town Hall of Munich, a brick edifice with a pinnacled stone gable, in the old German style of architecture. In front is a' bronze fountain, known as the Fischbrunnen, which commemorates the following circumstances connected with the guild of. butchers :—ln 1623 the city of Munich was desolated by a great plague, and on its abatement it was difficult to restore public con- fidence; so, in order to set at rest the minds of their fellow- citizens, the butchers assembled in their hall, and thence marched in procession to the market-place, where they plunged, one and all, into the cold water of the fountain basin, and returned dripping wet, without any ill effects or any fresh case of the terrible plague. In memory of the event the ceremony was kept up annually; and now, when the butchers' apprentices take up their freedom, amidst the other festivities of the occasion the young men have to take the Metzgersprung, or butcher's leap, into the fountain basin. The figure of a butcher's apprentice surmounts the fountain; at the base are crouching figures, representing plague and cholera.—" Cities of the World." Busiameie Carmc "LIFTERS."—In addition to his skill as a hunter, the Bushman also excels in an art quite as use- ful to him, but on the whole hardly so popular among his neighbours on whom it is practised. He is an adroit cattle- thief. The result of this is, that he is hated alike by Kaffir and Hottentot, who will even for a time forget their own never-dying feud to unite in taking vengeance on the com- mon enemy. If he cannot carry off the cattle, he will take to the inaccessible places where he can conceal himself, and leave the cattle to his'pursuers ; but not before a poisoned arrow has been left th each of the herd. If pursued, he will poison the watering-places on the way, and in- variably' endeavours to escape with his herd through places where horsemen or pedestrians less hardy than himself cannot follow. To follow the Bushman into his haunts among the mountains or inaccessible places is, however, 1 not a pleasant task. Lurking behind stones, under bashes, or among the long grass, the first inti- mation the unsuspecting traveller has of the vicinity of the enemy is one of those fearful little arrows entering his flesh. To escape with life after this is rare. Accordingly the Bushman is hunted down whenever a chance occurs, though he is everywhere feared, and is never, unless under I very favourable circumstances, openly attacked, as we have already hint3d. These arrows, which- render him such an object of dread, he keeps in a quiver on his back, though thcw for immediate use are carried in his hair, from which they can he instantly remoyed and strung on the bow. They are about eighteen inches long, and nnfeathered, so that they are only effective at short distances.—The Peoples of the World. ADVENTURES WITH LlONS.—Livingstone tells us that one morning, while enjoying a brisk ride he spied what he took to be a zebra a few hundred yards ;head. Dismount- ing he left his horse behind, and, gun in hand, proceeded in t.,443 direction pf the prey. Judge of his amazement when he discovered, as he presently did, that the supposed zebra was really a lion! The royal animal did not think it worth while to make a close acquaintance with the brave Doctor; but, in the most commonplace, not to say plebeian, style, turned tail. Livingtone followed as fast as he could, and was actually gaining upon the lion, when the creature was lost to view among the tall reeds which bordered a neigh- louring river. Chasing the lion is all very well, but being chased by one is decidedly unpleasant; at any rate Mr. Bal- dwin, another South African traveller, who experienced the sensation of being hunted by the lion which he intended to hunt, positively assures us that he never saw the like of it, and never wished to do so again. He had been hard at work all day mending the diesel-boom, or pole of his waggon, when an old Kaffir informed him that a lion was in the way and was being watched by a number of natives. Tired as he was, Mr. Baldwin was found ready, like Ben Battle, to obey the call of duty. Mounting his horse—which also was not so fresh as it might have been, having been ridden a long dikance in the morning—Mr. Baldwin in due time sighted the lion. Giving him chase, the animal ultimately came to a standstill in a thorny thicket. Leaving his horse for the moment, the hunter, at a distance of some 70 yards, fired at his "game," which collapsed so promptly that Mr. Baldwin thought it had been shot dead. Remounting and reloading, he took a short circle, and stood in his stirrups, to get a look at his victim. There he sat, crouch,cl in so natural a position, with fiercely flaring eyes, and ears erect, that it was evident he had not been struck at all. Mr. Baldwin had only put his horse in motion in order to get a nearer shot, when, ere he knew where he was, on came the lion at a tremendous pace. Urging his horse forward at its best speed, and mailing over a hard, flat ground, he soon found he was being rapidly overhauled. Glancing over his left shoulder, it seemed as if the lion took two strides for the horse's one. It appeared to be all up when the lion was felt to be within three boul4ids of him, but with an effort almost superhuman he managed to wrench the horse aside, and away the lion went flying past him, having, however' nearly unseated him'by gra ing his right shoulder. Mr. Baldwin pulled up as soon at he could, and the lion likewise slackened speed. Jumpingriolf his horse, the huntsman fired, and broke one of the hind egs orthe prey. Though the brave old lion made the ut ost efforts to escape, running hard even on three legs, Mr. Bald- win soon gained on him and slew him outright.—Little Folks Magazine. _

NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORTI- CULTURE, &c.

• At the • recent Stallion Show of the Peterborough Agri- cultural Society, Mr. Jas.Forshaw, of Blyth, Worksop, took the first prize of £7 for the best shire-bred cart stallion, foaled in 1880, with Waxwork Wonder. An apple in perfect preservation, although 96 years old, is in possession of a gentleman in Ulster county, Pennsyl- vania. As it rounded up from the blossom of the parent stem in the early summer of 1787, a bottle was drawn over it and attached to the branch, and after the apple had ripened the stem was severed and the bottle' sealed tightly. It looks as fresh as when first plucked. LUNCHEONS AT FARMING STOCK SALES.—At a meeting of the Gloucestershire Chamber of Agriculture, Mr. Bruton introduced this subject, and proposed—" That in the opinion of this Chamber the present practice of providing indis- criminate luncheons at sales of farming stock is a serious and unnecessary burden on the vendor, and it is recom- mended that a fee of is. be charged for the luncheon, to be -returned to purchasers." Various speakers supported the resolution, and it was carried unanimously. FREAK OF NATURE.—A few days ago, Mr. Blunt, veter- inary surgeon, Lutterworth, was sent for to go to Newham to a cow that was about to calve, when, from observations made on examining the animal, he ordered hepto be killed, and upon being opened a calf with two perfect heads on a a very large neck was found. By the direction of Lord Denbigh, the animal, which was of course dead, was sent to Coventry to be stuffed. The restrictions necessary ort account of the prevalence of foot-and-month disease in some parts of the country are apparently found rather hampering to trade. Two calf dealers named King purchased 43 calves in Wiltshire. Two they sent- off in one direction, and were fined £l6 10s. by the Wallington magistrates ; two went in another direction, and brought in a fine of £9 '4B. from the Henley magis- trates; and probably the calf dealers named King look upon their other 39 calves, if still unsold, as anything but a mine of wealth. HIGHLAND SOCIETY'S DIPLOMA.—The annual examina- tion for the diploma of fellowship of the Highland and Agricultural Society of Scotland has just taken place, with the result of five out of 17 candidates having passed. Two of these five are students of the Royal Agricultural Col- lege at Cirencester, their names being Tiffen and Basu. The latter, who is a native of the East Indies, holds one of the Bengal Scholarships. Only two other students from the Cirencester College were candidates on this occasion, both of whom—Messrs. A CLERGYMAN'S MISADVENTURES IN LIVERPOOL.

The Liverpool police are at present investigating a case of robbery in which a clergyman of the Church of England was the victim. The clergyman in question is a stranger to the city, and, at the time of the robbery, was in Liver- pool on a brief visit to a friend. During his sojournings in the city. he, at a late hour in the evening, or rather an early hour in the morning, whilst labouring, no doubt, under the influence of a powerful drug—probably chloroform—found himself in quarters where clergymen are not usually to be seen at such an hour. Somehow or other he was induced to enter a house in the neighbourhood, and, having been cordially received when inside the bewilderei parson was persuaded to disattire himself, and make himself comfort- able for th,e night. The soporific effects of the drug which we suppose the clerical gentleman was suffering from speedily wore off, however, and on regaining consciousness he found that not only were his gold lever watch and purse missing, but that the greater part of his wearing apparel had mysteriously disappeared. After much search- ing in the dark he succeeded in recovering most of his clothing, but his boots and stockings, like his watch and purse, were nowhere to be found. Thinking it dangerous to .remain longer in such a locality, this light of the Church beat a hasty retreat, leaving boots, stockings, watch, and purse behind him, and eventually made his way to the police station In Dale-street, where to a number of astonished clerks and policemen he related his strange adventures. The name of a friend being given, a messenger was despatched to the friend's house for boots and stockings, and these having been brought to the Detective Office the clergyman, by this time fully alive to his painful position', speedily donned them and without further delay proceeded, a much sadder and poorer man, to his hotel. It is needless to say that the clergyman's watch, which, it is said, was a presentation one, has not yet been discovered, the difficulty of tracing it being very much increased by the fact that the owner when he made his appearance at the Detective Office was in such a condition of mental haziness that he was unable to indicate to the_police the particular part of the city where these misadventures had befallen him.

Mr. Marko, assistant the latter part of their fourth season of being wintered Prosecuting solicitor, appeared in support of the charges, mostly on ensilage, and they are all healthy and ready for and Dr. O'Feeley, instructed by Mr. Quelch, appeared for the butcher, if needed for beef. There is not a Particle of the defence. There were present in court Col. Ford, R.A., exaggeration about these Statements. Col. Majendie, Dr. Dupre, the Prosecutor and Deputy- ' Prosmutor Fiscal of Glasgow, and Dr. Campbell Brown (public analyst of Liverpool). Tbe prisoners bore them- selves quietly, but with an assumption of indifference, smiling at each other frequently. Mr. Marks, in opening the case for the prosecution, said he would not recapitulate the evidence already given, but would state the purport of a mass of evidence obtained since • the prisoners were last before the court. He then detailed a number of circumstances which would be adduced to show the criminal intention of the prisoners and the terribly destructive nature of the explosives. The canisters were closely similar to the infernal machine foundin Glasgow in January last and at the Times office in London-. He would ask the magistrate to commit the prisoners not only on the charge of being in possession of the illegal explosives, but of conspiring together with other persons to 'commit felonies. On the application of Dr. O'Feeley the evidence previ- ously given was read over. Thomas Shannon was the first fresh witness called. He said he was a badge porter, and on the night of the 28th March he was on the Landing Stage when the Cork boat came in, and was employed by Deasey to carry a box to 34, Regent-street. When he got as far as the Waterloo Dock gates he was stopped by the police. Deasey was walking by his side, but did not assist to carry the box. Superintendent George Williams, chief of the detective department, described the searching of the two prisoners, and the examination of the box.. On seeing the contents of the box he sent for Dr. Campbell Brown, the city analyst, and handed them over to him for further examina- 'ion.

Samuel W. Conning, a sergeant of the Royal Irish Con- stabulary, at present stationed in Liverpool, described the arrest of. the prisoner Flannigan at Sutton near St. Helens, the details of which have already appeared. Dr. Campbell Brown stated that he examined the sub- stances found in Deasey's box. There was a packet of chlorate of potash and of sugar, each correctly labelled, and one of red orpiment or realger, which was not labelled. The bottle of oil of vitriol or strong sulphuric acid was not labelled. If the chlorate of potash and the sugar and the red orp:ment were mixed together, and were then touched by the sulphuric acid they would burn violently. The chlorate of potash and sugar mixed, without the realger, would burn violently if touched by the sulphuric acid. The tin can contained about a quarter of a cwt. of wood sawdust, mixed with a little chalk and saturated with nitro-glycerine. The lower part of the canister where the nitro-glycerine had oozed down through the sawdust contained nitro-glycerine in the proportion of 83 per cent., about the middle it was 75 per cent., and at the driest part at the top it was 67 per cent, an average of over 75 per cent. In the top of the canister there was a hole corresponding to a hole cut through the canvas which covered the canister, and in this was a tin cylinder five inches long and 1 inches diameter. A small piece of newspaper was loosely stuffed into the cylinder, and a cork fitting the hale was lying loose in the wooden box. Witness examined one of the three brass taps, and tried to ascertain whether it was an instru- ment known to anyone else, and could not find that it was. He then tried to puzzle out how it could be used with the materials in the box. He mixed chlorate of potash and sugar, and put it in a space between an inner and an outer brass cylinder. Two holes in the inner cylinder were covered by about eleven folds of paper similar to print- ing paper tied on tightly. After placing the mix- ture in the space indicated he screwed the tap into a hole in the canister, and turning it off he poured sulphuric acid into the tube. Then placing the instrument in an upright position, he turned the tap on and retired to some distance to watch the effect. In ten minutes he went back and unscrewed the tap, when he found that the acid had only eaten half way through the rolls of paper. He then cleaned out and recharged the instrument, but put two folds of paper less over the holes. In eighteen minutes after turning the tap it exploded, so that if he had completed the first experiment it would have exploded in twenty-two minutes. By using the tap in the way he had described, it caused violent com- bustion at the will of the operator, according to the manner in which the paper was wrapped round, thus regulating the time.—Cross-examined by Dr. O'Feeley : By an explosion he meant one similar to powdered gunpowder when ignited. He had not tested its explosive property.—Re-examined by Mr. Marks : On the following day, the 29th March, he examined the contents of the bag found upon the prisoner Flannigan, and found that the tin canister contained a mix- ture of chlorate of potash and sugar in explosive propor- tions. The liquid in the bottle was sulphuric acid. William Alexander Brown, Procurator-Fiscal of Glasgow, was next called, and said he remembered receiving, on the 24th January_ last, from the witness Brander (who was examined at the first hearing), a tin box, two pieces of brass tube, and a small paper bag containing a substance like sawdust. The pieces of brass were labelled, and were now produced. They were handed to Colonel Majendie on the same day. Dr. O'Feeley objected to this evidence, but his objection was overruled. Colonel Vivian Daring Majendie, Her Majesty's Chief Inspector of Explosives, was the next witness. He said the explosive described by Dr. Campbell Brown as having been found in the canisters was correctly designated as lignine dynamite, and it was not a legal explosive in this country. Two instances of the illegal use of lignine dynamite had come to his official knowledge in this country. One was on the 21st January last, at Glasgow, and the other was the else of the explosion at the Times office, on the 15th ult. There was only one dynamite factory in effective operation in Great Britain, and that was under Government inspection. No one could legally manufacture, import, or have posses- sion of ligsine dynamite. There was no licensed dynamite factory in Ireland. Dr. Dupre, F,R.S., professor of chemistry, also gave evi- dence as to the character of the explosive. ' Colonel Ford, R.A., one of Her Majesty's inspectors of ex- plosives, deposed to receiving from the witness Lawley, on , the 16th March, the tin box and other articles named. This being the case for the prosecution, the prisoners were then formally committed for trial at the assizes. DESTRUCTION OF THE BIRMINGHAM EXPLOSIVES. On Sunday morning the explosives which were found on Whitehead's premises in Ledeam-street were destroyed at the Sewage Farm, Salthy. Mr. Robert Macready, front Messrs. Noble and Co.'s, Glasgow, arrived in Birmingham late on Saturday night for the purpose of undertaking the danger- ous operation. Soon after nine o'clock Mr. Macready, ac- companied by Dr. Hill, borough analyst; Mr. Ferndale, chief constable; Chief Inspector Black, of the detective de- partment; and a strong force of police went to Virhitehead's premises in Ledsam-street, where Mr. Macready proceeded to turn into dynamite the nitro-glycerine which had been operated upon by Dr. Dupre. He started in the large carboy of 170Ib. of nitro-glycerine, which was so unexpectedly dis- covered on Friday last. It was in a highly dangerous state, not being free from acid, but the operator purified it by add- ing Hanoverian earth and chemicals. When the explosive material had been converted into dynamite, an operation which lasted until about mid-day, it was placed in seven buckets. These were transferred tá the prison van drawn by four horses' ' and escorted by a detachment of police and con- veyed to the Sewage Farm at Saltley, distant from Birming- ham about five miles. Following the van were three cars conveying a large number of constables. When the party arrived at tbe farm the dynamite was removed from the van, carried a good distance from any building, and spread in layers along the ground. It was then a supremely anxious moment, for a fierce sun was beating down upon the field, and Mr. Macreacy gave orders that the baize covering the buckets should not be removed. There was no necessity to tell the few spectators to keep at a respectful distance from the first little layer of deadly material as it was being ignited, and there was a feeling of painful suspense as the match was applied. But it was not of long duration, as all that could be perceived was a faint burst of flame, which increased with great rapidity till it consumed the compound within the space of a few seconds. There was not the slightest report, but even the most unscientific observer could detect the terrible potency of material from the powerful nature of the gases evolved from it. The success of the first experiment gave the few spectators fresh courage, and it was rather amusing to see how they shook off their timidity, and approached a little nearer the scene of the operations. The next experiment was' tried with a larger quantity of the explosive, the specialist striking a vesuvian match and applying it by hand with no more trepidation than if lighting a cigar. A fierce blaze shot out, and the entire mass was quickly enveloped. The peculiar rushing sound emitted by the flames produced a sensation which is not easy to describe, and those who happened to stand to the windward had the pleasure of inhaling some of the powerful fumes. The sun at this period was excessively hot, and the operator for vari- ous reasons decided to proceed more rapidly with his work. He took the entire contents of a bucket weighing at the most moderate computation 301b.' or sufficient, if properly applied, to blow up the largest building in the kingdom, and placed the material in a thin layer in the shape of a cross. - This time Dr. Hill applied the match, and the flames spread with tremendous impetuosity. The rushing sound, more omnious than the most angry thunder, could be heard for a long distance, and the heat was almost unen- durable. Almost before the flames had burnt themselves out, and the terrible material had been reduced to a harmless white ash, the operator had distributed the contents of another bucket in a similar manner. By this time the company had grown so courageous that they stood within a few yards of the dynamite as the match was struck, and the exciting work of destruction was continued. In this way the whole seven buckets were emptied and destroyed, the operations being carried out without the slightest mishap. The buckets were then carefully placed in the prison van, and removed to the Central Police Station. The whole work did not occupy more than half an hour. PLOT TO DESTROY LONDON. The authozities appear to be in possession of the outlines of the plot formed by the conspirators—a plot of consum- mate recklessness and brutality, and aimed, not against per.

annct in anthnritcr nr hnt criminateljr at the general public. It was seemingly pro- posed to place in different parts of London--in obscure lodgings in some places, in coffee-house lodging, in private and public hotels and other places—quantities of nitro- glycerine. There was to be no consideration given to nationality or creed in the matter; but on an appointed day and at a particular hour the machinery was to be set in motion for simultaneous destruction in different parts of the metropolis, similar to the plan attempted, on a lesser scale, at Playhouse-yard and at Westminster on the night of the 15th of March. The chief actors would probably have got safely off; while

if any of the subordinate workers had ',Teen taken their con- fessions would probably have been of no avail. The pot, if it had been successful, would have caused vast loss of life and property. Thirty-five years ago London was agitated by the apprehended Chartist revolution Even then, when the working men of London were led by agitators, and did not possess the political power they now enjoy, they refused to listen to the suggestion to use physical force to obtain the concession of their demands. To a greater extent than ever the working classes of London hold that "force is no remedy," and the detectives feel that they can rely upon the sympathy of the people in the streets even when making an arrest in a crowded placelike the Blackfriars-road at noon on a Sunday.—Times.

MORE ARRESTS. Several additional arrests have been made. An Irishman named John Kirton, who has lived some years in America, was apprehended on Saturday in London, where he had been staying three er four days, and was t-tken before the Bow- street magistrate and remanded, charged with being an accomplice of the other men captured in the metropolis for complicity in the dynamite conspiracy. He is supposed to be the writer of a letter in the possession of the police ad- dressed to "Thomas Gallagher, &q., Charing. Cross Hotel ' —one of the men remanded on Friday, all of whom are now for safe keeping confined in Millbank prison. Another 'arrest is that of Bernard Gallagher, brother to the prisoner above referred to, Dr. Gallagher. He was taken in Glasgow on Saturday, and st Inds remanded on the charge of being concerned in the destruction of a gasholder in that city last January. A young man named William Ausburg, 22, an Irishman, was arrested by the Scotland-yard authori- ties on Sunday morning. On Monday he was charged at Bow-street Police Court with being concerned with the four other prisoners now under remand—Gallagher, Wilson, Norman, and Dalton—in the possession of explosives, with intention to commit a felony. The prisoner seemed perfectly self-possessed, and he was remanded,

REMARKABLE ESCAPE. Some disclosures made on Wednesday in Birmingham show that an extraordinary escape from a disaster of an appalling nature was experienced at New-street Railway Station. The box containing a large quantity of nitro- glycerine, which was conveyed to the station by one of the men arrested in London, wasAaken charge ef by a porter. He placed it on a truck, which, whilst being wheeled along, tilted over the box, and the latter fell with a thud upon the platform. The prisoner who had charge of it appeared to be greatly disconcerted, and enjoined upon the man the necessity of taking great care, as the box contained articles of a very valuable and delicate nature. Had the contents exploded, it is estimated that some hundreds of lives would have been lost. THE BIRMINGHAM PRISONER BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

• The prisoner, A. G. Whitehead, was brought up at a special court at Winson Green Gaol, Birmingham, on Thursday morning, and further remanded for eight days. The proceedings, which were of a very brief duration, took place in the magistrates room in the prison, in order to avoid the excitement and risk of bringing the prisoner to the courthouse in the town. The magistrates assembled at half- past ten o'clock, and were Mr. T. C. S. Kynnersley, stipendary ; Messrs. White (mayor), Jaffrey, and Avery. They were accompanied by Mr. Hebbert, justices' clerk. The only other persons in the room were the chief of police, the chairman of the Watch Committee, Detective Black, Sergeant Price, several prison officials, and the repte- sentatives of the Press. As soon as the court had been constituted, the prisoner was brought in. He wore the prison garb of blue serge, and appeared by no means the worse for incarceration of from anxiety with regard to the result of his case. He is a much younger man than would appear from some of the des- criptions which have been published. His age is said to be between twenty-two and twenty-three, and with this his appearance fully agrees. He is decidedly a g )od-looking young man, short but broad shouldered, and well built, with short wavy dark hair, dark shaven face, and bright eyes of bluish grey. He stood ineide the door of the room when brought in, handling his prison cap, and carefully scruti- nising the magistrates and others into whose presence he had been suddenly ushered. Alfred George Whitehead, is that your name ? said the clerk, to which prisoner answered with a clearly pronounced yes. Chief Constable Ferndale then said :—This prisoner, your worships, has been remanded for a week under the 54th section of the 24th and 25th Victoria, chap. 97, charged with manufacturing a dangerous explosive—to wit, nitro- glycerine, with intent to commit a felony. On Saturday last I had a communication from the solicitors to the Treasury asking for a copy of the depositions taken last week and the police reports. Yesterday I received a further communication requesting that I should bring the prisoner before your worships this morning and ask for a further re- mand for eight days, without offering any further evidence or going more into the case. The Stipendiary (to prisoner).—All I have to ask is whether you have any reason to give why you should not be remanded for another week? The prisoner made some inaudible observation, and in reply to the stipendiary's question said, "I would wish the case to go on." The Stipendiary: But they are not prepared to go on with the case at present.—Prisoner: I have no particular objection. The Stipendiary: You are remanded till to-morrow week. —The Prisoner: To-morrow week? The Stipendiary: Yes. Prisoner was then taken back to his cell, and the pro- ceedings terminated. The arrival and departure of the magistrates' carriages was watched by a considerable crowd outside the building, but there was nothing else for them to see. The prisoner during these brief proceedings appeared by no means nervous, but manifested, rather than otherwise, an unconcerned air. A Central News correspondent was informed that though the prisoner at first disclaimed any religion he has since signified to one of the warders that he is a Roman Catholic, having stated that his parents were of that communion, and that if he was any religion he was the same. He was accordingly asked if he would like to receive the visits of the Roman Catholic chaplain, to which he replied that he would, and the chaplain saw him on Thursday morning. THE LONDON PRISONERS AT BOW-STREET. The hearing of the charge against the six men arrested in London in connection with the Fejiian plot commenced at Bow-street, on Thursday. Elaborate precautions were taken both for the protection of the yan in which the pri- soners were conveyed from Millbank, and for the security of the court. The prisoners were—Norman, Gallagher, Henry Wilson, Henry Dalton, John Ceirtane, and Wm. Ansbrough. Sir James Ingham presided. Three of the accussed had legal assistance. The six prisoners were brought up on remand charged with being concerned together in having possession of ex- plosives with intent to commit a felon Sr. Mr. Poland prosecuted on behalf of the Treasury, and in opening the case he said he should show that some of the prisoners camp from America to Glasgow in February, and ultimately established at Birmingham a manufactory of nitro-glycerine with a man named Whitehead. It would be shown that Gallagher, who was known on some occasions as Fletcher, had visited Whitehead at Birmingham, and that Norman and Wilson at least, among the other prisoners, had done the same. Documents found in Gallagher's pos- session clearly showed that he was entrusted with the management of the affair. Dalton would be shawn to have been in communication with John Devoy and O'Donovan Rossa. I Inspector Mackie and Chief-Inspector Littlechild proved I the arrests of the several prisoners, the discovery of letters and memoranda, and of a book containing a recipe for the preparation of fulminate of mercury. After luncheon, Sutton Edward Crowe, proprietor of Edward's Hotel, was placed in the witness-box. He said Norman came to his hotel on the 22nd March, and took a bedroom on the ground-floor. A gentleman representing himself to be a Mr. Fletcher called on the prisoner. Witness believed the prisoner Gallagher was the person. Laura Caroline de la Motte, of the Beaufort Hotel, kept by her mother.—Remember seeing the prisoner Gallagher on the 4th April. He engaged a room for a medical student who was going to walk the hospitals, and said he would want the rooms for two months. He gave the name of the student as John William Norman, and said he was coming from Birmingham. Norman arrived that night, and the police came the same night and arrested .him. Mrs. de la Motte, mother of the last witness, deposed to the arrival of Norman with a heavy box. Walter Savage, of Blackfriars's-road, a private hotel keeper, said that on Thursday, the 29th March, Augsberg came to his hotel and took a room for four nights. He had no luggage. While staying there, Gallagher called on him two or three times. Augsberg remained at his hotel till his arrest by the police. Rosa Evelyn Pryor, in the employ of the last witness, confirmed his evidence. Callagher (addressing witness) said: When you were at Millbank did you see anyone but us four? Witness : I did not notice any others. After formal evidence in identification of the other pri- soners, a remand was granted till Thursday next.

At Woolwich, on Wednesday, the nitro-glycerine recently seized in London was mixed with other material and burnt. A portion of it exploded with great violence, and several persons standing near narrowly escaped injury. Colonel Majendie, chief inspector of explosives, paid an- other visit to the illicit nitro-glycerine manufactory in Bir- mingham, and made a thorough examination thereof in order to sstisfy himself that there was no danger still lurking about the place. Two policemen have been specially told off to patrol the outside of the Bolton Town Hall by day, and during the night the patrol is doubled. A detective is on duty inside the building. At the gas works, also, special precautions have been adopted. The Glasgow expert who visited the laboratory in Led- sam-street, Birmingham, on Sunday, says the prisoner Whitehead has evidently remived a thorough education in the manufacture of nitro-glycerine, yet, considering the die-

Avaniarres under which he has walled, it 19 a marvel that the place has not been blown U. Dr. Gallagher, one of the prisons, who was arrested at Wilson's lodgings, has made a statement to the effect that he had met Wilson casually in the street, and .had only accompanied him to his lodgings because he had formed his acquaintance in America. Wilson corroborates this state- ment. _ .

A statement made on Saturday to the effect that some Fenian documents had fallen into the hands of the Salford police turns out to be incorrect. A quantity of papera were found in a tin box which was sold at an auction sale of household goods, and were submitted to the police for examination, but they had no reference to the Fenian Brotherhood, and not the slightest importance is attached to them. _ _

The military authorities in charge of the stores and am- munition lodged in the armoury at Chester Castle have deemed it necessary to take stringent precautions against attack. An extra guard has been placed around the Castle, and patrols are maintained night and day not only at the Castle but at the militia barrack and stores on the opposite side of Grosvenor-road. So recently as two years since an attempt was made to blow up the militia barrack. Late on Friday night the civil authorities at Preston were informed that an attempt would probibly soon be made to blow up the depot of the 11th (Preston) Volunteer Rifles, which contains upwards of a thousand stand of arms and a large quantity of ammunition. For several weeks past the public buildings in Preston have been under special police protection, but on receipt of the above-mentioned informa- tion the police guard was strengthened. The discovery of the nitro-glycerine "distillery " in Birmingham was brought about by the astuteness of Detective Sergeant Price, who first had his attention directed to the "oil and paint shop " by a person whose acquaintance he made last winter at the Board School science classes,who, like himself, had a taste for experimental chemistry, and who, having to deal with glycerine, was struck by the large arrivals of that article at Whitehead's place. In consequence of the marked ability and courage dis- played by the police authorities during the recent dynamite seizures, the Home Secretary intends to recommend Mr. Howard Vincent, director of the Criminal Investigation De- partment, Scotland Yard, and Mr. Jenkinson, director of the Irish detective force, for the distinction of K,C.8., and Mr. Williamson and Mr. Mallon (Dublin) to receive companion- ships of the order, the inferior officers being rewarded by money grants of a considerable amount. In accordance with instructions from the War Office, and in response to an urgent request on the part of the Mayor of the town and the Chief of the Police, the Birmingham borough gaol is being guarded by military sentries. The arrival of the soldiers at the gaol on Saturday night gave rise to the most extravagant rumours, and the greatest ex- citement prevailed in the neighbourhood. The gaol is now so well protected that there need be no apprehension of an attempt at rescue. The Governor of the Gaol made a request on Saturday to be supplied with some additional warders, and these were despatched at the earliest oppor- unity.

The police authorities at Liverpool are actively OR the alert, and it is believed that before long some further impor- tant discoveries will be made. Information has been com- municated to them of a treat to blow up the General Post Office in Canning Place. The postal authorities are reticent on the subject, but it appears the police have keceived infor- mation of a letter of a threatening nature baying been sent. As the Postal and Revenue buildings, as well as all other public buildings in Liverpool, are now being carefully watched by the police, it is not thought likely that any such attempt, if seriously contemplated, would have any chance of success.
So far the operations of the dynamite party have not been extended to Manchester, but some information _which ..

reached the police a few days ago has led them to believe that such an extension is contemplated, if not actually decided upon. Toe police were warned that an attempt is to be made to blow up the Town Hall. On more than one occasion threats have been uttered affecting the building, and measures have been taken to ensure its safe. These have now been renewed in the most stringent form. Other buildings in the city are being specially guarded, and it is fully believed that the measures taken by the Chief Con- stable will be sufficient to ensure their safety.

div.head: PRINTER'S DEVIL -I.
div.p: THE PRINTER'S DEVIL -I.
[BY ANGLO-SCOTUS.]

A book has recently been published called "The History and Pedigree of the Devil." As it does not contain anything about that mythical individual. the Printer's Devil, and as "Newtonian " has on several occasions not only implied that I have had some experiences of the vagaries of the chief satellite of King Carelessness, but expressed a wish that I should put them into print, opportrality having occurred for jotting them down, I have much pleasure in sending them to The .Examincr. According to the Talmu- distic calculation, there are said to be 7,405,926 species of devil in the world, exclusive of the Printer's Devil; and a curious instance of the Asiatic estimate of the relative power or strength of the right and left hands is conveyed in the belief that when a person is haunted by Or under the influence of these devils, 10,000 of them take up their posi- tion on his right hand and 1,000 on his left. Shakespeare says r—" Nay, then, let the devil wear black." Black being the prevailing colour of printer's ink may have some- thing Lu do with the presnito the imp* zo often play in typo graph's'. The following are a few instances that have come under my own observation. I hope they will interest the readers of The Examiner in general, and "Mac's merry men " in particular. Some time ago a well-known writer drew attention in the columns of a well-known journal to the fact that in criticising a picture called "The Grey Sisters," the compositor made him describe that work of art as " The Grey Whiskers." About the same time, another art critic, in describing, in a second journal, Sir C. Lindsay's gigantic picture," The Boat of Charon," by the vagaries or careless- ness of the compositor, in substituting an r for an o in the second word of the title was made the victim of a far more stupid and ludicrous blander than that of transforming " sisters" into "whiskers." Possibly the compositor who made the first blunder was aware that the male sex has not stood alone in the history of mankind as the sole possessors of hirsute appendages or facial adornments. The famous female prisoner of Pultow e. had a beard a yard and a half long; the "Great Margaret, Governess of the Nether- lands," had a long black beard; Wolfius also speaks of "a virgin with a long, black beard ;" whi:e in the year 1852 Mdlle. Bois de Cherie gave Londoners and others an oppor- tunity of interviewing a lady with a profuse head of hair, a strong black beard, large whiskers, and thick hair on her arms, neck, and back." But whoever heard of the son of Erebus and Nox,—" the old man with hideous countenance, long white beard, piercing eyes, garments ragged and filthy, and wrinkled forehead,"—being mentioned in the same con- nection with a mischievous or lively childi? Whatever Ckaron may have to do with the conveyance of the souls of grown-up people over the Acheron, it is hard to believe or conceive that the spirits of children will ever have to pass over the waters of any "bitter river" in the custody of ; such a ferryman. lam afraid that compositor had a bad temper and disliked children. In a third journal, the sub- stitution of an r for a c made another art critic descant on

the" bark of a red cow." Perhaps the Caxtonian hailed from Newton-le-Willows, and had heard of the "cow that yielded butter and sweet lard for making cakes." In a fourth newspver a literary critic was made to appear to write poetically about a "brooding mountain tree," the last word being substituted for "bee." Possibly this compositor had been indulging in an overdose of " Ovid's Metamor- phoses" and was thinking of the Thracian women,. those guilty dames who were visited with the vengeance of Lyceus and turned into trees. In the printing office of a fifth journal the influence of the "demon barber" must have been for a time predominant, as the following sentence will show, taken from the first proof of an article on "Lord Derby as a Liberal Statesman: 'The adherence of Lord Derby will be to Mr. Gladstone's Government what marriage with a county heiress is to the career of an eccentric eldest son, a comfortable comb which renders formerly disturbed well- wishers easy in their minds," Sze. The barberic metaphor proved too much for the printer's reader, even ; and thus, while in the process of correction " event " was very pro- perly substituted for "comb," "marriage with a county heiress" was duly chronicled as an event that had gener- ally something to do with the careers of eccentric eldest sons. "Reaping its chief paints" was another " confusion " that suggested the idea that the compositor had never seen anorchard or a field of growing grain • "paints" being sub- stituted for" fruits." I have often wonClered what impression Mr. Sims Reeves formed of printers in general when, some 26 years ago, he read the announcement in the columns of a journal, at that time devoted to music and the drama, that he sung with much artistic feeling and expression 'Come into the garden mud'!" Or what he would have thought or said had he been present in the composing room of the newspaper in question when the compositor was being called over the coals for having set up "mud " for " Maude." The compositor would not admit that the blunder was a stupid one, and told the overseer "that he could see nothing the matter with the sentence." " How can you justify such a remark ? " asked the boss. The reply to this question when it came convulsed the 'ship, and almost settled the boss; it was this :—" There would be mud in a garden on a wet day; wouldn't there ? " That was the only time I over heard the boss swear, or seem in the least perturbed. It is just possible the compositor hailed from the Fens, and had done all his own courting in damp weather. There are only two of us alive now and working together who heard that colloquy, but we often have a laugh over it, and a thought of regret for the other members of the 'ship who have gene over the border and joined the great majority. As Scott says in " Marmion,"— ..When mu lug on companions gone, We doubly feel ourselves alone."

CONVOCATION AND THE AFFIRMATION BILL. - The Lower House of the Convocation of Canterbury on Thurs- day debated the Affirmation Bill. Canon Lowe said that in the interests of religion he could not opdose the bill, and he moved, as an amendment to the proposal requesting the Bishops to oppose the bill, that their Lordships should be requested to watch the progress of the measure, not with the object of rejecting its principles, but to prevent it being enacted with retrospective powers. Canon Vaughan se- conded the amendment, remarking that one thing which made Mr. Bradlaugh's influence dangerous was the leeling which was abroad that he was an oppressed and injured man. Archdeacon Oenison vehemently opposed the amend- ment as dangerous and unsound, and on a division it was rejected. Eleven voted for and sixty-three against it.

THE PINENIX PARK MURDEES. TRIAL OF THE PRISONERS. Tl trlals of the Invincibles, looked forward to with so much interest, cemmenced on Monday, in the Green-street Courthouse, Dublin. Only six of the prisoners were brought down from Kilmainham Prison—Joseph Brady, Timothy Kelly, Thomas Caffry, Patrick Delany (the four who entered the Park en the car driven by Michael Kavanagh). James Fitzharrisi•alias Skin-the-Goat, and Daniel Curley. The five informers—James Carey, Peter Carey, Robert Farrell, Michael Kavanagh, and William Lamie—were also brought down to the Courthouse, their presence being required to give evidence before the Grand Jury. Mr. Justice O'Brien entered the Court at ten minutes past eleven, and took his seat on the bench. When he commenced his charge, the only members of the Bar present besides the Crown counsel, the Attorney-General, M.P., the solicitor-General, Mr. tames Murphy, QC., and Mr. Peter O'Brien, QC., were Mr. Philip Keogh and Mr. J. B. Killen, both of whom had been engaged for one or other of the prisoners in the preliminary investigation at Kilmain- ham. The office of Crown Solicitor was well represented in the 'persons of Mr. Matthew Anderson, Mr. Samuel Lee Anderson, and Mr. George Bolton, the last- mentioned of whom has had the most active charge of the Case throughout. Mr. Mallon, the Superintendent of the Detective Department was present, arranging for the attend- ance of the witnesses before the Grand Jury. The list of the prisoners against whom indictments were to be sept to the Grand Jury showed the number to be eighteen, Peter Carey having been removed from the list and added to the list of informers. His name, however, was not included in the list of witnesses to be before the Grand Jury in any of the cases. James Carey, his brother, is a witness in all the cases before the Grand Jury, with the exception of those of Edward O'Brien, Edward McCaffrey, and Daniel Delany. The informer for examination before the Grand Jury in the cases of Daniel Delany and Edward O'Brien is Robert Far- rell. In McCaffrey's case, Joe Smith, whose exact position as a witness is not defined, is one of the witnesses. There are only four cases—those of Peter Doyle, Thomas Martin, James Mullet, and George Smith—in which the Grand Jury will be asked to act on the sole evidence of James Carey. In all the otter cases they either have examined or will ex- amine independent witnesses. In his charge to the Grand Jury, Mr. Justice O'Brien explained the law relating to murders and mtaspiracies to murder, and pointed out that according to the depositions eleven persons assembled in the Phcenix Park on the evening of the 6th May for the commission of the crime. All these persons, he said, if the Grand Jury thought the evidence to be relied upon, were implicated in the actual murder—all just as much as the persons who in- flicted the fatal wounds or were present aiding or abetting; and moreover the persons who assembled in the Park on the sth May—the previous day—with the same object were in his opinion legally responsible for this particular crime of the 6th May directed against Mr. Burke. The crime was a most enor- mous one, but its enormity ought in no way to influence the Grand Jury to depart from the strictest lines of their ordinary duty; nay the very horror and indignation ex- cited in their minds by the occurrence ought to be an ad- monition to them to keep strictly within the lines of their duty. At the close of the charge the special jury lists were called. There were many cases et default, and a fine of £2O in each instance was imposed, with an intimation that the lists would be called day by day and that fines of £5OO might be levied. In a short time the Grand Jury returned into court with true bills against Joseph Brady for the murder of Lord Frederick Cavendish and Mr. Burke. At the request of the Attorney-General, the prisoner was arraigned on the charge of the wilful murder of Thomas Burke. He pleaded not guilty, but said he was not ready for the trial, having no counsel. His solicitor, Mr. M'Cune, said he had chosen counsel as provided by the Crown, but asked for a postponement for a few days. His Lordship, however, decided that the trial must go on on Tuesday. The Grand Jury again returned into court, and the foreman stated that a true bill had been found against Wm. Moroney ; true bills (two) against Timothy Kelley; true bills (two) against Daniel Curley; true bills against Patrick Delaney; true bills (two) against Joseph Hanlon; true bills (two) against Joseph Mullett; Laurence Hanlon a true bill ; Thos. Caffrey true bills (two');; and Michael Fagan true bills (two). Mr. Justice O'Brien said there were several other bills to be sent before them relating to the same charges, the witnesses in which would take some time to be ex- -ld

signalled with a handkerchief on the appearance fif Mr. Burke, and he said he did this by artier of James Carey. lie said he had no idea in identifying Mr. Burke .that it was for the purpose of murder, and he denied having made the remark about watching the sepretary. Twice afterwards Carey gave him money-13 each time, but he did not know what it was for. A woman who keeps the lodge at the Under Secretary's residence in the Park spoke to inquiries being made there by a man on the morning of the sth May, but she could not identify Brady as the man. She answered his questions, which were very minute, and had reference to Mr. Burke's personal appearance and dress. The eldest son of the in- former Carey, a lad of 15, described visits of several of the conspirators to their house, and stated that while his father was in gaol Brady and Patrick Delaney made a search for parcels in the loft of the house in Cumberland-street. The lad also furnished some corroboration of his father's evidence about the call which Carey Said he made at the Castle on the 6th May to get information about lan Burke's movements.—One or two witnesses were then called to identify Brady as one of the persons seen on the car or in the group in the park, and the case for the prosecution was brought to a close.—Dr. Webb addressed the jury for the defence, and in the course of his speech he asked them to believe that James Carey was endeavouring to save his own life by swearing falsely against Brady.—The defence was an alibi, to snpport which two or three witnesses were produced.—The Court then adjourned.—lt is expected that the verdict will be given this morning.

ELECTION OF GUARDIANS. -- PRESCOT UNION. The task of counting the voting papers in the election of Guardians of Prescot Union was accomplished by Mr. S. H. Hartley, the returning officer, at the Union offices, Whiston, on Thursday. The work was not so arduous as it often has been on similar occasions. Although contests were imminent up to a late period in several townships they were avoided by mutual arrangements and retirements in all but five townships, to wit—Eccleston (rural township), Halewood, Cronton, Huyton-with-Roby, and Much Woolton. The polling has issued in very little change in the personnel ot the Board. In Halewood an attempt to infuse "new blood" was made by putting up Mr. Thomas Woodruffe in opposition to the Rev. T. Chambers, but as will be seen from the polling it was signally unsuccessful. , In like manner an effort was set on foot to restore Mr. Jas. Ranson, an old and respected Guardian, to the position he had occupied respectably for many years as Guardian for the rural portion of Ecclestort ; but the ratepayers showed by their suffrages that they were se satisfied with the manner in which they have been represented during the last twelve months by Mr. Newsome, that they declined by a large majority to disturb him in a seat which he has un- remittingly endeavoured to make a useful one. The death:of Mr. G. J. Paris rendered the election of a new representative of Huyton-with-Roby essential. Four candi- dates took the field, with the result that the retiring member Mr. Dobell was re-elected, and Mr. William Gore Ashton, who was returned at the head of the poll, was chosen as his colleague. In Much Weolton the election re- sulein the substitution of a new member for Mr. Edwin Birch. In Cronton there has been no change. The follow- ing is a list of the Guardians returned, with the numbers ; polled where there were contests :—Bold (1) Timothy ; Eatock ; Cronton (1) Walter Bridge Longton, 72; John I Cook, 24; Ditton (1) Willoughby Gilbody ; Eccleston (Urban) (2) J. There were a few gentlemen present 'at the declaration of the poll, and Mr. NEWSOME moved a vote of thanks to the returning officer (Mr. Hartley) and the officers • who had assisted him in the election, for their impartial and gentlemanly conduct.—Mr. Everrs seconded the motion, which was agreed to, and put to the meeting by Mr. HALL, who expressed his confidence that Mr. Hartley had done all he could have done for the benefit of both candidates and ratepayers, and had conducted the election in a manner eminently satisfactory to all concerned. Referring to the change which the election being for three years involved, he trusted that they would have few difficul- ties and that things would go on to the satisfaction of the ratepayers.—Mr. HARTLEY, in returning thanks, acknow- ledged in warm terms the great assistance he had received from the assistant overseers and relieving officers, and from Mr. Chorley and Mr. Davies. He expressed a hope that the new board would work harmoniously with the rate- payers and officials, and that the officers would feel they were working for good masters and the masters feel that they had good servants.—Afterwards, Mr. NEWSOME, in the name of Mr. Hall, invited the assistant overseers and the other officers who had been engaged in the election to a knife and fork tea at the " Dragon." The invitation was accepted with thanks by Mr. DUNN on behalf of the officials assembled.

A" classical student" says, "You ask, 'lf Atlas supported the world, what supported Atlas?' The question, dear sir, has often been asked, but never, so far as we are aware, satisfactorily answered. We have always been of the opinion that Atlas must have married a rich wife, and got his support from her father." A crusty old curmudgeon, who was laughing over some- thing in his newspaper, being reproached by his wife for not reading it aloud so that she could share in the enjoyment, (testily said, "0, fudge, my dear! a thing that's funny enough to make only one laugh would be dreadfully stupid if divided between two."
