HOUSE OF LORDS.-MONDAY.

The Earl of Lytton called attention to the recent aclion of the Government in India, with special re- feronce of its effect upon the status of the native communi- ties and upin their relation to the British power. The Ex- plosives Bill was brought up from the Commons and passed.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MormAv. THE IRISH Mems.—Mr. Few= informed Mr. Gibson that the contract with the London and North Western Rail- way Company was to carry the Irish mails in ten and a half hours on the land and sea service combined. REFORMS IN ARMENIA.—In reply to Mr. Bryce, Lord E. FITZMAURICE stated that Her Majesty's representative at Constantinople had received full insttuctions with reference to the execution to the reforms in Armenia stipulated for in the Treaty of Berlin. No papers could be presented till the Government received a further report on the subject. MADAGASCAR.—In reply to Mr. Cropper. the noble Lord stated that, with a vie.w to the protection of British resi- dents in Madagascar, it was proposed to appoint immedi- ately another Vice-Consul, who would reside in the capital of the island, the present one being stationed on the coast. THE EXPLOSIVES BILL.—The orders of the day were postponed on the motion of Mr. GLADSTONE, and Sir. W. HARCOURT proceeded to introduce the Explosives Bill. The right hon. gentleman remarked that the Government had to deal with an organised conspiracy, not of men like the mere criminal of.the lower orders, but men in the higher walks of life, banded together against all the interests which keep society alive, men who like pirates were the enemies of the human race, and who ought to be treated as men who had no nationality. This new danger must be dealt with by new remedies, in a cool and resolute spirit. Having paid a tri- bute to the splendid services which the police had rendered during the past week—services which were equal to any for ffhich distinguished generals and victorious armies had re- ceived the thanks of Parliament--Sir W. HARCOURT proceeded to refer to the present condition of the law in relation to explosives, which he thought required immediate revision' and then explained the legislation he proposed to adopt. The right hon. gentleman laid special stress upon the fact that it is not only the man who makes nitro- glycerine that is dealt with in the bill, but every man, whether be is a British subject or not, who supplies money or who solicits or in any way procures, counsels, aids, abets, or who is accessory, shall be treated himself as if he were a principal, and suffer exactly the same punishment. It had been suggested that the bill should be temporary, but he thought there was nothing in it that ought not to be per- manent.—Sir R. CROSS agreed with the Home Secretary that the police deserved the thanks of the country quite as much as our soldiers and sailors who had gone through a campaign. He stated that those with whom he acted were quite willing, seeing the emergency which had arisen, to grant the powers asked for. When the Government came forward on au emergency the House ought to rise to the occasion. Leave was given to bring in the bill, which was at once read a first and second time. The House went into Committee.—Upon an alteration being suggested in one of the clauses, Sir R. CROSS recommended that the bill should be allowed to pass as it stood on the responsibility of the Government. The bill passed through Committee, and was read a third time amid chee.s. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAV.

The House met at noon, when the Royal Assent was given by commission to the Explosive Snbstances Bill, the Con- solidated Fund (No. 2) Bill, and the National Gallery (Loan) Bill. The ceremony occupied only a few minutes, and the sitting was immediately afterwards suspended.—At the evening sitting the LOBD CHANCELLOR moved the se- cond reading of the Representative Peers (Scotland) Bill, and an hour or two was devoted by their Lordships to the considerations of the fortunes of the Scottish nobility. The bill was read a second time, and the Earl of Galloway's Representative Peers (Scotland) Election Procedure Bill was rejected upon a division by 31 to 21. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. THE MARQUIS OF RIPON.—The report that the Marquis of Ripon would resign the Vice-royalty of India at the end of the present year was mentioned by Mr. A. BARTLETT, and in reply Mr. GLADVTONE stated that .he had not heard any- thing on the subject from Lord Ripon, nor did the Secretary of India know anything about it. COURTS Orrr.—Sir H. VIVIAN introduced the subject of "counts out," and suggested a remedy for the inconvenience and loss of time attending them. The hon. member for Glamorganshire moved that when it was found that 40 mem- bers were not present the question under discussion should be treated as a dropped order, and the House should proceed to the consideration of the next order of the day.—The mo- tion was opposed by Sir J. M'KENNA, who thought there never had been a more audacious proposition introduced in the House, for if it had existed some time ago it would have prevented Mr. Cobden and Mr. Villiers from bringing forward the question of the Corn Laws for years. Under such a regulation any Government could produce a count out for any motion not palatable to them.—Mr. B. HOPE was of opinion that the proposal would reduce the business of the House to a kind of intellectual leap-frog; and Mr. CowEN opposed it on the ground that it would simply have the effect of handing over to the Government the privileges of private members.—The PRIME MINISTER held that counting out did not bring about much substantial interference with business. It afforded oppor- tunities of relief at periods of heavy pressure upon body and mind, and it exerted a good deal of rough and summary justice upon motions of a class sometimes not well entitled to the attention of the House. He thought it would be well to give some further time to see the effect of the working of the new rules.—The motion *was then withdrawn. ham DISTRESS.—Mr. O'CONNOR POWER called attention to the subject of Irish distress, and moved that it could be most safely and efficaciously relieved by a judicious system of migration and optional emigration, together with a con- solidation of the holdings from which tenants are removed; that in the present condition of Ireland such a scheme can be successfully carried out only by a Government Commis- sion with certain statutory powers, including those of pur- chase and sale; and that the subject demanded the serious attention of the Government with a view to early legisla- tion.—The motion was seconded by Sir B. LEIGHTON.—An amendment was moved by Lord LYMINGTON to eliminate the iwords referring to migration and optional emigration, leav- ring the word emigration withont qualification. It was also proposed to omit that portion of the motion referring to pur- chase and sale. The debate was continued by several Irish members.—Mr. TREVELYAN declared that the scheme of the member for Mayo county was impracticable, as the expense would be ruinous, and there was not sufficient suitable land available for it. The House divided, with the following result :—For the amendment 99. against 33, majority 66.—Mr. GLADSTONE , said the Government proposed to negative the motion, as in 'its present form it gave a sense to emigration which they rlid not intend to convey.—Mr. O'CONNOR POWER stated that after the recent division he did not wish to press his motion.—The original motion was then negatived without a division.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-WEDNESDAY.

ELEUTIVE COUNCILS (IRELAND) BILL. Mr. BARRY moved tbe second reading of the Elective Councils (Ireland) Bill. The Bill was similar to one proposed by Mr. Butt in 1875. That Bill was supported by some members of the present Government. The present Bill proposed to trans- fer the control of the finances of the eounties from self) elected bodies to popularly elected and representative bodies.—After some discussion. Mr. TEnvErsaN opposed the second reading of the Bill. The Government could not deal with the subject this year, as they had too much in hand without it. If it were not withdrawn the ' Government would have to vote against it, although they did not deny the need for a reform of the present system.—Mr. PLUNKET expressed satisfaction at the decision of the Government, and went on to show that the Bill would put the expenditure of a million and a half of money in the hands of a wild and irresponsible body.— Mr. PARNELL said Mr. Trevelyan had. shown his ability to make a speech to order, and charged him with having sup- ported a similar Bill when in opposition. The Bill had no radical defects unless Liberal principles were radical defects. He looked to the reformed Parliament to settle this great question on lasting lines.—The House divided, when there voted for the second reading, 58; against, 231.—The House adjourned at five minutes to six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIMRSDAY. ' Lord Alcester took the oath and his seat on his elevation to thipeerage.—The Duke of SOMERSET called attention to the papers presented in reference to the alleged cruelty of agents of the Church Missionary Society towards saves, and the Archbishop of Canterbury was amongst those who took part in the debate which followed. —Viscount Smmotrrii moved for the appointment of a Select Committee to inquire as to the adequacy of the present naval forces of the country to meet the increasing demands made on their services, and such further demands as may hereafter arise in consequence of the augmentation of foreign navies.—Lord,Nowrnmoos argued that the navy is in a perfectly satisfactory condition, and the motion was withdrawn. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THIIRSDAY. SUFFERING IN THE WEST IliennuorDs.— In answer to Mr. Buchanan the LORD ADVOCATE stated that official reports disclosed a great amount of suffering among the population in the West Highlands. In most places the destitution did not amount to actual want of food, and there was not much unusual pressure on the parochial rates, but the people had no means of providing themselves with seed potatoes or corn, so that there would be a prospect of a famine next year if relief were not provided. Tux AFFIRMATION BILL: MR. BRADLAUGH.—In answer to Mr. M•Lagan, the ATTORNEY-GENERAL stated that the Government proposed to amend the Affirmation Bill o as to make it applicable to members elected after the passing of the bill.—Replying to Mr. Labouchere,Sir W. HARCOURT stated that he had received a letter from the Lord Chancel- lor respecting the presence of Lord Denman in the House of Lords when Mr. Bradlaugh's appeal was heard.—The LORD CHANCELLOR stated that it was competent for Lord Denman to attend the hearing of the case. If it had not been known that any opinion expressed by that Peer would not affect the result, a re- monstrance would no doubt have been made, as in the case of Mr. O'Connell.—Mr. GLAD STONE assured Sir S. Northcote that, in the event of Mr. Bradlaugh doing that which the Courts had deeldfd to be an illegal act, the Attorney-General would institute proceedings against him now that it was decided that a common informer could not do so.—ln reply to Sir 11. ala- well, Mr. GLAntrrown stated that it was not the intention of the Government to proceed against Mr. Bradlaugh for vet-
ng in the House without having taken the oath ;equired by law. _ _ _

THE BECHUANA CHIEFS. - Mr. GLADSTONE stated that the visit of Dr. Jorissen to this country was of an unofficial character, but he had informed Lord Derby that the Bechuana chiefs had made peace among themselves, and

that quiet had been restored. THE EGYPTIAN HEROES.—The PRIME MINISTER inti- mated that on Monday the House would be asked to take into consideration a message from the Crown in regard to the intention of the Government to propose a grant of certain annuities to Lord Wolseley and Lord Alcester for their services in Egypt.—Mr. LABorcuERE gave notice that he should oppose the vote on the second reading, and Sir G. CAMPBELL said be should support the vote to Lord Wolseley, but oppose that to Lord Alcester. THE CRIMINAL CODE BILL.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL moved the second reading of the Criminal Code (Indictable Offences) Procedure Bill.—Mr. MORGAN LLOYD moved an amendment which declared that no Bill would be satisfac- tory which in a trial for a criminal offence directly or indi- rectly compels the accused person or his wife or her husband to submit to cross-examination. This, however, was not seconded.—Several other amendments were proposed and. debated at considerable length by the lawyers in the presence of less than a score members.—The Bill was read a second time.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

The louse of a sheriff's bailiff at Tralee has been partially blown up with dynamite. A scaffold, on which several men were employed at the erection of a new house in Westport, Ireland, broke down on Wednesday. Several persons were injured—two, it is feared, fatally. From county Waterford comes a report of the house of a farmer who had rendered himself obnoxious to Nationalists having been maliciously set on fire, two cows and some poultry being burned to death. A. meeting of the National Land League was held in Dub- lin on Wednesday, when the receipt of £5,000 from Austra- lia was acknowledged. A letter was read, stating that the Placenix Park murder trial was doing the league much term in Australia, and interfered with the success of Mr. Red- mond's mission there. Writing to a Glasgow correspondent, Mr. Michael Davitt says that of all the insane projects ever condemned by common sense as certain to defeat a just, moral cause, the dynamite policy is the most idiotic and criminal. He pre- fers, if necessary, twenty years of slow work which will tell bit by bit for Ireland to the indulgence in the feeling that "revenge upon a tyrant is sweetest of all." The Recorder of Cork, in opening the Criminal Sessions, on Tuesday, commented at length on the provisions of the Explosives Act, and said the steps taken by the Govern- ment would make nitro-glycerine a hundred times more dangerous to the villains who used it illegally than innocent people whose destruction was intended. He deplored the state of affairs being disclos.-d in Cork in view of the National Industrial Exhibition about being held.

Stephens, the ex-Fenian bead centre, who has been in- terviewed in Paris, has declared that Mr. Parnell is on the "wrong track," and -he is ardently hoping and patiently waiting for the time when the Home Rule and Revolutionary party will form one com- pact mass with the whole of Ireland and the entiro population abroad to support it. He contends that every oppressed nation has a right to revolt, but he denies that any party can under any circumstances be excused for hav- ing recourse to assassination as a means to attain their ends; and he repudiates the use of the assassin's knife or of dynamite. COMPENSATION TINDER THE CRIMES ACT.—Tuesday night's Dublin Gazette contains a number of warrants to charge various districts in Ireland with payment of com- pensation under the Prevention of Crimes Act. £4OO has been awarded to Margaret Linnane, whose father-iklaw was murdered near Breath; £3OO to the wife of Patrick Halleran, who was fired at and wounded near Ballyhoo ; £4OO to the wife of John Doolagby, murdered near Knocka- man ; £4OO to the wife of Michael Conway, murdered near Kilmore ; £5OO to the wife of Michael Moroney, murdered near Leighort. All these cases were in the County" Clare. Smaller sums are awarded for injuries in the counties Cork and Clare.

SUPPOSED MURDER NEAR CLAREMORRIS,—A Claremorris correspondent telegraphs that a tenant farmer Prendergast, who was attacked near that town on Monday morning, died on Tuesday from the effects of a wound on the head. His assailants were two brothers named Coleman. The deceased, John Prendergast, left his house about 6-30 on Monday morning to fetch water from a well close to his farm. On the way he had to pass through a field rented by the father of the two young men now in custody. On his way back with the water, one of the Colemans stopped shim and asked him what right he had there. An altercation followed, and Preadergast drew a knife. The two Colemans then closed with him, knocked him down, and took the knife away. It is uncertain how the fatal wound on his head was inflicted.

LANCASHIRE FOOTBOLL ASSOCIATION CHALLENGE CUP.— The protest of Darwen against Beverley playing for the Black- burn Rovers in the final tie of the Lancashire cup competition was desided at an adjourned meeting of the ass, elation cam- mittee at Blackburn on Monday night. The result of a long discussion was in favour of the Rovers. who will consequently again hold the trophy. HATDOCK TEMPERANCE V. Every human soul is a battle ground where the: higher principles war with the baser passions. The current coin of life is plain, sound sense. We drive a more substantial trade with that than with aught else. No man can live wholly by the light of his own experi- ence, or be guided solely by his personal knowledge, but must, in many things, be dependent upon the testimony, and submit to the guidance of others. "And how does Oharlie like going to school ?" kindly in- quired the clergyman of a six-year-old. "I like going well enough, sir; but I don't like staying after I get there," was the ingenuous reply. Being about to depart, a gentleman who had been on a visit to some friends presented a junior member of the family with half a crown in the presence of his mother. "Please, is it a good one?" asked the little fellow. "Of course, it is!" replied the gentleman, surprised; "why do you ask?" "Because I'd rather have a bad one, and then they'll let me keep it. If I get any good money it goes into the bank, and I never get it again." A-NECDOTE OF CHRISTOPHER NORTll.—When Mr. Aytonn was wooing Miss Wilson, daughter of "Christopher North," he obtained the lady's consent conditionally on that of her father's being gained. This Mr. Aytoun was much too shy to ask, and he prevailed upon the young lady to ask for it herself. "'We must deal tenderly with his feelings," said hearty old Christopher. "I'll write my reply on a slip of paper and pin it to your back." "Papa's answer is on the back of my dress," said Miss Jane, as she entered the draw- ing-roora. Turning her round, the delighted suitor read the following words :—" With the author's compliments." —London Society. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, APRIL 14, 1883,

In both Houses of Parliament, on Monday, ttllB,l,lal alacrity was shown in the passage of Explosives Bill. The measure was only troduced in the Lower Chamber in the rternoon, but in less than an hour and a :,alf it had been duly considered, read a first, tDood, and third time, and sent up to tte Peers, by whom it was also quickly risPosed of. The measure would have beceived the Royal Assent the same evening, alit for the fact that the MARQUIS of SALIS- tielt"V Went out of his way to take up time un- cessa.rily by very unjustly charging the Go- c'e,rotnent with discourtesy to the hereditary :tatnber in introducing the Bill without ti(ll,t!ce• The noble MARQUIS also alleged the Ministry had resorted to what he Ced a manoeuvre, though in what the 03uvre consisted is not quite apparent, • would puzzle his lordship to point it f Of course there is no gainsaying the ttt that a very great deal of haste had been in not only framing, but in introducing Passing the Bill, a haste which is to be na-Precated except under the most extraordi- rY circumstances ; but we think it will be ken etikst -erallY admitted that in this case the cir- ances amply jutified the extreme course sitpte,h the Government adopted. It is for'etY no ordinary circumstance to be in- Cd that there is abroad a plot of "con- denlolate recklessness and brutality" to th,s,tr°Y a large portion, if not the whole, of hletropolis ; and that being the case, it is beePsarY, surely, that the Executive should de;irined with sufficient power to effectually suelL with the cowards who are the authors of bae,;..all atrocious conspiracy. The Govern- en— at the present time are confronted with atiesPiracy so grave, so threatening to life ProPerty, and so far-reaching in its ramifi- tation of s that delay in making the lair capable ithe°Ping with it would have been suicidal rc.,.eY are, moreover, called upon to deal in a t`o4olute manner with a new species of clime, nhilfined until recently to the scum of society I:the Continent, but unhappily it has spread has been adopted by a better educated tels of people in these islands. Fenianism LlPses the Socialism and Nihilism of tiern Countries. These two last-men- ',7sl disturbing elements aim, as a rule, viho`lie overthrow of persons in authority itna :refuse to redress grievances—real or tes,,atnary ; but here Fenianism is no thretor of persons, the friends and foes of aridec°,nspirators, the rich and poor, the peer alik„'T Peasant, and the property of all are tion-Piaeed in imminent danger of annihila- Nket ,We hope, however, that the law just torlane.Q Will be sufficiently strong to crush this there in its embryo stage. The fact that Ito carnips no scarcity of money with which •orie on the dynamite war, that manufac- (l, isensy" the dangerous compound have been • b red at Birmingham and Cork, and that • eing indiscriminately carried about in liertii.alld boxes and deposited in public and siespilhlic places for an unlawful purpose is tliorelei,it to give rise to serious alarm, all the uistensifit 1 when we know that the esPrient for such offences previous to °,ffetie4aY was altogether inadequate to the hlckte. Itwas scarcely the thing, as the HOME 7111/1,141c1' said on Monday, that the man Zlitt 0„--4E-A-D—n0w in custody at Birmingham, Natitif' whose premises the nitro-glycerine 6refitisecs iaetkcirY was discovered— could not be hav °lb uY the authority a license to have , e dynamite, that is to say if he could 4'`orld it out of prison and demanded it; ;ru tI equally unsatisfactory that a per- terlt P,Dssession of dynamite with a felonious 'eary .suould be able to escape with only two thaelse ItnPrisonment. This is no longer the ' ft heti sonspirators had better remember theireetorth they will be severely punished 6criminal designs and acts. The bill Crt ex new become law does not deal I).Psives which result in the loss of ita roahl'e. for the very sufficient reason that he Lc'duces an explosion by which life th`q for guilty of murder, and is dealt the eurder under the common law of tie Point The bill takes up the question at t, . which is short of murder, and by :Leans Jo it is provided that if a person by illalicio,;l_,explosive substances unlawfully and t7Y causes an explosion of a nature in,e,?ldanger human life, or to cause ct ,"e111; inittrY to property—and it would be 't ‘eulate,deed to Produce an explosion not to cause injury to life and pro-

pErty—the punishment shall be penal servi- tudt for life, whether injury to person or property has actually been caused or not. Anuther clause deals with a case where there has not been an explosion, but where there has been intent and an attempt to cause an ; explosion; and this clause is so framed that ; whether a person conspires within or (being a subject of Her MAJESTY) WithOUl Her MA- JESTY'S dominions to cause an explosion, or ' makes or has in his possession or under his control any explosive substance with intent by means thereof to endanger life, he shall be punished with 2o years penal servitude. The object of this clause is of course to punish English conspirators in France, America or any other foreign country when they return to England, if ever they should do so. If any ' subject of Her MAJEsTY, -then, takes part in the approaching dynamite convention in America, and subsequently returns to this country he will be liable to punishment on conviction. The next important provision in the bill is that which relates to a person who makes or simply has in his possession or un- der his control any explosive substance under such circums ances as to give rise to a reason- able suspicion that it is not so made pos- sessed, or controlled for an unlawful object, and the punishment for this is 14 years penal servitude. The onus of proof, be it observed, that it is used for a lawful purpose will rest upon the person possessing it,after the reason- able suspicion has been raised by the police; and we may safely assume that any honest person will be able and anxious to give an account of how he became possessed of ex- plosive materials and for what purpose he uses them. Such, in brief, are the chief clauses of the measure, but it contains others of minor importance which will, we should think, ba of immense assistance to the police in detecting those who unlawfully traffic in explosive materials, as for instance in the power it confers on magistrates, to hold in- quiries ; at the same time the innocent will be sufficiently protected by the Act, one great safeguard being that no prosecution can be instituted except by consent of the ATTORNEY- GENERAL. It is a matter for regret that it should be necessary to pass a bill of so strin- gent a character, and it is, too, rather re- markable that the law was so inadequate to meet an emergency of the nature which .has arisen ; but as an Irish judge remarked on Tu sday nitro-glycerine should be a hundred times more dangerous to the villians who use it illegally than to the innocent people whose destruction is contemplated, and this we hope will be the outcome of the new bill.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST IMPROVEMENT CLASS.-Mr. Stringfellow presided over the weekly meeting on Tuesday evening, when a paper was read by Mr. Palmn on the subject 'Does the Salvation Army supply a public need?" Mr. Palin took the affirmative, and a good discussion ensued.

HALTON PARISH CHURCH SI-CK CLUB.—The balance sheet of this club shows that there is a balance of 160 to the credit of the society, notwithstanding the increased ex- penditure owing to the fever which was prevalent in the neighbourhood in the autumn. Mr. Jeacock and Mr. A. Povev are the trustees for the ensuing year. RESULT OF LEATHER'S LIKING FOR Luauou.—At Run- corn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Peter Leather, whose face was well known to the magistrates, was summoned on a charge of being drunk andlrefusing to quit the)Three Crowns beerhouse. On the 6th inst. Leather entered the beerhouse in a state of intoxication and called for a glass of beer, but the landlady noticing his condition, declined to comply with his request. He thereupon created such a disturbance that the assistance of a policeman was obtained. As there was a "a black list" against the defendant, who had pre- viously been fined 40s. and costs for a like offence, he was mulcted in a similar penalty, with the alternative of going to gaol for a month. DEATH OF Mn. JOHN WRIGHT, OF HA.LTON.—The se- vere weather of March has carried off another familiar figure in the person of Mr. John Wright, of Halton. The deceased gentleman was well known and highly respected in Halton and neighbourhood. He was the eldest son of the late Mr. Peter Wright, of Alvanley Hall,and came to reside at Halton nearly 50 years ago, settling down as a farmer at Highfield House. Here he led an active life for upwards of 35 years, when, owing to ill-health, he was compelled to give up busi- ness pursuits and seek repose and retirement. Before church rates were abolished and the Halton farms contributed to the Parish Church rate of Runcorn, Mr. Wright was co- churchwarden with the late Mr Rigby, of Runcorn, and in his own parish took a deep interest in all public matters. He served the township as a Guardian for about 12 pears, and WAS most diligent and painstaking in the performance of his difficult duties. Before the present church at Halton was built, Mr. Wright was chapel-warden of the Halton Chapelry, and it was he who seconded the proposition that the old bhapel should be removed to make way for a new and more handsome building. He acted as overseer of the poor, and had, in fact, filled every office in the township, and by his neighbourly kindness, and his just and honourable conduct, he was rempt..cted alike by rich and poor. The deceased gentleman was 79 years of age, and was interred at Al vanley Church on Thursday.

ALLEGED MILK ADULTERATION AT RUNCORN.--At Run- corn Petty Sessions, on Monday. James Sayle, milkseller, Portland-street, and Catherine Murphy, carrying on the same trade in Mersey-street, were each charged wtth selling adulterated milk.—P.C. Bossoms stated that on the sth of March he purchased a pint of milk from each of the de- fendants and informed them that the milk was intended for analyses.—Superintendent Williamson said the result of the two analyses was as follows :—" This milk, judged by a yer poor cow, contains two per cent of water, bat if judged by a sample of milk which Superintendent Williamson obtained from the farmer this milk will then contain ten per cent of water. No change has occurred in the article, therefore, that would interfere with the analysis." Mr. Williamson observed that he had caused the process of milking to be watched and a sample then taken, and the result of the analysis was a very good m4k.—Mr. Lake, who appeared for the defendants, said Mrs. Cook, from whose farm the milk came, would prove that out of 20 cows kept by her, 15 were in calf, and by being milked much longer than they ought to have been, the milk was of a wretched character. Mrs. Cook had honestly come forward to admit that the milk was below the standard it ought to be, and the fact that it was so was borne out by the result of the two analyses which were precisely similar. He contended that if dilution had taken place the results would not have been similar.,-Mrs. Cook, of Halton Gate Farm, corroborated the advocate's statement.—The Beach said the defendants should have the benefit of the doubt there was in the case, and the case was dismissed. •

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 14, 1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 14, 1883.

ASSISTANT-OVERSEER FOR HALTON. On Monday, at Runcern Petty Sessions, Albert Woodier was appointed the assistant-overseer for Halton at a salary of £45 per annum. SERMONS AT BETHESDA CILA.PEL, RUNCORN. The Rev. J. T. Maxwell, of Over, on Sunday preached two sermons in the above place of worship. Collections were made at each service in aid of the Manse fund. NEW POOR RATE FOR RUNCORN.—Captain C. W. Haele- hurst and Mr. John Brundrit on Thursday sanctioned the laying of a poor rate for the current half-year at Pd in the pound. Mr. W. Sutton, who made the application, said it was calculated to realise £1,865 7s. The Hon. Alan de Tatton Egerton, the recently-elected member for Mid-Cheshire, was entertained to luncheon by his election committee on Wednesday afternoon, at Maccles- field. Mr. W. C. Brooks, M.P., Mr. Heath, ex-M.P. for Stoke, and Mr. Egerton Percy Milford spoke, condemning the policy of the Government, and urging Conservatives to be ready for emergencies. COST OF PAUPERISM IN RUNCORN UNION. It appears from a return which has just been issued by order of the House of Commons giving the cost of in-maintenance and out-relief in each Union in England and Wales for the last half of the parochial year, 1832, that the in-maintenance in the Runcorn Union during that period cost £7Ol, and the out-relief £1,750, £52 of which was given in kind. WIDNES ;.!..CHOOL BOARD AT WORE—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Mr. G. H. Danby, clerk to the School Board, prosecuted the following_ persons for breaches of the Education Act :—Henry Shepherd, Henry Amees, James Carr, Michael Daley, Thomas Carr, James Hopkins, Patrick Farrell, John Keenaghan, Patrick Murray, Timothy Kinsella, Thomas Toole, and Adam Green. Thu usual fine of 53. was imPosedin each case. FURIOUS DRIVING AT WIDNES.—On Wednesday, at the Widnes Petty Sessions, Bartley Purcell, a young man, was chawed with furiously driving along the street.—P.S. McGregor said at half-past twelve o'clock, on Tuasday, the 3:d instant, he saw the defendant driving a horse and cart along Lugsdale-road. He was standing in the cart, and floggiug the horse with the reins, making it travel at a speed that was dangerous, as there was a large number of people in the street.—A fine of 53 and costs was imposed. WATERING Rust AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Ses- sions, on Monday, Robert Dyer, of the Blue Ball public. hours, Fryer-street, was summoned for unlawfully selling a pint of adulterated rum to P.C. Bossons on the 3rd March. —Superintendent Williamson said the analysis showed that there was 45 per cent. of water in the rum, which was 20 per cent. more than was allowed by Act of Parliament.— The defendant set up the pretext that his wife sold the rum to the constable froth i a jar which contained the adulterated spirit. It was not the article which be sold, and was a mis- take on his wife's part.—He WAS fined Ll and costs. RuNCORN BURIAL BOARD ACCOUNTS.—On Thursday evening, a meeting of ratepayers was held in Bethesda school to receive the report of the auditors of the Burial Board accounts. Mr. J. J. Speakman presided, and there were present Messrs. W. Handley, J. R. Frith, B. Bisbrown. Thomas Riley, W. F. Salkeld (-secretary), and W. Sutton (assistant overseer). The balance sheet presented was adopted on the motion of Mr. Frith, seconded by Mr. W. Handley. It showed that the Board had a balance of £219 us 21 in the bank. It was decided that the accounts should be published in the newspapers, and the balance sheet will be found in our advertising columns. RUNCORN AMATEUR BICYCLE CLUB —The annual general meethig of this club was held on Saturday evening, under the presidency of Mr. F. A. Smith. Mr. Thomas Norman was unanimously re-elected the president of the club, and Mr. F. A. Smith' was appointed secretary in succession to Mr. J: Thiamine, who was thanked for his past services. The following runs were 'arranged :—To-day, Froisharn ; April 21, Daresbury ; April 28, Northwich ; May 5, Grappenhall ; May 12, race; May 19, 1100 Green; May 26, Delameri. In- stead of the usual championship race, it was decided that a handicap be run on May 12th on the Aston course thelimit not to exceed four minutes. The statement course, showed the club had a balance in band of £7 101 11d. RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB.--The Runcorn Football Club may point to the record of the past season's work with par- donable pride. They have played about 25 matches, and have had opposed to them some very strong teams, but in all their contests they have never been:declared beaten, and their card does not show one lost match. The club is yet in its youth, but the members have proved that they are not lacking in strength and courage. Crewe, Northwich, \War- rington, Birkenhead, and Edge Hill have all in their turn been defeated, and the successful club next year will set their caps against clubs of higher fame than even these we have named. Financially the club has also been very suc- cessful, and several local charities have been the recipients of large sums of money. On Saturday next a team will op- pose the Warrington Club, and the proceeds will be given to the Aged People's Treat fund. On the following Saturday a match will be played at Warrington on behalf of the In- firmary.

...... . WIDNES CRICKET CLUE.—This club, of which Mr. F. H. Gossage is president, will commence the cricket season to- day (Saturday), when the Ist eleven plays " Pilkington's Team "at Widnes. The other fixtures are :—April 21, Egremont, at Seacombe; April 28, St. Helens and ground, at Widnes; May 5, St. Helens Recreation and ground, at Widnes: May 12, Latchford, at Widnes; May 19, Chester College, at Widnes; May 26, Birkenhead Victoria, at Widnes; June 2, Warrington, at Warrington; June 9, New- sham, at Liverpool; June 16, Bootle and ground, at Bootle; June 21, Chester College, at Chester; June 23, Birkenhead Victoria, at Birkenhead; June 30, Bootle and ground, at Widr.es ; July 7, Newsham, at Widnes; July 14, Frodsham, at Frodsham; July 21, Athletic sports, Widnes; July 28, St. Helens and ground, at St. Helens; August 4, Frodsham, at Widnes; August 11, E,tremont, at Widnes; August 18, Latchford, at Latchford; August 25, St. Helens Recreation and ground, at St. Helens; September 1, Warrington, at Widnes; September 8, Briggs' benefit match. RUNCORN BURIAL Boeum—The monthly meeting was held at the Cemetery, on Wednesday afternoon, under the presidency of Mr. W. Whittaker, the chairman. There were also present :—Messrs. Mess, Norman, Rhodes, Cole- burn, Rhodes, Littler, and Salkeld (secretary).—The Secre- tary reported that the interments for the year ending March 25th were 406. an increase of 147 on the previous period. The fees received for the same time amounted to £379 16s 3d, being an increase of £l2B 198 id on 1881. Since the opening of the cemetery there had been 6,075 inter- ments.—Mr. Moss moved the confirmation of the Finance Committee's minutes,which showed that accounts amounting to £l4 14s 2d were passed for payment; £23 4s was due to Mr. Hazlehurst for interest.—Mr. Littler seconded the motion, which was carried.—Mr. J. J. Speakman, and Mr. B. Kniveton, the auditors, certified that they had examined the books and accounts of the Burial Board, up to the 25th ult., and found them correct in every particular.—This was the whole of the business of public interest.

TAQUEST AT RUNCORN.—On Tuesday morning, at the Navigation Hotel, Runcorn, Mr. Coroner Ridgway held an inquest touching the death of Alice White, a married woman living with her husband at 17, Canal-street. Mrs. White, who was 41 years of age, was confined on the 24th March. She was attended by a woman named Mrs. Riley, but as she became very ill Dr. MacDougall was sent for on the Ist April. She appeared, when that gentleman visited her, to be suffering from bronchial congestion, and was rather feverish, but he could not say she had puerperal fever. On the 6th April Dr. Bagnall visited the deceased, who was then in a moribund condition and beyond human aid. She died on Sunday night last.—The Coroner observed that it rested with him to decide whether or not there should be an inquest, and from the evidence before him he thought it was the duty of Dr. Bagnall to give a certificate. The Coroner, at the close of the inquiry, informed the deceased's husband, who is a bricklayer, that puerperal fever some- times arose from the unsanitary condition of the dwelling. house, and he cautioned him to keep his dwelling cleaner than it had hitherto been.—The jury returned a verdict to the effect that death resulted from puerperal fever. THE PERCY MURDER CASE: A QUARRELSOME FAMILY. —At Widnes Petty Session., on Wednesday, William Percy was charged with refusing to quit licensed premises when requested to do so, and also with assaulting Ann Whalley. —Mr. T. J. Peters appeared for the defendant, Mrs. Whalley, who is the sister of the defendant, said she kept the Blackburn Arms public-house, Lugsdale. On the 14th inst. the defendant entered the house in a state of drunken- ness. He demanded three glasses of beer for himself and his companions, but she refused to serve them, and brought the defendant some bread and cheese instead. The defen- dant seemed displeased at this and struck her three times, knocking her to the ground. She ordered him to leave the house, hut he refused.—Thomas Painter confirmed this statement, while another witness said when Mrs. Whalley brought in the bread and cheese and the defendant refused it, the complainant attempted to put him out of the hodse. Defendant then struck her. She told him that it was all through him that her father was where he was.—Mr. Peters, for the defence, characterised the case as a trumpery one, the proceedings being actuated by spite. The defendant bad undergone a good deal of persecution at the hands of his family, members of which had appeared in that court to answer charges.—The Bench ordered the defendant to pay costs for the assault, and dismissed the other case.

- - HOUSEBREAKINct BY BOYS AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Thos. Sullivan (14) and Hy. Smith (13) were charged with breaking into the lock-up shop of Edward Martley, bookseller and stationer, Anne-street West, some- time between eleven o'clock on Saturday night and nine pan. on Sunday, and stealing therefrom is. sd. and a key, value is.—Mr. Martley said a few minutes before eleven o'clock on Saturday night he locked up the shop, leaving Is. ed. in the money drawer in which he left the key. The key produced was his, but the chisel and mallet did not belong to him. In consequence of a communication made to him he went to the shop on Sunday night, when he found that half of the back kitchen window had been taken out, and an entrance thus effected. Inside he discovered that a panel had been taken out of the middle door leading into the shop; the money was gone from the till, and the key was missing. The property had also been damaged to the extent of 10s.—P.C. McMasters said on Sunday night, seeing a light in Mr. Martley's premises, he went round to the back, and entering the yard, found the prisoner Smith crouched under the kitchen window. He seized him, and deminded what he was doing there. The prisoner replied, "I am doing nothing," and witness NYIS about to burst open the door, when a voice inside said, "Don't burst it open; I will come out." Prisoner Sullivan then emerged through the window. He was wearing neither coAt nor cap, but in his waistcoat pocket were two threepenny bits and lid. in copper. The knife and chisel produced was found on a table near the middle door which had been broken, and Sullivan claimed the implements as his property.—Smith pleaded not guilty. —Both prisoners were committed to take their trial at the next Liverpool Quarter Sessions.

THE COST OK WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.—At an adjourned meeting of Widnes Local Board Mr. F. H. Gossage, the returning officer, .presented his bill of the cost for the election. It, amounted to £59 4s. CLAIM FOR STREET MAKING AT RIINCORN.—Mr.LinakOr, clerk to the Commissioners, applied_ at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, for an order to be made upon Mrs. Elizabeth Billingsley for £I6 4s. Id., for private improve- ment expenses, being her apportionment of an amount ex- pended by Runcorn Improvement Commissioners for the making of Ashridge-street. The defendant did not appear, and the case was adjourned until Monday next. The new High Sheriff for Lancashire, Mr. Thomas Ashton, will this (Saturday) morning entertain a large number of guests at breakfast at his residence, Ford Bank, Didsbury. After breakfast the High Sheriff, together with his chaplain and other officers, will be escorted by a proces- sion from Didsbury to the Queen's Hotel, Manchester; and subsequently he will meet the judges of assize on their arrival from Carlisle at Victoria Station. The commission for the assizes will be opened in the afternoon.

THE MERSEY SALT AND BRINE COMPANY, LIMITED.— On Thursday, an extraordinary meeting of the shareholders of this company, convened by Messrs. G. E. Kaye and Co., solicitors, of King-street, Cheapside, on behalf of a large number of proprietors, was held at the City Terminus Hotel, Car.non-street, London. Mr. F. M..Cobbitt was voted to the chair, and in opening the proceedings he called upon Mr: Guedalla (ef Messrs. Kaye and Co.) to explain the cir- cumstances under which the circular was issued calling to- gether this meeting, which was convened on behalf of some of the largest shareholders in the concern, for the .purpose of considering the present position and prospects of the company. Without desiring to anticipate the explanations which might be afforded by the board, it was idle to con- ceal that their position was most grave, when they con- sidered that the expenditure upon the works had largely exceeded. the anticipated amount; • and, in his opinion, it was th.refore necessary that the shareholders peremptorily insisted upon the most searching investigation into the circumstances under which all payments bad been made by the Board, in order to arrive at the cause of this unsatisfactory state of things. The works should have been completed in October last, and the great delay which had taken place, and which still continued, in the completion, was seriously prejudicial to the interests of the undertaking. Little or nothing had been accomplished teleards fulfilling the promises held forth in the prospectus, and the time had certainly arrived for the Board, who had called up the whole of the capital, to give an account to the shareholders of the manner in which they had discharged their trust. He con- sidered it impossible that Mr. Cecil Baikes, M.P., who was chairman of seven or eight other companies, could pay suffi- cient attention to the concerns of this small undertaking, besides attending to the interests of the other companies with which he was connected and his Parliamentary duties. —After some conversation it was agreed that no further action should be taken by ;he sbareholders until after the meeting summoned by the directors, which would be shortly held.
LAUNCH OF A VESSEL AT RUNCORN

Messrs. Brundrit and Co., of Runcorn, added one more success to their long list of achievements in shipbuilding, when from their yard on Saturday morning last, was launched a three-masted schooner of excellent design and workmanship. The rare occurrence of such an event, and the bright and genial weather that prevailed, attracted a large concourse of spectators to the spot, while on the Lan- cashire side some hundreds of persons were eagerly ,on the watch for the vessel's appearance on the river. Miss Dun- I bavand having performed the ceremony of christening the vessel, which received the name of "Fox," the order was given to release it from the stays, and for a few moments excitement was general. Everything, however, went well, and as the "Fox" glided gracefully into the water a hearty cheer was raised, and a canon was repeatedly fired. Built from designs of Mr. John S. Davies, manager and draughts- man for Messrs. Brundrit, the new vessel is acknowledged to be superior to any of her predecessors and is classed twelve years A 1 under special survey at Lloyds. Her re- gistered tonnage is 99.71, and she is expected to have a- carrying capacity of 220 tons. Her dimensions are 90 \feet inches on the keel, 211 feet beam, and 10 feet 3 inches depth of hold. The frame of the vessel is of good English oak throughout, while the keelson is of pitchpine the out- side bottom planking up to bilges, rock elm; and the decks yellow pine. The vessel has been rigged by Mr. John Bate, and a full suit of sails supplied by Mr. S. R;tvenscroft. Mr. George Yarwood has done the painting and decorative work, and Mr. Clotwerthy, of Liverpool, was entrusted with the whole of the carved work. The figurehead of the vessel is a fox, while the appropriate figures of a huntsman and hounds adorn the stern. In the internal arrangements of the "Fox" are incorporated all the latest improvements likely to con- duce to the comfort of the captain and crew, and she has been fitted with double action steering gear and patent double action pumps. We may state that the vessel has been built to the order of Messrs. Thomas Cooper and Co., of Runcora, for genaral coasting purposes, and under the command of Captain Dunbavand. late captain of the" Redtail." She left the Mersey on Wednesday, with a cargo of salt for Aberdeen. Messrs. Brundrit, it is interesting to know, are at Tiresent en- gaged in the erection of a much larger vessel for several Inca' gentlemen.

div.head: WIDNES CHORAL SOCIETY'S CONCERT.
div.p: WIDNES CHORAL SOCIETY'S CONCERT.

Only a moderate audience gathered in Widnes Volunteer Hall, on Thursday evening, to hear the members of Widnes Choral Society give their last concert of the season, and it is doubtful if the receipts will cover the expenses. No doubt the proceedings at Hartland Chapel contributed in some degree to this result, which is the more to he regretted as he music was varied and bright. Rossini's " Stabat Mater" composed the first part of the programme, "The May Queen" the second, and miscellaneous pieces the third. Although not numerically so strong as on former occasions, the chorus, conducted by Mr. W. I. Argent, acquitted itself of the somewhat difficult pieces it was called upon to render with taste, precision, and harmony. True, weakness was at times noticeable, but at the same time we feel constrained to congratulate the members on their suc- cessful performance. The principals were Miss Emily Stewart (soprano), Miss Frances Armstrong (contralto), Mr. Arthur Tuer (tenor), and Mr. Morel! (bass.) Mr. Tuer sang parts allotted to him with cultured taste and power. His rendering of " Cujus animam gem3ntem " was very fine, and he was no less happy in his singing of Sullivan's song "My dearest heart." Miss Stewsart has previously gratified a Widnes audience with an evidence of her power as a vocalist, and her flexible voice on the present occasion was heard to great advantage. The recitative "The Queer's greeting," in the May Queen, and also the song which followed, was an enjoyable piece of vocalisation. Miss Armstrong suc- ceeded in securing the marked attention of her audience, who rewarded her with a well-merited encore for the charm- ing song "The lost chord," which she sang with great ex- pression. A similar token of appreciation was awarded Lb Miss Stewart and Miss Armstrong for their admirable inter- pretation of the duet" Quisest homo," their voices blend- ing most harmoniously. Mr. Morell gave a careful render- ing of the parts assigned to him, but his voice lacked power and expression, and the fine air, "Pro peccatis," awakened no response from the audience. As on former occasions, the orchestra was equal to the calls which were made upon its skill, and to it must be ascribed the effkctive rendering of several of the choruses.

div.head: RUNCORN GUARnIAN'S' ELECTION.
div.p: RUNCORN GUARnIAN'S' ELECTION.

By withdrawals and comprctnises contests were avoided in the townships of the Runcorn poor law union, with the exception of Runcorn and Weston. In the former place feeling ran somewhat high. The Ratepayers' Assniation, which was inaugurated last autumn, decided to enter upon a test of its influence, and nominated five candidates whose names are slessrs. F. Rigby Wm. Mellor, F. Fairhurst, Wm. Handley, and W. Whittaker. A slip issued "by order of the committee" asked the ratepayers to support these gentle- men because they were "not nominated to protect private interests at the expense of the general body of the rate- payers," and because they were pledged to a policy of the strictest economy. The other two candidates were Mr. Thomas Norman, who has served the town as a Guardian for a great number of years, and Mr. Philip Speakman; and these gentlemen received the support of what is termed the " Works." "An indignant ratepayer " issued a handbill chiefly in support of Mr. Norman's candidature. He declared that an unscrupulous attempt was being made by an "irresponsible organisation " to deprive the ratepayers of the services of Mr. Norman, "your oldest and most trusted Guardian," and asked them to show their appreciation of his faithful services in the past, and their condemnation of the "petty clique" by voting for Mr. Norman, Mr. Speakman, Mr. Fairhurst, Mr. Whittaker, and Mr. Handley. On Monday, when the vot- ing papers were distributed, canvassers in large numbers were at work, and the probable result of the contest was much discussed. The papers were collected on Tuesday, and counted at Dutton Workhouse on Wednesday. Time result was as follows:
W. Whittaker W. Handley 9BB T. Norman 955 F. Fai hurst F. Speakman 677 W. Mellor 593 F. Rigby 584

It will thus he seen that two of the candidates receiving the countenance of the ass niation were defeated, while Mr. Norman, against whom strong efforts were unsuccessfully made, occupied the third place. A rumour went the round of the town on Wednesday that an uaple leant incident or two was likely to arise from the contest. It was stated that there were several clear cases of tampering with Toting papers, and that the advisability of prosecuting the offenders was under consideration. Of the votitrx papers collected, 750 were either blank or spoiled, and 400 more wore ren— dered useless owing to non-delivery, throug,h deaths and re- movals. The result of the Toting at Westeo was :
Rev. Canon Barclay 2ll F. G. Claudet 172 Jameg Handley ll9
Considering the forces arrayed against him, Mr. Hardley has made a brave fight, being only 60 below the second candidate.

div.head: Wetter to the gaitor.
div.p: Wetter to the gaitor.
THE RUNCORN RATEPAYERS' ASSOCIATI ON AND THE LATE ELECTION.

Sir,—On perusing the mandate, which, issued by order of the committee, was supposed to seal the doom of Mr. Norman in his capacity as a Poor-law Guardian, my admir- ation of the sentiment of each stirring paragraph was equalled only by my amazement at the startling discrepan- cies continually occuring between the high sounding theories and the practical applications of the policy which is there set forth. For instance, while demanding fresh vigoares a stern necessity, they begin by excluding from their list the gentleman, who, of all others, has been ex- emplary in the regularity of his attendance on the onerous duties of a Guardian, and whilst tirading against private interests, they select as their foremost candidates two gentle- men officially connected with our guaranteed ten per cent. gas monoply. Again, while endeavouring to raise a false issue on the question of assessments, they unhesitatingly demand the dismissal of the youngest member of the Assessment Committee, throwing at the same time the cloak of their organisation round Mr. William Handley, their nominee, who, as a much older member of the said committee, and an overseer of some years standing, must of ne:essity be doubly responsible. Supposing for the moment the irregularities they insinuate have any existence, and one wonders which to admire most, the keen and impartial discrimina- tion,of these local dictators, or the manly straightforward- ness of their financial authority. The combination has, however, been frustrated. Mr. Norman has weathered the storm which spleen and jealousy strove so hard to raise, and the result of the election should teach our newly- fledged association that before they can wield that power to which they aspire, they must prove that their organisa- tion can only be employed in the interest of those they affect to serve, and that misrepresentation, no matter how specious, is impotent to command their co-operation. And, in the meantime, I leave them to extricate themselves from the toils in which a clique has encircled them, and to bear as best they may the onus of having caused an unnecessary election, the cost of which, whether defrayed by township lor union, must certainly come out of the pockets of the ratepayers.—Yours truly, COMMON SENSE.

div.head: STRANGE DROWNING CASE AT .RUNCORN.
div.p: STRANGE DROWNING CASE AT .RUNCORN.
EXTRAORDINARY CONDUCT OF A PUBLICAN.

Mr. Ridgway, the coroner, held, at the Burial Board Offices, on Tuesday afternoon, an inquiry into the circum- stances by which a woman named Ann Gibson, 29 years of age, met her death. The body of the deceased had been found in the Bridgewater Canal at Top Locks that morn- ing. _ _

'Elizabeth Abbott, wife of Thomas Abbott,l4, Fryer-street, said the deceased was the wife of Thomas Gibson of no settled residence. When in Runcorn the deceased lodged at witness's house. On Monday morning deceased said she was going to Chester after her husband, but at four o'clock she came into the house drunk, and -later in the evening went out. The last time witness saw her was about 10 o'clock, when she was at the top of Fryer-street with two sailors. Shi. did not appear to be drunk then, and seemed quite able to take care of herself. Witness did not know the sailors, and could not recognise them again if she saw them. Deceased went away with the sailors. When in drink she was very short-tempered. Mr. Richard Rowles, New Inn, High-street, stated that he last saw the deceased alive at a few minutes past ten on the previous night, when she was standing in his vaults. A man named Thomas Hodgkinson was with her. Hodg- kinson looked perfectly sober, and he paid for a small glass of port wine for the deceased. The deceased drank her wine and went out, and Hodgkinson remained some minutes later. He did not think Hodgkinson went out of the house with the intention of following deceased. Thomas Hodgkinson, keeper of the Feathers Inn beer- house, Church-street, on being asked by the Coroner whether he was with the deceased at the New Inn on the previous night, said he did not remember anything of the sort. He was so very intoxicated that he did not remember being at the house, nor did he remember paving for any wine for the deceased.

The Coroner: Am I to understand then that you were so intoxicated that you cannot remember what you were doing? was.—The Coroner said he would candidly tell the witness that he did not understand Mr. Rowles coming there and saying he seemed to be sober, and that he served him with drink, and then the witness telling them he waq thoroughly drunk and knew nothing about it. He did not know what course the police might pursue, but it was certainly a shocking state of things.—Witness : I can give you no evidence at all.—The Coroner: You were so intoxicated that you knew nothing Do you know where you were at all? I think I was at Hayward's —Do you remember being with the woman? Ido not.— Do you remember being with any woman? No; but if the woman had dodged him it was quite possible he trid!f have paid for some drink to get rid of her, knowing what sort of a woman she was. When he went home be was Very drunk, and pulled his boots off and went straight to bed.—You know, Mr. Hodgkinson, it is a very serious matter. You must really look at it in a serious light. Do you really mean to tell me that you were so full of drink that you knew nothing of what was going on? I can remember nothing at all of her.—lf it had happened that Mr. Rowles had been summoned for permitting drunkenness, the chances are a hundred to one you would have ca.llel a score of wit- nesses to prove you were perfectly sober. lam sorry to say it, but I don't believe you are telling us the whole truth. Mr. Wright (a juror) questioned witness as to whether he, remembered being at the Nelson Hotel about halt-past nine on the previous night.—Witness replied that he had no recollection of it.

Mr. Wright said the pretence of the witness that he had not been there was all nonsense. Hodgkinson c tiled at the house at that time, and was served by him. He (Mr. Wright) was looking after the Nelson, as the landlady was in some trouble, and he remembered the circumstance well. The Coroner (to witness): Just listen to me, sir, anl just aemember you are sworn to tell the whole truth. It is a rerious matter, and do not make so slight of it. Witness: I cannot say any more.—You have given me the impression, rightly or wrongly, that you are treating this inquest in a very improper manner, and treating me as coroner in a most impertinent manner, besides behaving most disrespectful to the jury. (Hear, hear.) Stand up, sir, and remember von are in a court of justice. I am told you were at the Nelson at half-past nine last night, and were served with a glass of beer. Were you sober then? I cannot say I was sober at the time.—Were you drunk? Witness was understood to to say that he did not think he was sober.—What time do you remember being sober, to begin with? I was " fresh " when I left home, about seven o'clock in the evening. I was sober at twelve o'clock, because I had a meeting with the magistrates at that time. Then I was drunk in the afternoon, and went round for a walk and got a glass at one place and anotber.—Do you remember being at the Nel- son at 9-30 ? I don't remember the time.—Where did voa •go from the Nelson? To the Queen's Head. Whet -had you there? I had beer there. Did you stand anybody treat? Yes. A fiddler, a big fellow, an Irishman,—Where did you go to from there P To Hayward's. I cannot tell where I went to. I was knocking round, i and the missals said it was about ten o'clock when I came in.— Well, I don't believe it.—Witness : I have witnesses to prcve it.—The Coroner : I don't believe it at all. I believe it is an attempt on your part—for I believe Mr. Bowles—to get out of a discreditable business. I sincerely hope the teolice will take notice of your conduct. They can prosecute you for an offence under the Licensing Act, and I hope they will take notice of it.—Witnees : I am very sorry if I have committed an offence, sir.—The Coroner : Accordirl to your own statement you want to make us believe you were drunk, and I cannot credit one word you have said.—Wit- ness: Will you allow me to send for evidence P—The Coroner: No, indeed. Go out of the room, sir. I shall not allow you anything for your attendance.—The witness hav- ing left the room, the Coroner observed that for some reason known only to himself the witness Hodgkinson had tried to keep something back. It would have been much better for him to have told the whole truth than to have acted in the may he had.—A Juryman informed the coroner that Hodgkinson had been fined on the previous morning for harbouring women of immoral character in his house.—The jury concurred in the remarks of the coroner, and strongly commented upon the way the witness had conducted him- self during the inquiry. The Coroner remarked that he had known Mr. Bowles for many years, and quite believed all he had said; yet here was a man like Hodgkinson who had attempted to get twelve men of common sense to believe his statement that he was beastly drunk at ten:o'clock. If he had been charged with drunkenness he would have got ten or a dozen men to prove that he was sober. It was not often he came across a man who had no respect for himself.— Joseph Booth, Canal Constable, deposed to finding the body or the deceased in the canal at a quarter past three that morning. The hands had been crushed in the lock gate.— P.C. Noden stated there were no marks of violence on the body. He had been unable-to trace the sailors who had been with the deceased on the previous night, but from in- quiries he bad made be believed Hodgkinson was the last man who saw the deceased alive. He did not think there had been any foul play, and it was his opinion that the deceased had fallen in the water in passing ander Waterloo bridge, where the footpath was awkard and narrow. A constable saw Hodgkinson leave the New Inn at a quarter past ten, and he was seen by Inspector Hollingworth near the Holy- head harbour at a quarter to ten. He seemed to walk straight and was going towards home.—The Coroner said the fact that Hodgkinson was seen on his way home a few minutes after Mr. Bowles said he was at the New Inn, cleared up a grave doubt in his mind, and if this had not transpired he should have felt it necessary to adjourn the inquiry. Hodgkinson had knowingly and wilfully told untruths, and if anything arose through his conduct he had only himself to blame.—The jury returned an open verdict.

div.p: A TIOLENT LODGER.-At the St. Helens Police Court on Monday, a man named Bernard Cullen, who had been pre- viously fined for drunkenness, was charged with having committed damage, to the extent of 245,,, to the house 69, Lowe-street, where he lodged.' It appeared that the prisoner had gone to his lodgings on Saturday night in a very drunken and disorderly state, and having been put out the house by his landlord, he broke the windows and sashes with a spide. —Mr. Kitchen gave evidence as to the extent of the damage done, and prisoner was ordered to pay 24s damage and a fine of 2s tid and costs, or, in default, 28 days' imprison- ment.
LATEST
NE WS.
MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL SCHEME
The Manchester hip Canal Bill was yesterday re- argued before the Standing Orders Committee of the House of Lords. Earl Redesdale presided, and sixteen Other noble lords were present.

Mr. COATES, who appeared for the promoters' explained the main provisions of the Bill as altered by the Standing Orders Committee of the House of Commons, and as now presented to their lordship's House. The only part objected to on the Standing Orders was, be said, the first part of clause 26, which had been struck out. This provision gave the promoters power to improve the navigation of the Mersey between Runcern I and Garston ; but the promoters contended that even wite- ont this power the Mersey Conservancy Board, consisting of I three Cabinet Ministers, could by virtue of the Act under which they were constituted, authorize the promaters to carry out the works which they contemplated. The inten- tion of the .promoters was not to make a new channel alto- gether, but to improve the channel which already existed. It was in evidence that at high water vessels of between 500 and 600 tons however, could go up to Runcorn, which was just below ;he place where the entrance to the canal avoula be placed; and it was a fact that 225,000 tons of I shipping annually went up the river to be discharged at the I very place. At low water there was a channel of four feet close to the entrance to the canal, and the depth gradually increased towards the sea. It had been said tint they would require to dredge the bed of the river to the depth of thirty feet, but he was able to assure the committee from a section which had been made that the depth of scouring would not require to be more than 12 feet at the entrance to the dock leading to the canal. No doubt a low water channel would be extremely inexpedient, but a low water channel was by no means an essential of the scheme. Experiments which had recently been made showed that steamers after' passing the bar at Liverpool at flood tide could travel quicker than the tides, so that in three and a half hours from the tide flowing up at Liverpool a vessel would be at Runcorn on the flood tide and thus gain access to the canal docks. The persons promoting the Bill were promo- ting it not as a speculation, but in the interests of the dis- trict, and that was proved by one of the clauses which pro- vided that the undertaking could be transferred to a trust on payment of a small percentage for the use of capital inves- ted by the company. Sir THEODORE MARTIN said he represented the Mersey and Irwell and Bridgewater Navigation Company, and he had to address the committee on their behalf, and also on behalf of the other petitioners against • the Bill. He asked their lordships to look at the Bill and see what the scheme was. When it was first introduced it was a scheme to make into the port of Manchester the whole-of the estuary of the Upper Mersey from Garston to Hunt's Rank in the city of Manchester, that was to say, a distance of 11 miles, in an es- tuary varying in breadth from threeemiles to thirty or forty yards. A canal through dry land by itself was proposed in this Bill. Was it not an absurdity on the face of it? Means ought to have been7provided for approach by the canal from the sea' otherwise how could the canal as set forth in the recital of the preamble be made available for ocean steamers? He maintained that thera was nothing in the Bill for the committee to consider, as the most essential portion of it had been eli- minated by the Standing Orders Committee of the other House. No provision was made in the Bill for raising funds to deal with the channel in the estuary of the river, and he submitted it would be contrary to the practice of their lordship's House to send such it Bill to a Select Committee. Mr. REIS also spoke against the Bill on behalf of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, and Mr. Pierre, in the interest of the London and North-Western Railway Co. After a brief deliberation in private, The Committee decided by ten to six to suspend the Standing Orders, so that the Bill will be allowed to proceed in the present Session.
THE PHCENIX PARK MURDERS.
BRADY SENTENCED TO DEATH.

The trial of Joe Brady for the murder of Mr. Burke in Phcenis Park, on the 6.11 May, was continued yesterday morning in Dublin. The jury catne into their box at 10 minutes to 10, but it was not until shortly past 10 that Judge O'Brien put in an appearance. He was quickly followed by the counsel for the defence, and subsequently by the two law officers of the Crown Mr. Murphy, Q C., and Mr. P. O'Brien, Q.C., for the prosecution. Brady was immediately afterrwards placed in the dock, which, as usual, was strongly ptiotected by police, marines, and plain clothes detectives. James Edward Kennedy, examined by Mr. Sullivan for the defence, said: In May last I lived at 6, Upper Dami- nick-street. lam a clerk. I know Joseph Brady well. I remember the night of the murders well. I SAW Brady on that evening coming up Upper Dominick-street. That was about five or ten minutes past seven. lam perfectly cer- tain it was Brady. I saw there was a girl with him whom I had never seen before. He did not pass me, but he stopped me, and stood talking to me for three or four minutes. This was opposite my own door. lam perfectly certain about the hour. I left my house at tow miuutes to seven, as I had an appointment. I, should know the girl again if I saw her.

Cross-examined by the Attorney-General : I knew Brady well, but not especially well. I used to meet him, perhips, once a month or two months. I recollect seeing him in April and February, but I could not say about January. I first gave my evidence last week. I heard of the charge some time ago, and I knew the man was inno- cent. It didn't strike me particularly when I heard that my old friend was charged with murder, but I knew he was innocent. I saw the girl yesterday morning and again in the afternoon, and although I had never seen her except on the 6± with Brady, I recognised her at once. No one was with me when I recognised her. There was some one with her, but I don't know who it was. I met Brady fiye or six times after the 6th of May, ana before he was arrested.- I do not recollect the times nor the places of these meetings, hut I recollect the 6th well. Everyone in Ireland has cause to remember that. As Joe and the girl passed on I remmber making the remark to my- self, "What the devil is Joe for now ?" I have been in Little's public-house twice, and each occasion was last week. I saw Brady the day after the murder, and said it was a ter- rible thing. He replied, "Yes, it has ruined Ireland." I never met him after that until the evening he was arrested. I don't know when that was now.—Brady was arrested on the 13th of January this year,•and you have already sworn that you did see him in June and July. Did you see him ? I might have, but not to speak to him. I don't think I did. —But you have sworn a few minutes ago that you did see him .—I did, but that was through a mistake. Mr. :11'Cline then fetched in the witness Meagher and wit- neFs identified her as the girl he had seen with Brady. Dr. Webb intimated at this point that the case for the defence was closed, and asked his Lordship whether he would hear the objection he (Dr. Webb) would have to raise elncerning the evidence adduced by the Crown.—His Lordship assenting the learned counsel submitted that be respectfully objected to the reception of all evidence which went to show the existence of any conspiracy prior to the 3rd of May, 1882. He also objected to the production of any evidence of any conspiracy to murder Mr. Burke before that date, except so far as the evidence consisted of the acts or words of the prisoner himself, or the words or actions of others in his presence. The learned counsel contended that the charge under which the prisoners were brought up at Kil- mainhann was framed in the charge of conspiracy, which was a misdemeanour, and followed up by a charge of murder, which was a capital offence, a combination which, in the learned counsel's experience, had no precedent. His Lordship reminded Dr. Webb that the indictment in the present case was framed on the charge of murder alone Dr. Webb, continuing his argument, submitted that a conspiracy to murder must be to murder some definite in- dividual. The law which regulated the evidence of pri- soners in the second degree, or alders and abbettors, and the rule of evidence which referred to the conspiracy, was not applicable to a crime like the present. Mr. Sullivan supported the contention of his learned friend. The Attorney-General reminded his lordship that the evidence of conspiracy had only been adduced to such an extent-as it affected the doings of the prisoner prior to the actual murder. His Lordship concurred with the Attornev-General, and said he could not accede to Dr. Webb's proposal as one con- tained in the statutes. Mr. James Murphy, Q C., deprecated the action taken by ' Dr. Webb at Kilmainham, and repudiated the contention that Carey was driven to give evidence as a result of the nature of the charges made against himself and others. He had given evidence to save himself. His Lordship ultimately declined to allow that the con- tention of Dr. Webb had, been proved, and thereupon Mr. Adams addressed the jury in closing the case for the defence. He said the jury had to decide between the testi- mony of Annie Meagher, the pure and unstained young girl, and that of Jamas Carey, the infamous informer. Let them weigh James Carey against Annie Meagher, and he would await their verdict without fear. The Judge having summed up, the jury retired and found a verdict of guilty. Brady was then sentencedite death

div.head: CETEWAYO STARVING.
div.p: CETEWAYO STARVING.

The Daily ire w s says :—Cetewavo, having had to borrow £5O from Mr. Saul Solomon, of Cape Town, to buy "domes- tic appliances "on his return, has sent messengers to return the money. It is said, however, that he is almost in a state of starvation, as those who have obtained his lands will not give them up.

div.head: 'THE GLENDALE CROFTERS.
div.p: 'THE GLENDALE CROFTERS.

In consequence of the threatening attitude the Glen- dale crofters, the summonses of eviction have been sent through the post-office. The documents were all posted at Portree on Thursday night, in the presence of witnesses,and it is believed that the court will hold this service sufficient. The crofters are in an excited state, and precautions are again being taken.
TUE ATTEMPTED ASSASSINATIO-N OF PRINCE
MILAN.

A Vienna telegram of yesterday's date says :—At Belgrade on Thursday, Helen Marcovio, who attempted to assassinate Prince Milan in October last, committed suicide in prisor. Helen Knitjaniu, who was implicated in the same crime, committed suicide in prison lately. The State trial, at which disclosures of a remarkable character were expected will thus be stopped.

div.head: DEATH OF A LADY UNDER CHLOROFORM.
div.p: DEATH OF A LADY UNDER CHLOROFORM.

Mrs. Duncan Mackintosh, Inverness, died on Thursday night under distressing circumstances. She was having some teeth extracted. Chloroform was administered and two teeth were removed from the lower jaw. The next tooth to be taken out was an upper molar, and in the process of extraction Mrs. Mackintosh recovered from the influence of the chloroform, raised her hands to her head, and immediately expired. The deceased was a young woman.
A POTTED MEAT MANUFACTURER SENT TO
PRISON.

At the Birmingham Police Court, yesterday, a potted manufaeurer named Henry Bryan, of Great Lister-street, who carried on a considerable business, was sentenced to three months' imprisonment, without the option of a fine' for having on his premises 150 pieces of diseased horse flesh and 60 pieces of pork from an animal that had been suffer- ing from swine fever. THE PROPOSED CRIMINAL COURT OF APPEAL

Addressing the grand jury at Chester Assizes, yesterday, Mr. Justice Hawkins, referring to this bill, said he could not say much about it, as it had not been submitted to some of Her Majesty's judges. Of course it would be a very good thing for everybody to have an appeal to the very highest tribunal, but it might involve a great deal of difficulty. It would be much better if they had a little more care bestowed on the investigation of cases in the first instance and he could not help Waking that the applications which were made to the Hot .e Secretary for the revision of sentences or for the revision of the verdict of juries, were made very much in consequence of the imperfect way in which cases were now presented to the court.

Lord GRANVILLE brought up the message from the Crown proposing pensions of £2,000 per annum to Lords Wolseley and Alcester.—Earl DIINRAVEN called attention to the condition of agricultral labourers in Ireland, and moved a resolution in favour of legislation on their behalf—Lord CARLINGFORD pointed out difficulties in the way of legislatkn, but promised attention on the sub- ject.—The motion was withdrawn.—The, Army Annual Bill passed through comm.itise and the House adjourned.
