div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Mr. TREV/ILYIN, replying to Mr. O'Brien, said no unfair advantage had been taken with witneves to be called tortilla defence in the Phoenix Park murder trials, and the whole course pursued had been as fair and above-board as murder trials usually are conducted. THE EGYPTIAN HEROES.—Mr. GLADSTONE brought Up a messige from the Crown asking the House to enable Her Majesty to grant pensions to Lord's Wolseley. and Alcester of £2,000 per annum.—Messige to be taken into consideration on Monday. _

TUE TRANSVAAL.—On the motion for resuming the adjourned debate on Mr. Gorst's resolution regarding affairs in the Transvaal, and on Mr. Cartwright's amend- ment thereto being read, Mr. CARTWRIGHT said he could not accept the amendment to his amendment Mr. Gladstone proposed to move, and therefore he asked leave to withdraw his amendment.—A discussion ensued as to the difficulty that would arise if such a course was pursued.—The SPEAKER pointed out that leave to withdraw the amendment rested with the House.—Sir S. NoirritcorE said the present difficulty had been occasioned by want of straightforward- ness on the part of the Government in not giving Sir. M. Beach the opportunity of bringing forward his motion censuring the Transvaal policy of the Government. The best way out of the difficulty was for the Government to say whether or not they would give the hon. baronet the op- portunity he d-eired. If so, it would get rid of the difficulty these shiftings had brought about. Mr. GLADSTONE complained of the accusatory attack made on the Government, and said he should be quite prepared to add the words to his amendment making it corn- plete.—l'lle motion that the amendment be withdrawn was negatived amid cheering.—Sir H. HOLLAND then resumed the adjourned debate. He attributed the whole of the diffi- culties that had ar;rn in the Transvaal to the shifting policy of Her Majesty's eleeevernment, as they had failed to maintain and uphold the dignity Of England. The Govern- ment, it appeared to him. had not yet made up its mind what to do. The Government had made a convention with the Transvaal Government which the latter Government had broken, and vet Her Majesty's advisers were not prepared to act with decision in the matter. The best thing to be done was to abandon the sham suzereignty, as the charge had been brought against them of having deserted their allies, and that charge they were not prepared to deny. He insisted that complicity existed between the Transvaal Government and the Boers.—Mr. LEATHAM e,aid in great English constituencies it was thought that armed interfer- ence on behalf of the Bechuanes would be positive prostitu- tion of the resources of this country. He condemned the action of the missionaries, who, he said, were religious free- booters, filibustering in the territory of others. He supported the amendment, which set out that any interference in the very grave complications that existed must be confined to the limits of absolutely unavoidable obligations. Lord JOHN MANNERS severely condemned the policy of the Government. He characterised that policy as paltering, pitiful, huxtering, and further degradation for England.— Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said the policy of the opposition ap- peared to be to make war speeches and propose peaceful resolutions; and he insisted that to have continued the war after they had-abandoned the territory would have been an act of unparallelled wickedness. The present state of affairs was the result of the meddling policy which brought about the 'Zulu war, and while he admitted they were under some obligation to give reasonable support to the chiefs, which they had proposed to carry out by the offer of money and lands, they were under no such obli- gation as regarded the tribes, which numbered over 50,000. He thought that if the chiefs united amongst themselves they could secure respect from the Boers, but under any circumstances the Government would not be driven into a war which nobody in the country wanted, and which, if en- tered into, would be perfectly unjustifiable. The Hon. SIDNEY HERBERT thought the Government exhibited great weaknese in not compelling the Boers to respect the property of others.-Mr. GoscrtEsee thought this country had lost some of its influence as regarded the protection of native races, and the fact that our agent at Preetoria was agent of the party that had been defeated by the Boers might have had something to do with the present circum- stances. He earnestly entreated the Government to make up its mind whether they would withdraw their agent from Prretoria and give up the !suzsreignty, or else that the British resident should be adequately supported in his re- monstrances. Drifting between two opinions could only land them in disaster.—Mr. STUART WORTLEY condemned the inactivity of the Government—On adjourned—Sir jornountd—si the motion s tio.nNoofßATln: Mr. W. FOWLER the debate wag again COTE asked that a reguler evening might be given to conclude the debate.—Mr. GLAD STONE said if they could agree to definite proposals instead of a string of amend- , Inmate on paper, he would willingly give a night. Some arrangement might be come to by Monday.—Sitting sus- pended.—The Spesher resumed the chair at five minutes'past nine, when the House was counted. Forty members being present, Mr. MONK proceeded to call attention to the marriage laws in the United Ringdom.—The House was again counted, and 40 members not beiges preeent, ties House adjourned at 9-15.

A despatch from Berlis states that several officers of the Russian army will shortly be brought before a court- martial on the charge of treason. They have been induced to join the Nihilists by a woman whose husband is among the batch of prisoners now on trial before a special tribunal. WOMEN AND CHILDREN CUT DOWN BY TROOPS.—A de- monstration against the authorities has occurred at Grijau, near Zaitchar, Servia. A troop of mounted gendarmes charged a crowd of men, women, and children, cutting down many with their sabres. Others were trampled under foot by the horses. The inhabitants have sent a telegram to the Government and the King, asking for a commission of in-

From Cairo it is reported that a Commission has been nominated to arrange the details of the plan for the estab- lishment of a Representative Chamber, this being the scheme which at present chiefly occupies the attention of Lord Dufferin, who is anxious that the decrees embodying, not only the basis sketched out in his despatches, but also pro- viding for the effective working out of his instructions, should be promulgated before his departure. THE PARLIAMENTARY OATH IN SPAIN.—A Madrid tele- gram says,—The HOMO of Deputies has approved, by 164 votes to 42, the Parliamentary Oath Bill, which allows Freethinkers and Protestants to enter the Cortes. Senor Castelar made a splendid protest in the name of the Repub- lican minority against the oath. He upbraided the Conser- vatives and Liberals for sacrificing the religious test rather than the Royalist's oath, when they ought to recollect that King Amadeus and the Spanish Revolution never exacted any oath from the Alfonsists. Spanish history for the last fifteen years proved how little statesmen observed such en- gagements, which were repugnant to the conscience. A SHAMEFUL TiticK.—A shameful trick has been played on the French Academy of Sciences. The Kiinigsburg student, Hermann Minkowsky, who, with the late Professor Henry J. S. Smith, was declared to have gained the great mathematical prize of 3,000 f, had simply pirated Professor Smith's communication to the Royal Society, in 1868, on the representation of a number as the sum of five squares. He had even copied a slight error hi it. The Academy, therefore, at a secret session on Tuesday, annulled its original decision, and decreed that the whole prize had been gained by the distinguished English Professor, who, unfor- tunately, has not lived long enough to expose the hoax. AN EASTERN ABDUCTION CASE —A curious story comes from Central Asia about the abduction of a woman from Baku and her transference to the harem of the Shah. The event is said to have occurred some months ago, and it is understood that the woman has only been restored to her husband after a strong representation on the part of the Rus- sian Minister at Tegieran. The interest in the matter does not arise altogether from the fact of the abduction or restora- tion of the woman, but is rather found in the incidental re- marks that are made in the course of the story as to the re- lations of the Emperor of Russia and the Shah. These two potentates, it appears, have never shown a very friendly feel- ing towards each other; and the present incident is appar- ently being seized upon by Russia as a basis for the exchange of anything but complimentary messages with the Govern- ment of the Shah. AFGHANISTAN.--It is a common opinion that on the Liberal Government assuming office Lord Beaconsfield's Afghan policy was completely reversed and all the advantages, if there were any, of the costly campaigns in that country thrown away. A statement to this effect having been made at the close of a work recently published, which gives a strictly accurate account of the military operations in Af- ghanistan, and is consequently likely to be regarded as a standard history of the campaign, Sir Lepel Griffin, who was the person chiefly concerned with the political arrangements under both Administrations, gives the assertion an emphatic contradiction. He declares that, "instead of the Liberal Government completely reversing the policy which had been pursued by their predecessors, they maintained that policy intact, and the only portions of it which disappeared were those which were inherently impracticable or mischievous, such as the occupation of Herat by Persia, and the creation of an independent kingdom of Candahar, both of which died a natural death, and did not need any action of the Liberal Government to hasten their dissolution." - - A terrible explosion is reported by the Paris paper to have occurred at Revel, a town in the Gulf of Finland, and not far from St..Petersbug. More than 2,000 spectators were witnessing a theatrical performance, when a tremen- dous explosion suddenly took place, throwing the audience into a state of panic, and the building in complete darkness. When, after some delay, lights were brought, a frightful scene presented itself. In the rush for the exits hundreds of the spectators had been hurled to the ground and trampled up,m. Some could be seen lying where they had been literally crushed by falling beams and masses of stone. Others hurled against the wall by the force of the explosion, lay mangled and bleeding, rending the air with their agonising cries. Help was however happily at hand, and in a comparatively short time the building was cleared of the bodies, the wounded being conveyed to the hospital and the dead con- signed to their relatives. The number of fatalities is not known. The disaster is attributed to an escape of gis from gutta pacha bags employed in the lighting of the theatre.

GALLANT RESCUE AT TIM LIVERPOOL LANDING STAGE. --On Wednesday night, about 10 o'clock, a rather "damp- ing "wind up of a day's outing was experienced by a younc, woman named Leech. on the Landing Stage. Miss Leech', it would appear, Is a domestic servant living at New Brighton, and on Wednesday bad a "day out." In the morning she crossed over to Liverpool to visit some friends residing in Toxteth Park, and stayed there all day. At about 10 o'clock at night she arrived on the Landing Stage escorted by a young man. Just as the ferryboat for New Brighton was starting Miss Leech ran to the end of the stage and flourished her umbrella. It was no use, the gangways were up. and the boat was already on the move. Miss Leech, however, who was in a hurry to cross, hazarded a leap from the stage. The passengers on the beat cried "Don't," and the people on the stage echoed the cry; but the boat must be gained at any risk, and the leap was taken, but, alas for the holiday attire! Miss Leech undershot the mark, missed the now rapidly-moving boat, and vanished into the dark waters of the river with a plunge and a scream. A young man named W. B. Godfrey jumped into the river and succeeded in keeping Miss Leech afloat I until Captain Johnstone, of the ferryboat Seymour, seeing the accident, without divesting himself of his clothing, except his hat, also plunged into the river, and succeeded in catching Miss Leech, and supporting her above the water nntil a lifebuoy was thrown to them. They were hauled on to the sage by means of a rope by several men who were present. Miss Leech was taken to the receiYing-house at Prince's Dock and cared for, and was little the worse for her jrnine!lion, Godfrey got up by a ladder to the stage.

The grand committee for the consideration of law bills met on Thursday for the first time, and made some progress with the revision of the clauses of the Court of Criminal Appeal Bill. One of the " houses" in the gunpowder mills at Sedgwick near Kendal, exploded on Thursday, and three men were very seriously injured. Tyr9 pf o.leni are not expected to Survive. , InNienation received from Lloyd's on Wednesday niOrning states that the flue new iron steamer Alora, of Liverpool, 729 tons register, is missing with all hands, anti the insurance office.s have given up all hopes of her safety. The vessel sailed on the Oth February from Swansea for Valencia, to load a cargo of fruit, and has not been seen or heard of since. She is supposed to have foundered during the heavy storm of the 13th and 14th February, and the whole of the crew have, there is no doubt, perished with her. The quarterly meeting of ironmasters took place on Thursday afternoon, and, as usual, was largely attended. Inquiries were numerous, but the volume of business trans- acted was comparatively small. Prices for the most part remain the same as they have been for several weeks past, but the recent reduction in wages and a downward tendency in fuel fortifies consumers in bringing pressure to bear in the direction of lowering the prices of finished iron. The marked bar basis of £7 103 with the extra 12s 6d for the Earl of Dudley's brand is continued. Unmarked birs are to be had as low as £6, but the majority of houses do not care openly to quote less than £6 2s 6d. The galvanised sheet trade is depressed, owing to over production, and at a meeting of makers it was decided to lay down no fixed basis. A feeling prevailed among those present in favour of restricting the output, and a resolution was passed to carry it into effect. Galvanised sheets average at present about VI 103 per ton for singles, bat there is much under- selling. The Welsh tinplate makers also met. Trade was very quiet, particularly as regards the American demand. No definite prices weie fixed, but the usual price for Welsh cokes is 163 per box. The demand for pig is dull, but prices are more firm than in the case of finished iron. Native all mine hot blast rules from £3 to £3 53 per ton; part-mine , about £2 103 ; and cinder £2 to £2 ss. Northampton and I Derbyshire makes vary from £2los to £2 17s. THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADES.—Business continues very quiet im the Lancashire iron trade. For pig iron the inquiry is extremely small, and although makers still ask late rates, there is an easier tendency in the market which, so far as district brands are concerned, would enable buyers to place out orders at a little under quoted rates. For delivery equal to Manchester Lancashire pig iron is quoted 47s 6d to 48s, and Lincolnshire brands at from 453 6d to 468 Gd. less 21- per cent. for forge and foundry qualities. In the manufactured iron trade orders still come forward very slowly. Where business is at present being done it is on the basis of £6 2s 6d to £6 5s per ton for Lan- cashire, and .£6 5s to £6 78 61 per on for North Staffordshire bars delivered into the Manchester district.- -The reduction in the prices of coal announced at the com- mencement of the month by the leading Manchester firms has not as yet been followed by a downward movement in ether districts to any material extent. In some cases there as been a little giving way, chiefly upon the common classes of round coal. The 'better qualities of round coal still !move off fairly well for house-tire purposes. Engine ' fuel is only in moderate demand in the Manchester district, and common yard slack is plentiful, but in ether districts good pit ?lack is scare, with an upward tendency in price. At the pit mouth prices average about Os 8J for best coal, 78 61 to Si for seconds, 6s 6,1 to 7s for common house coal, 53 6d to 6s for steam and forge coal, as Gd to 5s for burgv, and 3s 6d to 4s for good ordinary slack, with special sorts fetching about 4s 3d to 4s Gd per ton. Shipping has shown rather more activity during. the past week, but prices con- tinue low. For coke there is a fair demand at about 8s to 9s:for common up to about us and 12s for the better sorts at the ovens.

- - ASHTON. ASHTON RECREATION SOCIETY.—A meeting in connec- tion with the Ashton Recreation Society was held at the Local Board Offices, on Tuesday evening last. Mr. J. Gaskell occupied the chair, and there was a very good atten- dance of members. Several proposed new rules were dis- cussed and passed, and arrangements were made for the opening of the ground to-day (Saturday.) The question of the appointment of a paid secretary was also considered at I some length, and it was decided to call a special committee meeting to prepare the programme for the annual sports on

_ Whit-Monday. ODDFELLOWSHIP AT AS hTON.-011 Sunday afternoon week, the quarterly committee meeting of the Ashton-in- Makeraeld District of the Independent Order of Oddfellows, M.U. Friendly Society took place at the Gerard Arms Hotel, Ashton-in-Makerfield. The delegates met at the customary hour, viz., three o'clock. Prov. G.M. Moses Battersby oc- cupied the chair, and Prov.D.G.M. Charles Hodgkinson, the vice-chair. At the concltision of the bushuss the Prov. G.M. entered into a friendly criticism of the balance sheets of the various lodges, and a friendly d!scussion followed, after which the meeting closed, and the company adjourned for dinner, whidh was served in the commercial room of the hotel. Dinner over, the customary after dinner speeches were freely indulged in, and the proceedings, which through- out had been of the most amicable nature, terminated _ _

_ shortly after six o'clock. ASHTON CHURCH ASSOCIATION: TEACHERS' MEETING.— The half-yearly meeting of the teachers in connection with the Cave Browne Protestant Institute, Heath-lane, Ashton, was held on Saturday afternoon last. Several business matters were considered, and at the close of the meeting about 40 of the teachers and friends sat down to an excel- lent tea, which was served in the lower room. The ladies presiding at the tables were Mrs. Hill, Mrs. I'. Naylor, Miss HOdgkinson, and Mrs. J. Pennington, and to all appearance the tea was thoroughly enjoyed by all present. An adjourn- ment was made to the upper room, and Mr. C. Hodgkinson was appointed to preside. He explained the object of the gathering, after which an excellently varied programme of readings, recitations, &c., was gone through. The singing was very well conducted, and the recitations and readings were given with much effect. Mr. Thomas Jameson pre- sided at the harmonium with his accustomed ability. At the close of the entertainment, which was a thoroughly pleasant and enjoyable one, a hearty vote cf thanks was accorded to the ladies who presided at the tables, the accompanist, chairman, &c. THE LOCAL BOARD ELECTION: RESULT OF THE POLLING. —Considerable interest was centred in the annual election of seven members of the Ashton Local Board which took place last week. As the voting will show, all the retiring members, with the exception of Mr. Thomas Aspinall, who was not re-nominated, have been re-elected though Mr. Wm. Boardman, one of the defeated candidates last year, made a good fight and secured a large amount of support in his efforts to secure a seat on the Board. The work of counting the votes was commenced on Thursday last at the Local Board aides, before the returning officer (Mr. J. Gaskell), several of the candidates having sent representa- tives. As the task was not completed on that day, the work was resumed on Friday. In the afternoon Mr. Gaskell issued the following declaration of the poll A. B. Moubert 930 votes, T. D. Grimke 813, J. Wright 766, T. Crompton 688, Rev. H. Siddall 675, J. Pimblett-584, E. Burchall 560 (these seven were elected), Wm. Boardman 541, Wm. France 484, John Lyon 463, John Fairhurst 341. At the close of the business a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Gaskell on the motion of Mr. C. Hodgkin- son, seconded by Mr. W. Lowe, and Mr. Gaskell briefly acknowledged the compliment. ASHTON CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH : RECITAL OF SACRED Music.—A recital of sacred music, the proceeds of which were to be devoted towards clearing off the debt on the church, was given in the Congregational Church, Gerard- street, Ashton, on Monday. The selections included the greater portion of Humberstone's cantata, "The entry into Jerusalem," and pieces from the works of Beethoven, Ben- nett, Costa, Handel, Mozart, and Mendelssohn, and had evidently been selected with much taste and knowledge of the abilities of the performers. The principal vocalists were Miss Jones, of Wigan; Miss Smith and Miss Swift, of St. Helens; Mr. J. T. Elliott, of St. Helens ; and Mr. McClure, of Wigan; the choruses being rendered by members of the Earlestown Musical Society, under the efficient conductor- ship of Mr. John Hayes. Mr. Jas. Unsworth presided at the organ. The congregation was a fairly large one, and though no applause was accorded, owing to the, idea that such actions would appear unseemly in the sacred edifice, the various selections were thorougly appreciated, as was testi- fied by many expressions at the conclusion of the recital. After the meeting had been opened with singing and prayer the programme was commenced, the first part of which was solely selections from Humberstone's cantata " The entry into Jerusalem," with the exception of the overture to 4,andel's " Occasiottal oratoria," which was given as an organ solo by Mr. Unsworth. Miss Jones followed with the recit. "When they drew nigh," and Mr. Elliott gave the recit. "Go into the city," and air "The Lord bath need of him." Miss Jones next sang "All this was done," the choruses "Rejoice greatly" and "Mightiest monarchs" being the next items. "And when he was come" was rendered by Miss Jones. Mr. Elliott gave "If thou hadst known," and Miss Smith sang "Come unto I Him." After the choral prayer, "Save us now, we beseech Thee," Miss Jones again appeared to sing "And when he was come" and " Jesu, the very thought is sweet ; " Mr. McClure giving "Where is the promise ? " The chorus, "This God is our tiod," brought the first part to a close. Mr. Unsworth opened the second part with an organ solo, con- sisting of Handel's overture to "Samson," which was fol- lowed with the mottet "0 God, when Thou appearest " (Mozart). Miss Smith next sang "0 rest in the Lord" (from Mendelssolm's "Elijah "), and Mr. McClure gave "Why do the nations" (Messiah). The ever-popular "God is a spirit" (Bennett) was given as a quartette by Miss Swift (who kindly took the parts allotted to Miss Jones in the se- cond part of the programme) Miss Smith, Mr. Elliott, and Mr. McClure, after which the stirring - air and chorus " Philistines, hark "(Costa), was sung by Mr. Elliott and the choir. Miss Swift, of St. Helens, next sang a selected air, and the concert concluded with Beethoven's "Hallelu- jah" chorus (from" Mount of Olives.") The singers and a few friends afterwards retired into the schoolroom and par- took of refreshments before starting for home. On behalf of the committee, the Rev. H. Wilson, pastor of the Church, sincerely thanked the vocalists for their services, and Mr. Hayes briefly responded on behalf of the choir. The party then separated.

Mr. Ellison stated, were occupied by large families and were entirely without water. Others had had their privies changed into water closets, minus water, the consequence being that they caused a serious nuisance.—The CHAIRMAN said there was no doubt that there was some very bad property in that locality.—lt was agreed that the surveyor should inspect and report upon this property—Alderman MCBRYDR said the surveyor might at the same time report upon the condition of some cottages on the road to Marshall's Cross about which he had heard many complaints.

THE KEEPING OF PIGS IN THE BOROUGH. The CHAIRMAN called attention to the fact that the minute of that committee recommending that pigs should not be allowed to be kept within 100 feet of dwelling-houses had been sent back by the Council.—The MAYOR said the reason why he had not approved of that minute was that it would not have given any additional powers to the inspec- tors of nuisances or to the medical officer, but would rather have been restrictive on their present powers. They (the Corporation) had powers to remove all pig-styes which were a nuisance and injurious to health.—The CHAIRMAN Said the resolution was more in the direction of giving the sur- veyor some idea as to the sort of cases to bring before the sanitary authority.—Mr. BELSHER thought all that was re- quired was that the nuisance inspectors should make com- plaints where they ought to be made, and not that the com- mittee should preclude pigs being kept at all, which the resolution passed at their last , meeting would have done. Mr. WILCOCK said that he would propose that the pig question be left alone altogether. They had plenty of power to check nuisances without telling people that they should not keep pigs at all. As for the medical men, there was not a medical man in St. Helens to- day that would not say pigs were a nuisance no matter where they were.--The CHAIRMAN said Mr. Spears himself said the Council had made a mistake in referring back the resolution.—The MAYOR said that perhaps they were aware that they bad farm houses in the district.—The CHAIRMAN: I suppose Mr. Spears is sufficiently acquainted with the dis- trict to know what it is. The MAYOR considered that it should be left to the nuisance inspectors to report nuisances caused by pigs, and they would be held responsible. Dr. McNicoLL said that if the nuisance inspectors thoroughly did their duty in that matter it would amount to the same thing—all pigs would be excluded from St. Helens. Mr. CRACK here said that he had received a letter containing the following memorials to the committee :—" Gentlemen,— Referring to the memorial to the Mayor, Alder- men, and Councillors of the borough on the subject of the proposed restrictions as to the keeping of pigs in the borough presented at the last Council meeting, we are requested to inform your committee that a meeting of ratepayers was held last night at the White Hart Hotel, Church-street, at which upwards *A 200 inhabitants of the town were present, and -many others were unable to get into the room on account of its being cro atded, and at which the following resolutions were passed —‘ That this meeting protests in the strongest possible manner against the resolution of the Health Com- mittee with regard to the keeping of pigs in St. Helens, and would suggest that in lies of fixing a limit as to the distance from a dwelling-house within which pigs shall not be allowed to be kept, the existing powers of the Corpora- tion shall be enforced against those pig-keepers who do not keep their styes in a clean state. 'That a committee of 12 ratepayers representing each ward of the borough be ap- pointed to arrange the preparation of a memorial to the Health Committee on the subject, and that meetings be held in each ward for the purpose of discussing the ques- tion and ascertaining the feelings and opinions of the rate- payers thereon.' The committee was duly formed, and the necessary steps will at once be taken to carry the foregoing resolution into effect, but as it appears that the meeting of your committee is to be held to-day there is not time to hold the meetings, and we, therefore, beg respectfully to urge upon your committee the desirability of delaying the further consideration of the question until the meetings have been held, when the views of the ratepivers of the borough will be fully known.—We are, gentlemen, your obedient servants, PETER MCKINLEY, chairman of the meeting; JOHN ROUGHLEY, secretary."—This memorial having been read, a little further conversation took place on the subject, and ultimately it was agreed on .the motion of Mr. BROOK, seconded by Mr. FOSTER, that the attention of the sur- veyor should be called to the provisions of the Public Health Act, 1875, and the St. Helens Improvement Act, 1869, relating to the keeping of swine, and that he be instructed to report to that committee all cases of swine being kept so as to be a nuisance. Dr. McNicola, (medical officer) reported as follows : Sankey Brook: Samples taken from Eccleston branch by Inspector Williams from the usual places between Spray Bridge and Messrs. Lyon's bottle works are found to be free of acid.—lnspector Houghton has taken samples from Hard- shaw brook district. One taken from Mr. Kurtz's drain contain acid; and those taken from St. Helens Chemical Works are acid, but of less strength than formerly. Some acid was found in the stream flowing into Rainford Brook from Messrs. MOrydes and Co's. works. This was caused by accident, and was at once repaired.—Health of the Town: The mortality of the past month has been great throughout England according to the Registrar General re- ports. I regret to say that St. Helens has not been an ex- ception. Our rate has reached 30.89, the excess having been caused by diseases of the chest. The east and north winds have prevailed, bringing a low temperature, which have proved fatal to many. The total number of deaths during the month had been 139, namely, 85 were males and 52 females. The births numbered 199. THE MEDICAL OFFICER'S ANNUAL REPORT. The MEDICAL OFFICER (Dr. McNicall) presented his 10th annual report. He had, he said, to express regret that the facts and figures would not permit them to congratulate themselves as on former occasions. The mortality, which had been moderate for several years previous to 1882, was increased in that year by an epidemic of measles which pre- vailed during the first quarter, and was very fatal. During the year the local registrar had recorded the deaths of 1,502 persons, of these 776 were males and 726 females. This made the death-rate of the year to be 25.5 against 2147 the previous year. The births in the year had been 2,574, of which 1,283 were males and 1,291 females, making a birth- rate of 43.7, being 68 more than in the previous years when the birth-rate was 43.52 per 1,000 of population. The birth - rate had been highest in Parr ward, and lowest in Sutton West ward in pro- portion to population. Previous to 1881 the birth rate of St. Helens, indeed thronghout the country, had declined from year to year, but during the last two years the numbers in St. Helens had increased to 437. The average birth rate of St. Helens for the last ten years was 451, while the average rate of 20 large English towns was 36.1.—Zymotic Diseases: There had been an unusual prevalence of this class of dis- ease, which had caused the death of 506 persons, being fully one-third of the total deaths. This made the death-rate in St. Helens from infectious diseases to be 8 61. Of small- pox no single case had come to his knowledge; but with regard to measles, which had been an epidemic in the early part of the year, they had caused the death of 250 children, of which 233 were under one year of age. div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

SUBSIDENCE OF LAND AT GOLBORNE.—During the past few weeks a large portion of land near Golborne Smithies has been gradually giving way, and not only has some un- easiness been occasioned, but considerable damage has been done. It is believed that the subsidence has arisen owing to the coal workings beneath the surface, but this fact has not been properly established. The highway has giyen way to the depth of over a foot, and the gas and water pipes have been drawn out of their sockets, causing numerous leakages, while even the railway has suffered, and it has been found necessary to raise the rails. The curbstones on the road side have bgen bred:en, and some damage was done to pro- perty belonging to Mrs. Atherton—the walls having cracked, and the doorposts thrown out of the perpendicular. The dropping was noticed more particularly last Friday, but aft yet there is no cause for any serious alarm. I MAY-DAY PREPARATIONS. Extensive preparations are I already being made amongst the Golborne people for their I May-day fete, the principal attraction of which is the 1 "Crowning of the May Queen," preceded by an imposing procession of merry juveniles in gay attire. Although the custom is somewhat new in this district it bids fair to attain considerable notoriety and has already gained the hearty appreciation of the entire inhabitants of Golborne and sur- rounding district, increased interest in the event having been manifested year by year. Amongst the juveniles the great piestion discussed—long before the " merry month " approaches is—" Who is to be queen ?" This was decided on Monday week, when 09 girls, between the ages of 9 and 13, assembled on the ground now known as the "May Queen field." Considerable anxiety was manifested amongst the little folks who evidently regarded the event as of no little importance. One of the girls was elected to hand round the slips of paper from a bowl amongst which was the word " Queen." The coveted treasure tell to the happy lot of Miss Louis Yates (youngest daughter of Mr.R. Yates, Golborne Colliery), who is now looked upon as the heroine of 1883. The "train bearers" aria "maids of honour," &c., having been appointed nothing remains but the favour of fine weather to ensure success. The arrangements are again in the hands of an active committee. HAYDOCK.

Sr. JAMES'S CHRISTY MINSTRELS.—The troupe of local " minstrels," known as the " St. James's Christy Minstrels," gave an entertainment in the National Schools Haydock, on Monday evening. There was a crowded attendance, and many of the selections by the performers were much appre- ciated, Mr. W. Pomfret, Mr. J. Hazelden, Mr. T. Taylor, and Mr. E. Barnett meeting with the greatest favour. The instrumentalists very ably fulfilled their engagements, and taken altogether the entertainment was an enjoyable and amusing one. The introductory overture, "Emma Snow," was well given; after which Mr. James Cnnliffe sang " I'm as jolly as a sandboy." Mr. T. Heaton gave " Does your heart beat true to me ;" Mr. J. Richardson sang a, comic song, entitled " Bill of fare ;" and Mr. J. Speakman sang "Don't be angry with me, darling." For capitally singing v "He isn't, a marrying man," Mr. W. Pomfret received an encore, and an equally amusing selec- tion—" You're a dirty boy "—was given. Mr. I'. Aspinall next sang, "You are a lucky fellow, John ;" and Mr. J. Hazelden received a well-merited recall for his song " Only to see her face again." "The Skidmore guard " was given by Mr. Edwin Leyland, and was followed with "Save the bay," a piece excellently sung by Mr. T. Taylor, who was re-called. Mr. E. Barnett favoured the company with an effective rendering of "The jolly little nigger," which was also encored ; and the first part of the entertainment was brought to a close with "Say a kind word when you can," sung by Mr. J. Hunt. The second part opened with a "Scotch dance," in which Messrs. E. Leyland, W. Pomfret, S. Naylor, and P. Aspinall took part. Mr. J.4Hunt afterwards sang "Tom Bowling," and Messrs. W. Pomfret and E. Burnett gave "Mulligan Guards." A violin solo was given by Mr. T. Taylor with marked ability, after which Mr. Edwin Leyland sang " Nobody knows the troubles I've seen." After Mr. M. Wilson had sung "He's an old 'un," Mr. G. Strong gave an amusing " stump " speech. div.p: PRESCOT HIGHWAY BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board, was held on Tues- day. Present Mr. W. L. Evans(chairman), Mr. Willis, J.P. ; Messrs. Leatherbarrow, Whitfield, Tyrer, J. Lowe, Cross (clerk), Goldsworth(surveyor).—The SURVEYOR reported that he had received a letter from the Water Committee, of the Liverpool Corporation, asking permission to lay down two wash-out pipes at Rainhill. When the Cor- poration had applied for their Water Works Act of Par- liament, he had pointed out that it was desirable these pipes should be placed underneath the road instead of discharging on the surface, and the Corporation now pro- posed to carry them underneath the road down to the brook.—The application was agreed to, with the condition that the Corporation should restore the road when the work was done, and that the Board should have a right to dis- charge surface read water into the pipes.—Mr. LEATHERBARROW protested against the passing of the amounts which had been allowed at last meeting with reference to team labour done at:Rainhill by Mr. Lowe.—lt was stated the work had been done by Mr. Lowe's son, but Mr. LEATHERBARROW contended that Mr. Lowe derived an indirect benefit from it, and that for him to deal either directly or indirectly with the Board was a contravention of the Highway Act, IB62.—The CHAIRMA.24 remarked that Mr. Leatherbarrow ought to sow that Mr. Lowe had some direct benefit—Mr. LOWE said he had no benefit at all.— Mr. LEATHERBARR.OW intimated that he would appear before the auditor, object to the passing of the account, and explain the circumstances under which the work had been done, and submit to the auditor that Mr. Lowe had a beneficial interest in the work. Tenders for team labour were then considered, when it appeared that the , offer of Mr. Matthew B. Lowe was the lowest.--Mr. LEATHER- BARROW inquired who Mr. M. B. Lowe was, and whether he was a waywarden ? to which Mr. Lown replied that he was his son and not a member of the Board.—A long conversa- tion ensued as to whether Mr. Lowe had any interest in work done by Mr. M. B. Lowe, in the course of which it was pointed out that if a waywarden wished to do work in his own township in connection with the Board he must obtain a certificate from the justices, and Mr. Lowe intimated his intention of applying for a license to do such work at Rainhill. Mr. LEATIIERBARROW now said notica would have to be given by Mr. Lowe of his ; intention, and a special meeting of the Board would have to , be held to authorise his making the application.—Mr. LowE said be would give notice.—Mr. LEATHERBARROW observed that Mr. Lowe admitted the accuracy of what he (Mr.

Leath erbarro w) had said.— Mr. LOWE explained that be meant his application to have refer- ence simply to casual work and not to any contract.—ln the course of further conversation the CHAIRMAN suggested that it would be better to refuse the tender of Mr. M. B. Lowe, and Mr. LEA.THERBARROW moved

a resolution to that effect.—Mr. LOWE thereupon protested and threatened to resign, and several members of the Board having urged him to give the matter further consideration the subject was allowed to drop.—On the motion of Mr. WILLIS, seconded by Mr. TYRER, a vote of thanks was given to the Chairman for his services during the past year, and on the proposition of Mr. LEATHERBARELOW, seconded by Mr. WILLIS, a similar acknowledgement was made of Mr. Lowe's services as vice-chairman.

BISHOP-MAKING IN THE ESTAB- LISHED CHURCH. The Liberation Society has just published a pamphlet on the subject, which will be read with much interest. The Government has recently been called upon to select an Archbishop of Canterbury, and bishops for the sees of Truro and Llandaff ; and taking advantage of the interest which this circumstance has created in the subject of episcopal appoiritments generally, the society has prepared a statement of the various provisions of the law on the sub- ject, and the legal and other formalities which have to be obesrved in connection with these appointments. It is altogether a very opportune publication. It is divided into three sections. The first sets forth in order all the various formalities observed; the second deals with the cases in which attempts have been made to test the reality of some of the forms which are employed on these occasions, and the decisions which have been given in regard to them ; and the third gives an account of the posi- tion in regard to the appointments to the episcopate which is occupied by the Free Episcopal Churches of Ireland, the colonies, and America. One of the first things which will strike the reader is the fact that the entire procedure in regard to the steps to be taken in the appointment of a bishop in the English Establishment is still regulated by an Act of Parliament passed in the reign of Henry VIII. Nothing could better indicate the antiquated, dead-alive character of the formalities observed than this simple fact; and the detailed information which is given with respect to the various stages of the appointment, only serves to deepen the impression of the hollow formalism of the proceedings. Reviewing these formalities the pamphlet says : " That they are - antique and to the last degree com- plex and cumbrous, is the least of the objections to which they are open. Their naked Erastianism, their subordination of all that is spiritual or elevating to what is merely secular, legal, and technical, must strike the most cursory observer; while the Episcopalian who regards the Church as a spiritual institution, receiving its commission from Divine and not human authority, cannot but feel shocked at so ostentatious a disregard of everything which is characteristic of primitive Christianity, and even of the religious feelings of our own time.' The information which is given in the second section will be specially in- teresting. It brings out in a very striking manner the utter helplessness of the Church of England in regard to these appointments to its highest offices, notwithstanding all the elaborate pretence of freedom of action which is made in the forms employed. The proceedings in connection with the appointment of Dr. Hampden to the See of Hereford and Dr. Lee to Manchester in 1847, and of Dr. Temple to Exeter in 1869, are noticed at some length, and the ac- count given will leave upon the mind of the reader a pain- ful sense of the profane mockery which is involved in much of what takes place on the occasion of such appointments. In the third section a far more agreeable story is told; for this deals with the p/osition of the Episcopal Churches of Ireland, the Colonies, and America, which, as they are not supported by the State, are not controlled by it, and have the selection and appointment of their chief officers en- tirely in their own hands. Some very remarkable facts are given as to the beneficial results in the Churches concerned, of this power of self-government, both with regard to the spirit which it evokes' and the facility with which it enables the Churches concerned to add to their episcopate in proportion to their needs. The pamphlet closes with the following passage :—"lt is unnecessary to spend many words in pointing the moral of the subject. The Church of England can escape from the humiliation of its present position in regard to these appointments, and can obtain the freedom of action in which its sisfer Churches rejoice, in only one way. It is true some of its leaders are indulging the hope that means may be found for granting to it the liberty of self government without withdrawing from it the advan- tages of Establishment. But that is a vain dream. If the Church of England would enjoy the blessings of freedom she must be willing to pay the price of D:sestablishment and Disendowment."

Captain Shiel, late of the 75th Regiment, committed suicide at Ihninster, on Wednesday night, by cutting his throat. Mr. Dean, on behalf, of the Church Association, applied to Lord Pefizance on Thursday morning to pronounce sentence of absolute deprivation upon the Rev. A. H. Mackonochie, and he agreed that if by exchanging livings with Mr. Suck- ling the defendant exempted himself from all the conse- quences of his ecclesiastical disobedience, then the law might be broken by any number of clergymen with impunity. After hearing Mr. Jenne on the same side Lord Penzance said he would take time to consider his judgment.

div.head: HALE.
div.p: HALE.

ENTERTAINMENTS AT HALE.—Last week, at the Drill Hall, Hale, two entertainments were given in aid of the Liverpool Royal Infirmary and the Hospital for Women, both being under the patronage of Colonel J. Ireland Black- burne, M.P., whilst the use of the hall was accorded by Lieutenant-Colonel Mewburn. The first part of each enter- tainment consisted of songs and glees, after which there were readings and a lecture on "Mesmerism," by Mons. Duveuthal. A dramatic performance by the " Hale Strollers" brought the programme to a close. The two gatherings were a great success, and will result in sometking substantial for the charities in whose aid the entertainments were given.

HELSBY. AcTioN AGAINST A HELSBY BEILDEIL—At the Birken- head County Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. Swetenham, Q.C., deputy judge, tke trustees of the Wirral Children's Hospital sued John Dixon, builder, Helsby, for £lO damages in trespass.—Mr. Carver (instructed by Messrs. Whitley, Maddocks, and Co.) appeared for the plaintiffs, and Mr. Walton (instructed by Mr, Knowles) for the defendant.—lt was alleged that the plaintiffs bought, in July last, a portion of the land belonging to the hospital, and were strictly within their, rights according to.the conveyance to them and the plan, and had no more than they had paid for; but the defendant, who was a subsequent purchaser from the same Ivendor of an adjoining piece. had trespassed upon the plain- tiffs' land with his drains and erections, and claimed as his property, under his conveyance, about fifty-five yards of the land belonging to the hospital —The contention of the defen- dant was that he had conveyed to him ard had taken no more than he had paid for, and that as he bought from the same vendor as the plaintiffs, he was not answerable for any mis- take.—His Honour held that the vendor was bound by the deed of conveyance to the trustees, and that tke defendant could not claim any part of that which had been so con- veyed, and gave judgment for the plaintiffs for £lO, with costs on the higher scale._ ____
HUYTON. CONFIRM4TION.—On Wednesday the Bishop of Liverpoo confirmed 81 candidates at St. Michael's Church, Huyton. HUYTON QUARRY.

CHILD BURNT TO DEATH. -1:11 inquest was held on Wed- nesday, at the Seal Arms, Huyton Quarry, before Mr. Bar- ker, coroner, on the body of a little girl named Alice Gore. From the evidence it appeared that at eight o'clock on Mon- day morning the little girl, who was about nine years of age, was standing before the tire in her night dress, and, during the absence of her mother for two or three minutes, her dress caught fire'. She rushed into the back yard, and her screams attracted the attention of her mother and Mrs. Jones, a neighbour, who together put out the flames. Deceased was attended by Dr. Gorst, of Huyton, but her injuries were of so serious a natnre that she died at half-past six on Tuesday morning. She was the daughter of Henry Gore, banksman, Wigan-street, Huyton Quarry.— The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." LYMM.

CONCERT.—For the purpose of raising funds with which to buy a number of new instruments for the drum and fife band in connection with the Lymm branch of the Church of England Temperance Society, a concert was given in the National school on Thursday evening. A short time pre- vious to the commencement of the concert the band paraded the streets, and played a number of popular airs. The school was well filled, and the Rev. G. W. Guest presided. The programme, which was a varied and interesting one, was gone through in a manner which reflected cred,:t on those who took part in it, several encores being accorded. It consisted of the following :—Selection, by the'band,: song,

- "The Steertnan's song,' Mr. Blackmore ' • song, "Early years." Master W. Simpson; overture, "Figaro," piano, with accompaniments for flute, violin, and violoncello; song, "Doughty deeds," Mr. Guest; pianoforte duet, Messrs. G. H. and H. C. Bayley; Dutch song, "Kaizer," (in character), Mr. Hindle; new grand march, the band; song, "The outlaw." Mr. Guest; flute solo, Mr. T. Gregson ; song, " Love me little love me long," Mr. Blackmore ; overture, "Caliph of Bogdad," piano, with accompaniments for flute, violin, and violoncello ; Dutch song (in character), Mr. Hindle. The concert was brought to a close by the singing lof the National Anthem. TEE LYMM PERJURY CASE.—With the object of seeing what can be done in the case of William Rowbottom and others, who are undergoing terms of imprisonment for perjury, a largely attended meeting of the residents in the neighbourhood of Lymm was held in the Assembly-room at the Spread Eagle, on Thursday evening.—Mr. Hall presided, and in the course of his remarks he referred to the late trial, the result of which, he said, was deplored by a great many of them. He expressed his opinion that there had been a miscarriage of justice in this case, and said it rested with the meeting to say what steps should be taken to bring about an alterition of the sentence. While admitting that the judicial Bench had endeavoured to carry out the'func- tions devolving upon them, he said it sometimes happened that they perpetrated blunders, and he thought it was a matter for regret that the same judge had previously heard a case in which Rowbottom was concerned.—Mr. Whitham (Warrington) expressed his opinion that, from what he knew of the case, Rowbottom had had an injustice done him. He suggested that a committee be formed with the object of bringing about a commutation of the sentence.—Mr. Nash. Mr. Barf, and Mr. Wood (Manchester) also addressed the meeting, and a committee was ultimately formed with the object above-mentioned, and a number of subscriptions were handed in. It was stated that subscription lists were being filled up in different parts of the district.—A vote of thanks to the chairman brought the meeting to a close. • ORMSKIRK. LOCAL BOARD ELEOTION.—The fcllowing is the result of the voting for three members of the Ormskirk Local Board of Health :—James Eastham, 518; Josiah Wainwright, 441; Frederick Gardiner, 367; William Newshatn, 288; Walter Wright, 157; Peter Forshaw, 42. CRTJELTY TO AN Ox.—A labourer named John M‘Donough and a butcher called Green were convicted at Ormskirk, on Tuesday, for cruelty to an ox' and received well-merited puniskment. The animal had been driven by a lad from Liverpool, and, being tired, lay down on the roadside. While it was there M‘Donough and Green amused themselves by beating it, kicking it, and jumping upon it, and squirted to- bacco juice in its eyes. A month's hard labour in gaol will teach M'Donough to avoid sport of this kind in future, and it may be hoped that the fine of 40s. and costs inflicted upon Green will have a salutary effect upon that gentleman. 1— Liverpool Post.

div.head: ROBY.
div.p: ROBY.

THE BISHOP OF LIVERPOOL AT ROBY.—The Bishop of Liverpool preached in Roby parish Church on Sunday, on behalf of the diocesan institutions,'which include Warrington institution for the relief of widows and orphans of the clergy, the society for tha augumentation of poor benefices, the Board of Education, and the Church Building Society. The offertory amounted to £22. BAZAAR, &C. AT ROBY.—It may be remembered that a week or two ago we narrated the circumstances under which the exterior of Roby parish Church had been embellished with a new clock. It was then stated that what deficiency there might be in the cost of the improvement would be en- deavoured to be made good by a sale of work or bazaar This sale of work, which on a small scale was a pleasant fancy fair, took place on Saturday, in the Huyton and Roby Schools, Damhouse-lane, and was accompanied by a tea party and miscellaneous entertainment provided by mem- bers of the congregation. The result was in all respects satisfactory.

div.head: SANDBACH.
div.p: SANDBACH.

THE SMALLWOOD MURDERS: ALLEGED STABBING BY ONE OF THE WITNESSES.—At Sandbach, on Tuesday, John Stack, one of the principal witnesses against the person in custody charged with the double murder in Cheshire, was charged with stabbing Martin Corcoran, on Saturday night. A quarrel took place between several persons, and the prosecu- tor alleged that Stack stabbed him with a knife in the eye, and three times in the breast. Dr. Archer said that he examined the prosecutor, and found an incißed wound above the left eye two inches in length. There was also a contused wound on the head. Prisoner was committed for trial.

div.head: WHISTON.
div.p: WHISTON.

SINGULAR FATAL COLLIERY ACCIDENT.—OR Wednesday, Mr. Barker held an inquest at the Carr's Hotel, Whiston, respecting the death of Joseph Thomas, 52 years of age. On the 12th December last deceasid was getting coal in one of the pits of Prescot Colliery, when a lump of coal fell, striking the end of his pick and driving the shaft of that implement violently against his stomach. He worked in- termittently for some weeks, but afterwards b came so ill that he had to cease work. Dr. Brindle, of Prescot, attended him, and the case being a peculiar one the services of two Liverpool surgeons were obtained, and a surgical operation was found necessary. Deceased died on Sunday. The evi- dence of the surgeons showed that the immediate cause of death was a tumour on the liver, and a verdict of "Acci- dental death " was returned. WINSFORD.

SHIP LAUNCH.—An occurrence of which too few of the sort have taken place at Winsford lately, a ship launch, called for notice on Wednesday noon. From the slip of Mr, R. G. Cross the vessel " Ammonia " took the water. It is intended for the alum trade at Goole, in Yorkshire, and is made with cisterns for the purpose. SALT TRADE.—The demand for salt, as was reported at the beginning of the month, has continued abnormally small, and so no decrease in stocks has been effected. This is .partially due to the very late winter in the Baltic. No official change has yet been made in the prices as given last month, so none need be made in the present list. The comparison of March, 1883, with 1882, is not very favourable except to some of the minor markets, yet as compared with former years there is room for hope and con- fidence. Times in the silt trade have often been worse. But to look at some details, in which we will confine our- selves to March, 1883, and March, 1882, by comparison, at , the same time saying that the shipments for last month exceed those of March, 1877, 1878, 1879, and 1880, but full below 1881 and 1882. TIF, LEVEL CROSSING NUISANCE AT
WI DNES. IMPORTANT COMPROMISE: SUGGESTED CENSURE OF THE COMMITTEE.

A special meeting of Widnes Local Board 1t".% held yesterday afternoon for the purpose of receiving the report of the Parliamentary Committee on the London and North- Western Railway Extension Bill and the Ship Canal Bill. Mr. F. 11. Gossage presided, and there were present Messrs. E. Carey, F. H. rankhurst, T. Handley, D. Forster, D.Wright, J. Midwood, J. E. Johnson, S. Sadler, R. Webster, Dr. O'Keeffe, and J. T. Allen (clerk).

- Mr. ROBERT DAVIES (the Board's solicitor in the opposi- tion) read the following clauses which had been agreed upon between the Parliatnentary Committee and the Elilway Company:—(l.) The company shall not stop up or interfere with the footway leading from Ann-street East to the Iron Bridge and Marsh in Widnes aforesaid, shown on the de- posited plans as crossing the enclosure numbered 63 on the plans, but shall at all times hereafter have the same open for traffic as before the passing of the Act. (2.) The Local Board may at all times hereafter maintain the sewers and gas and water mains and pipes in their present positions under or across the site of the said level crossing, and may from time to time repair, relay, and enlargs the same, and shall and may have and exercise under or across the site of the said level crossing the same, and as full rights for such purposes as the said Local Board would have had or enjoyed if the said level crossing had not been stopped up and discontinued, but such rights shall

not be exercised so as to prejudicially effect the Present or any future lines of railway of the company. (3) The company shall construct the said new street in the position shown on the deposited plans to the reasonable satisfaction of the surveyor of the said Local Board, and shall for ever thereafter maintain and well and sufficiently light the san e at their own expense, and notwithstanding anything shown on the deposited plans or sections, the gradient of the said new street on the easterly side of the bridge bp which the same is to be carried over the railway of the company shall not be steeper than one foot in twenty- four feet, and on the westerly side of the said bridge not steeper than one foot in twenty feet, and the width of the said new street shall not be less at any point than 30 feet. (4.) The company shall at all times hereafter maintain and keep open for the public use with right of access thereto from Ann-street, the present footbridge over the site of the said level crossing, and if the company shall at any time hereafter widen their railway at that point, the comnany shall construct for the public use as aforesaid, and to the reasonable satisfaction of the surveyor of the said Local Board, and henceforth maintain a new footbridge over the said widened railway in lieu of the present footbridge. (5.) The company shall simultaneously with the omstruction of the said new street construct to the reasonable satisfaction of the surveyor of the said Local Board, and of a width not less than 12 feet, with a gradient not steeper than one foot in eight feet, and with sufficient hand rails, a passage or slope from the said new street to Elizabeth-street in Widnes,, and parallel to that street as a means of communication for the use ef the public from the said new road to Elizabeth- street, and the company shall for ever maintain and suffici- ently light the same passage or slope at their own expense, provided that if at any time the said slope shall be used by the public for the passage of the carriage traffic (other than hand-carts or wheelbarrows) the liability of the company to repair the said passage or slope shall cease, and the Local Board shall thenceforth repair the same at their own ex- pense. Mr. DAVIES said in addition to these clauses, and it was the opinion of those best competent to form an opinion, that if the Board had gone before the Commons they would not have got better terms, he had asked Mr. Itamts, on behalf of the deputation, to pay costs. He twice refused, but on pressing him a little he said a lump sum would he contributed towards the Board's cost. He (Mr. Davies) found that if the Board had gone in opposition, the expense would have been between £4OO and £5OO. He submitted that they had got everything they could reasonably have expected the Committee of the House of Commons to grant; and without any expense to the ratepay6rs, for he was told that £.500 would mean an addition of 2d. in the £ on the rate.

The CHAIRMAN remarked that the deputation ought to be considered by the Board as having been very successful in their negotiations with the company. The slope was quite practicable, and wide enough to bring a loaded cart up and down. Mr. WEBSTER wished to know how the committee came to the conclusion that they could not get the main road from Ann-street if they had gone into opposition. Mr. HANDLEY said they were advised by the solicitor and counsel that very likely Parliament would not grant the road.

Mr. CARET said the committee were very distinctly assured by Mr. Davies' Parliamentary agent, and by the best legal advice, that they could not get 'any better terms probably not even so good as they bad obtained, if they bad

" • • _ Ltie l'arliianvenum: „ox anxious to do away- with level crossings, and that if the 1e9141 Board wished ia:v e unreasonable terms, or if their to : terms were mpracticable. and would prevent the abolition I of the level crossing, the Board would ni.:7itably be beaten by the railway company. Therefore the deputattQll made the best terms possible. Mr. Davies had saved a large expense to the ratepayers by not goirg into cpposition, and the Board were much indebted to him for the advice he had given them, and the way in which he had cenducted the negotiations. His interest was certainly not to discourage opposition, but rather to forward it as a prefessional gentle- man ; but he had given the most honest advice possible, and bad urged upon them no course which many a professional man would have done. He had great pleasure in moving the adoption of the report. Mr. HANDLEY seconded the proposition, and spoke favour- ably of the terms which had been obtained. The CHAIRMAN said they had been as successful as they possibly could have been by the opposition. Mr. SADLRR wished it to be understood that he had been no party to the arrangement, which gave up the rights and privileges of a large number of residents in Ann-street simply to gratify the ambition of a grasping railway com- pany. There were 4,000 people using the crossing each day, and he thought if it was abolished the private property ;per s would experience great inconvenience and serious loss.

Tho CHAIRMAN said Mr. Sadler might rest assured of one thing—that the Committee of the House of Commons would not have offered any opposition to the London and North- Western Railway abolishing the crossing. Mr. SADLER: There is no one can benefit by this scheme except the railway company, and Widnes Foundry Company There may be ems or two indirectly affected by it. Dr. O'KEEFFE said while he had every confidence in the gentlemen who represented the Board, ani in the probity of Mr. Davies, he should not vote until he knew more about the agreement. Mr. DAVIES pointed out that the terms were agreed upon by the committee in London, only Mr. Sadler dissenting, and he did not see what good voting would do. Mr. HANDLEY said the Parliamentary Committee had full 13nir to make an arrangement they thought proper. Mr. DAVIES said they were advised that any property owner agrieved by the London and North-Western Railway Company's Bill was bound to appear in person, and the Board could not take up the case of a single property owner in Widnes. That was proved by Mr. George Bolton appearing in person and fighting his own battle. He (Mr. Davies) would no doubt have pleased everybody a great deal better by allowing the matter to be fought, but when he knew that the expense would be about £5OO, he did ad- vise that if possible that money should be saved, as he felt that they could get as much without going into opposition. Their parliamentary agents, who were men of large prac- tice, scouted the idea of throwing out the Bill on any ground the Board could bring forward, and the terms were agreed upon, and afterwards made into clauses, which were now part of the Act of Parliament. He could not under- stand the Board deputing rive or six people to act lot them, and meeting then with the apathy which ha .`,71 been shown that day. Mr. CAREY said they asked for the approval of the Board, but if they could not get that, the agreement would still etand. Mr. SADLER said the statement made by Mr. Kershaw to Mr. Worthington that the Board's plan as first submitted would coat £lO,OOO, had had a very prejudicial effect upon the matter. Mr. CAREY observed that the committee informed the company's representatives that it would not cost more tban £5,000. and they were prepared to prove it. Dr. O'KEEFFE said Ann-street had been ruined in conse- quence of the inertness of former Boards. Mr. SADLER asserted that if the company had purchased Railway-street, they could have made a road thirty feet wide. _ _

-Mr. DAVIES ,-aid the value of that street would quickly have risen. Mr. SADLER: That is the qutstion. tion of expense. Mr. DeinEs stid if the Board had wished him to oppose and not compromise, be ought to have been instructed to that effect. He contended that they had made the best arrangement possible, but it was impossible to satisfy oiveryone. The motion was put to the meeting, but only two mem- bers voted for it, and it was suggested that the meeting should be adjourned. It was remarked by a member that if the report was not adopted it would amount to a vote of Censure on the committee. The CHAIRMAN said he had no objection to an adjourn- ment. If there had to be a vote of censure he should pre- fer it to be passed by a full Board. Mr. CAREY ohsurved that should the censure be passed, the Board would have to appoint another Committee for the Ship Canal Bill. 24r. DavtEs : And another lawyer too, sir. The CHAIRMAN: If it is adjourned I shall certainly move that a new Committee be appointed for the Manches- ter ship Canal Bill. The motion was then passed, several metnbers abstaining from voting. A shrt discussion then ensued on the Ship Canal Bill, and it was decided that Mr. Davies should forward a clause to the promoters, and the meeting rose.
It is simply a ques-

It had reference to surcharges made upon the Board for -the year ending Lady Day, 1880, the total amount surcharged being £3,105 73. Id. The entire su Ti had been remitted. TRE WAYLE&TE 4IIESTION.—THE ARBITRLTrox ctikne.

The following letter was read : Warrington. 31st March, 1803.—Dear filir.—Widnes Local Board and Hutchinson's Trustees,—We have to report that this matter came before the umpire and arbitrators at the Lion Hotel, hens, on Thursday and Friday. The case of the trustees, as stated by their counsel, was that thoy claimed ss. per yard for the whole length of the sewer, so much for p tank- ing tits end of the new dock for fear of percolation in coose- quence of the proximity of the sewer, so much for restoting their sewer damaged, as alleged, by the new Fewer. and other sums for trespass and land rendered useless; making a total claim of £3,200 to £3,300. ltri)on Mr. Boutledge, the only wit- ness called, p oducing the leases made by Mr. Hutchinson's trustees, as he was compelled to do by notice to produce having been served, and admitting on cross-examination that the lessees and others had rights of railway and cart road on the surface of such of the length of the new sewer, !he counsel of the trustees said he was not prepared to go on, and the umpire required that a pan should be furnished by the trustees accu- rately showing and defining these rights, and adjourned the further hearing to Saturday, the 19th May, at 10 o'clock.— Yours truly. ROBERT DAVIES & 00.-51 r. Alien, Local Board Offices, Widnes.

div.head: SEWERAGE SCHEME-DISORDER DISAPPEARING.
div.p: THE SEWERAGE SCHEME-DISORDER DISAPPEARING.

The CHAIRMAN said he had received from Mr. Pierpoint a certificate to the effect that Mr. R. Jeffries was entitled to £243 56 4d on account of work done on account of Widnes main sewer.—Mr. PIERPOINT explained that Mr. Jeffries was anxious to know his position with the Board, but as he (Mr. Pierpoint) stated at the last Board meeting, he could not possibly find out without measuring the whole of the work done since the commencement. This he had done with Mr. Scholes, the surveyor, to Mr. Farrar, the civil engineer, of Bury, and he should be glad to show the Beard how the figures given In the certificate were arrived at. He and Mr. &holes did not agree by a considerable amount, the latter statingthe balance duo was about £4OO, while Mr. Pierpoint mede it into £243. He gave Mr. Jeffries a detailed copy of the account, and explained everything to him, and although not perbaps as well satisfied as he would have been if he could have had a larger balance, he fell in with it. He (Mr. Pierpoint) should be glad at any time to prove the correct- ness of his report..—Mr. WEBSTER moved that the certificate be referred to the Cemmittee.—Mr. MIDWOOD said things had been in such a disorganised state that they had not been able to have this matter before the Committee. Mr. Riffles had been a good deal knocked about lately, and kept out of money that was due to him on account of the dis- satisfaction that existed with regard to the sewer; but now he (Mr. Midwood) supposed that everything was "square," and that Mr. Jeffries was going en with his work satisfac- torily. Under these circumstances he thought it was hardly fair fcr the Board not to pay the money certified as due.— Mr. Webster's motion found no seconder, and on the motion of Mr. MIDWOOD, seconded by Mr. SHIITTLEWORTH, it was resolved that the money be at once paid.

div.head: GAS AND WATER COMMITTRE.-THE _YEAR'S WORKING.
div.p: GAS AND WATER COMMITTRE.-THE _YEAR'S WORKING.

The minutes of the Gas and Water Committee contained the Engineer's report, which stated that during the four weeks ending the 14th March, 45,049,331 gallons of water had been pumped, and 35,816,008 delivered, being a decrease of 12-4 per cent on the corresponding period Fast year. There were 6,328,000 cubic feet of gas made during the same period, and 6,293,000 delivered. The illuminating power of the gas during the month had averaged 15-66 candles. The rates for the hire of gas and water meters had been reduced. It was recommended that the salary of Mr. A. Redfern be increased from £65 to £BO per annum. The CHAIRMAN moved the confirmation of the minutes, and read the following statement of the yeat's working of the gas and water works :—The de- pression of trade at Widnes during the season of 1882 had been such as to cause a decrease in the consumption of both gas and water, but the decrease in gas for the year ending March 31, 1683, was an improvement upon the years of 1881 and 1882. Seeing that new blood had been infused into the gas and water departments, and the financial matters had been greatly improved, they might look for- ward to good results. The engineer was now erecting a new setting of retorts by which when completed they would be able to make gas at a much cheaper rate than they had hitherto dune. The quantity of water pumped at Stock's well for the year 'ending December 31st, 1882, was 298,831,315 gallons, and the quantity of water pumped at Netherly for the year ending December, 1881, was 327,977,630 gallons, being a decrease of 888 per cent for 1882. The quantity of water pumped at Nether's, for the year ending December, 1882, was 202,637,771 gallons, and the quantity of water pumped at Netherlv for the year ending December, 1881, was 204,496 846 gallons, being a decrease of 90 per cent for 1852. The total quan- tity of water pumped from all sources for the year ending December 31, 1882, was 501,469,086 gallons, that pumped for the year ending December, 1881, was 532,474,476 gallons, being a decrease of 582 per cent for 1882. The total quantity of water delivered for the year ending Decent- .-- eeee, eeeeeee,oee fee fee year enaing Dee:twee. 01, 1061, e aza,reeelee gni lone being a decrease of 4.50 for 1882. The total quantity of gas made during the year ending March 31, 1883, was 70,897,000 cubic feet, that made for the year ending March 31, 1882, was 73,234,000 cubic feet, being a decrease of 3.19 ner cent for 1883. The total quantity of gas sent out for the ear ending 'arch 31 was 73,074,000 cubic feet, that sent out for the year endin - March. 31, 1883. was 71.240000 yg cubic feet, being a decrease of 2.50 pr cent for IM3. The average yield of gas per ton of coals for the year ending March 31, 1883. was 10,000 cubic feet, that for the year 1882 was 9,841 cubic feet, being an increase of 117 per cent. for 1883. The illaninating power of the gas for the past year has been equal to 16-48 candles. The coal consumed for the year ending March 31 was 7.120 tons 12 cwt., that carbonised for March 31, 1882, was 7,441 tons 14 cwt., being a decrease of 431 per cent. for 1883. Mr. FORSTER seconded the motion for the passing of the minutes.—Mr. Joneesole remarked that for some time past the Board had been trying to reduce the salaries of its officials, and now, apparently not satisfied, were going in for increasing them. He thought it was a serious step for the "old Board" to take, and therefore moVed that the minute with regard to salary be referred back to the committee, so that the new Board could deal with the matter.—Mr. MiD- woon concurred with these remarks, and seconded the motion. Referring to the reduction in the terms for the hire of meters, he slid that course would induce people to burn more gas than they had hitherto done, the large deposit of £l, and the high terms for the meters having pressed be-I'o'y unnn the householders. He hoped the time would soon come when every cottage in the town would be illu- minated with gas, and the inhabitants benefiting themselves would benefit the Board.—Mr. FORSTER said he considered that Mr. Redfern deserved the increased salary, and he ought to have received it long before this time. It was the wish of all the members to watch closely the expenditure at Board's ter in present, bi3t a servant ought to receive due remuneratio- for his services.—The CHAIRMAN said the committee given the matter their serious consideration, and an"n. favour of the increase. Redfern had been .in t/e employ four years, and never during that 'wee k.iad crease.—Mr. CARE, in explaining the reasons why 111 had recommended the increase, said he had made many -altera- tions in the office work. It was w-Ai. known that previous to his coming to Widr,„ the office hours were from nine o'clock to five.. Now the office was open during the whole of the ti:,ne the men were on the works, viz, from six o'clock i -P. the morning until the men left work. Of course it w".es necessary for someone to be there, and he had arrange with with Mr. Redfern to work the hours he had named, as he had done with the other young fellow in the oft" etce.- The details of the mains, and the distribution: of gas and water, about which they knew absolutely notl,mig, were questions that would have to be gone into, s'd would entail a considerable amount of work, and more, than he was in a position to do himself. If any- thfin went wrong with the mains he was quite in the hands o the workmen, because he did not know where they were, and the Board had not the information which they ought to have. It was to get this extra work done that he had re- commended the increase. Mr. Redfern was very energetic and deserved better remuneration than he was receiving at the present time. Mr. Carr mentioned other special work that was proceeding.—The amendment was =fled, and the question of salary having been referred back, the minutes were passed.

div.head: UIGHWAY COMMITTEE.
div.p: UIGHWAY COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of the Highway Committee on the 2tlth March, the Clerk reported that Mr. Jowett, contractor, had offered £2O in settlement of the claim for damages done to roads by the extraordinary traffic caused by the Yyrnwy scheme. It was recommended that the offer be accepted if the money was paid at once. Letters dated the 22nd inst. were read from Mr. Hartland and Mr. Proctor about the making or repairing of Irwell-street where Hartland Chapel is situated. The Surveyor was instructed to prepare plans and estimate for making that portion of the street between Cholmondeley-street and Mersey-road. The Surveyor was also instructed to place two of his men to asceitain the number of footpassengers, vehicles, ikc., using Ann-street level crossing.—Mr. MiDwooD moved the confirmation of the minutes. He remarked that he had seen Mr. Hartland with respect to Hartland Chapel, and had informed him that the committee could not carry out the request made by hina which was that the Board should find the materials and the chapel authorities do the labour of forming the street. The only course the committee could take was to make the street and adopt it, and they were quite willing to do that.—Mr. Surrnxwoarw seconded the motion.—ln reply to Mr. Webster, Mr. MIDWOOD said 4,000 persons and vehicles passed over Ann-street crossing in a day.—The minutes were passed.
