ASTONISHING IGNORANCE_ At the Court House, Ruecorn, on Thursday, Mr. Ridg- way, the coroner, held an inquest touching the death of Emma Robert, lie'eai in a court on Mill Brow, with a man named White. On Monday the deceased had a dis- agreement with a woman named -Mrs. Poulton, and whilst engaged in it she received an injury to her back, of which she afterwards complained. Apparently with the object of allaying the pain, she took a dose of laudanum on Tuesday af•ernoon. Shortly afterwards she went into a heavy sleep, and although a number of neighbours visited the house, and one even stayed by tbe woman's side for two hours, no doctor was sent for until too late to save her life. She died about half-past seven on Tuesday evening. The following evidence was given : Joseph White, fisherman, of Heath-road, said the deceased had lived with him about 22 years. She had been in the habit of drinking very heavily. He last saw her alive on Tuesday morning about nine o'clock, when she ap- peared in her usual health. He knew of no reason Why she should take laudanum, and she was not in the habit of doing so. Mary Wilson, daughter of Joseph Wilson, living at Mill- brow, said she was 13 years of age. On Tuesday afternoon, about half-past four, she saw the deceased in the street near her house. The deceased asked her to fetch 2d. worth of "stuff to rub her back." She thought the name of the stuff was laudanum. She fetched it from Mr. Buck's shop, and a boy served her. She returned with it to the deceased, who put it in her pocket, and walked into the house. She thought deceased was sober. Mr. Buck cross-examined the witness, who now said Mr. Buck served her. She asked for 2d. worth of laudanum to rub a person's back. She did not say her mother wanted it. Martin Rafferty, son of John Rafferty, who lived on Mill- brow, deposed to fetching for the deceased 3d. worth of laudanum from Mr. Brown's at five o'clock on Tuesday afternoon. When he was returning with it, Mrs. Hignett met him, and took the bottle from him.—By Mr. Fairhurst (the foreman) : Mr. Brown did not ask him what he wanted the laudanum for. Elizabeth Wilson, of Mill Brow, stated that she saw de- ceased several times on Tuesday, and she "seemed put out of the way." Deceased informed her that she was expecting a summons. About fivo o'olools oho -rrent into tho bongo of the deceased, who was then standing by the doer with the cup produced in her hand. She said she had drunk the laudanum which had been in a bottle that was on the table. Witness said "It will do you harm," and deceased replied "Oh, dear no ; it will only ease me." Witness did not know that laudanum was a poison. and therefore she did not send for a doctor. About half-past seven witness visited the de- ceased again. She was then lying on the sofa asleep, and she died without awakening. Witness did not think the deceased drank the laudanum with the intention of killing herself. Mary Ann Hignett, wife of George Hignett, of Heath- road, said the deceased complained on Monday of the way in which Mrs. Poulton had treated her, and said the latter had thrown some water upon her and had hurt her back. Her heart, she said, felt broken about her niece Maria, who had gone into service. On Tuesday morning, deceased told witness that she did not feel as bad as she did on the previ- ous night, but, pointing to her chest, she said "I feel very bad here, and I think my heart will burst." Several times that day witness visited the house, and about five o'clock deceased told her that she had drunk some laudanum to do her good, and if it did she would have some more. Afterwards witness took 3d. worth from the boy Rafferty.Phe did not see deceased again alive. She did not think deceased meant to kill herself. Mrs. Poulton, wife of 'rhos. Poulton, titter, of 16, Union- street, was then called, and stated that deceased on Monday created a disturbance in her house, and witness put her out. In doing so the deceased's foot caught in the mat, and she Iwas thrown to the ground. The deceased was drunk, and she shut the door in her face. Martha Johnson deposed to the deceased appearing troubled about her neice on Sunday night. About half-past five on Tuesday she went to the deceased's house, and found her lying on the sofa with a quart jug in her hand. She took it from her, and asked her several questions, but she only stared. She left the deceased on the sofa as she had heard that she had taken laudanum, and spoke to the neigh- bours about it. The deceased went to sleep, and breathed thickly. Witness remained with deceased up to the time of her death. The Coroner here examined all the witnesses with regard to their knowledge of laudanum, but all they appeared to know was that it sometimes "slept people to death." The Coroner said it appeared that the last witness allowed the poor woman to remain in a dying state for two hours without sending for a doctor. He asked Mrs. Johnson why she did not send for a doctor, and she replied that she spoke to the neighbours about it. The Coroner expressed his astonishment at the ignorance of the witnesses, and said Mrs. Johnson would have been a great deal more of a neighbour if she had never gone into the house at all. Mr. Croley remarked that the deceased lived amongst a poor class of people who did not like sending for a doctor without having money.—The Coroner said from his ex- perience of the medical gentlemen of Runcorn, he felt sure that if a doctor had heard a woman had taken poison money considerations would not have prevented them attending.— Dr. MacDougall: Certainly. Dr. MacDougall said he had made 11, noee-mortem examination, and so tar ao ho could gqiNTIRIn Tao deceaecd bad ktic..l tiastnsshan ovcrdoco of poison. The jury, after a few minutes consideration, returned a verdict that deceased died "From misadventure through an overdose of opium taken by herself."—During the inquiry the Coroner said laudanum was one of the poisons that dil not come within the Act, and there was no restriction on its sale.

OPENING sat:lt:ES. rs.al'i,lisod Wesleyan Chapel, which has been in course of erection since July last, was opened under favourable ans- pices on Thursday afternoon, The edifice has been built by Mr J. A. Chapman, of Bradford, from the designs of Mr. Isitt, the style adopted being mixed Italian. Patent brick, with stone in string courses, is the material used in its con- struction, and although the building is not of a pretentious appearance, it is an architectural feature in the neighbour- hood in which it is situated. The appointments of the inte- rior are of first-class workmanship and design. Pews of stained deal, and constructed in the form of benches, occupy the ground floor, while running round three sides of the building is a commodious gallery. The rostrum and its fur- niture are of an artistic design. Opposite is placed a new harmenium, which has been procured from Mr. Burroughs, of Myrtle-street, Liverpool, at a cost of about £5O, and will be a great aid to the conversational singing, which enters so largely into Wesleyan worship. The edifice has cost over £2,000, but it is to a large extent free from debt. As a token of the esteem in which they held Mr. Via Hartland, whose name the chapel bears, Mr. F. H. Gosssage and Mr. T. S. Timmis each gave a donation of £5OO, and by various means several additional hundred pounds had been raised. The Rev. Charles Gar- rett, the president of the Wesleyan Conference, performed the dedication services on Thursday afternoon, when the sacred edifice was filled with a crowded congregation. Pre- vious to the service, the Rev. R. Harper, the superinten- dent minister of the Widnes circuit, announced from the ros- trum that the chapel had been duly registered as a place of public worship. Then the hymn" Behold Jehovah's awful throne" was sung, followed by prayer. A portion of the 103rd Psalm was read by the Rev. Charles Gar- rett, who gave a lucid explanation of the various passages. Before commencing his discourse, the rev, gentleman said he rejoiced that they had secured such a suitabre chapel ; it seemed to be just the place they needed; and by God's grace, when they had freed it from debt it would be a place in which they would all delight, and which, he trusted, God would fill with His glory. They must remember that it was not finished until it was out of debt. They had very much better live with a debt upon their own house than upon the flouoo of God. Tho Alo.ot,r muot oomo boforc tho vant. If they wanted tO enjoy every blessing of that house of prayer, see to it that not a penny of debt rested upon it, that they might be free to do the work of God. Unless they freed it from debt, they would leave a great stain that would hinder them at every turn. The rev, gentleman took for his text Genesis, 49th c. 10th v.: "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor the law giver from between his feet, until Shilok come; and unto him shall the gathaing of the people be." He said the death-bed was always a solemn scene, terribly solemn when it was a sinner who was dying---a life to end, eternity to begin; to see the door of hope shut, no Saviour essaying to make intercession, and darkness and doom his portion for ever. The harvest past, the summer ended, and he not saved. The death-bed was a solemn scene when it was a good man who was dying. Only fools were not solemnised, for a thoughtful man must feel the solemnity of the scene—the work-day ended, the seed time over, conscious that eternity would be abundant or scanty according to his conduct in the past. His text introduced them to a good man's death-bed. Jacob's troublous life was ended. Jacob's morning and noonday was cloudy, but the eventide was bright. His natural strength was exhausted, his eyes were dim, so that he could not well discern those round about him. But in that moment when it seemed as though every- thing was ending God gave him a new vision, God took the opportunity as Jacob slipped down the gulf of time to unroll before him a panorama of the future, and he saw the history of the descendants of all his sons. - He saw Christ, and heard the millenium call. Jews and Gentiles were agreed that the text referred is the coming of the Messiah, and the first name Jesus given Jesus before he came upon the earth was Shiloh. Shiloh was one of those wonderful words that was dark with excessive light. Scholars had gathered round it for generations, and every one seemed to discover some new beauty in the marvellous word. One said it meant the "longed for" or the "desired of all nations." Was net that an expressive description of Christ? For no nation could have permanency, or prosperity until that nation was Christ's, then there was solidity, purity, and prosperity too. There was His gracious coming, "until Shiloh come," coming into the world to save sinners, to rank himself with humanity that it might be for ever. He laid his glory by, left the adoration of the skies, and came to the earth to be received, nay, to be rejected. The people took him with cruel wicked hands, and dragged him to calvary, and in that one word they had the whole history 1 from the rough manger to the cross. The ' rev, gentleman traced how the prophecy was fulfilled, and I said the sceptre had departed, and the Jews had ceased to be a nation. Would Judah ever be a nation and have a sceptre? He could not tell, but when that question was asked the solemn words of Paul always seemed to be sound- ing in his ears—" God can graft them in again." There he left them and looked at the last of these three glorious promises—" Unto him shall the gathering of the people be." There was no uncertainty about Christ's triumph. How any man could doubt the ultimate triumph of Christianity in this world was beyond his comprehension. Tr, its..a :a s;esee sts-aa and when a scorner talked about the decay of Christianity he did not know what he was talking about. Take an - illustration. At Preston was Joseph Livesey, the founder of the Teetotal Society. His eye was clear, his heart was warm, and he was as loyal and true as in the days of yo:e. He (Mr. Garrett) dare not say that some of those present would not live to see the millenium call. Look at what had been done in Joseph Livesey's time. When i!ie WAS born there was no missionary spirit in the world, and he himself said his great work was to call the Church. It was a fact that three-fourths of the world when Joseph Livesey was born was wrapped in midnight darkness. America was a semi heathen country; India, but a name, a.strange country where adven- turers went to win honours and get gold; Africa, a fringe of population bordering upon a great desert. Japan was but a name; China a kind of dream that bad an inexpressible charm for children ; Fiji unknown; Madagascar visited but once or twice ; South Sea Islands were just being des- scribed by Captain Cook. That was the state of the world when Joseph Livesey was born. Look at it to-d ty. At honse,the Church full of life' and with a healthy missionary spirit, each striving which shall ;be first to tell the glad tidings of salvation. America was standing at our side, if not a little in front of us in all missionary enteric'. lee ; India was open to the Gospel, which could be preached in every village without let or hindrance; China open to the Cross, hundreds of Godly men and women there preaching the Gospel ; the island of the sea not in midnight darkness but ringing with the songs of Zion ; Madagascar, now a Christian nation with a Chistian 'queen, and Fiji, now a I Methodist world. All this had been accomplished in one man's life ; was it then too much to hope that the boys present would see the millenium. The world was open to them on every side, and nations were hastening to Christ. Why was that chapel built? It was not that they might have their dear friend's name on the front. It was to gather m'n to Christ. How beautifully these chapels stood. They kept him running from pillar to post to open them, yet men bad the audacity to talk about Christianity decay- ing. Who did not know that the intellect of the world was gathering round the cress Same of our would-be clever men scoffed as if nobody but weaklings sided with Chris- tianity. But he told them that the mightiest men of intel- lect in the world were gathering round Christ. Nobody ignored Christ now. They might hate Him, but they could not ignore Him. They could not help seeing Him when the sun was ever shining brighter and nearer. People were gathered to Christ in many ways, but the mightiest argument for the truth of Christianity was the consistent life of a professor. They had an illustration, which he could not but hint at that afternoon, of the influence of a noble, Godly life. Let them try to win those round them to Christ our Saviour. May all be gathered to Him. Mr. HARTLAND rose whilst the collection was being taken, and said he daresav most of those present had heard of the handsome gifts of Messrs. Gossage and Timmis at the com- mencement of the building. They each gave £5OO, and when the foundation stone was laid they also each gave him a£s note to put on the plate. But they grew better as they grew older, and to-day they had sent him a letter, enclosing two .£5O notes—one each—for the collection that afternoon. They owed a great debt of gratitude to Mr. Goesage and Mr. Timmis, and he Prayed that their lives might be spared and their souls conver id and brought to God. Then they would lead a happy life, have a triumphant death, and a glorious eternity. The Rev. CHARLES GARRETT observed that it was a grand thing to have Methodist representatives who had in- luence with their employers, and the young 'men present had in Mr. Hartland an example of a Christian life, which he exhorted them to imitate. The proceedings then terminated. Afterwards tea was provided in the old school chapel. and in the evening another service was held, the preacher being the Rev. R. N. Young, the secretary of the Conference. A collection was made.

div.p: HEALTH COMISITTEIC.

The MEDICAL OFFICER reported to the Health Com- mittee, that during the month of March there had been 73, or 35 04 per 1.000 births, and 35, or 16.8 deaths, including 10 children under one year, and six betvreenone and five years. Zymotic diseases caused two deaths.—The receipts from the market for last month were £lB Bs. 5d., being a decrease of 7s. as compared with March, 1882. Four shops were now let. 82 pigs were killed in the alaughter-house last month.—The minutes were passed on the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. JouNsorr.

FINANCE. At a meeting of the Finance Committee a letter dated 30th March, was read from Mr. Oppenheim, giving notice that the Moss Brook Bridge case might come on any day, and asking for £5O for counsel's fees and witnesses' expenses.— It was recommended that the following accounts be paid and charged against the year of 1883-4 :—G as, £234 lls. 3d. ; water, £lBO Os. 6d.; highway, £lO6 4s. 7d.; hospital, £24 17s. 4d.; health, £7O 2s. 6d.; market, £lO 14s. 9d.; sewer- age, £l5 155.; and Finance Committee, £2,326 lls. 11d.— The minutes were confirmed on the motion of Mr. MID- WOOD, seconded by Mr. SHuTTLEwourn.

div.head: GAS MANAGER AND HIS MEN.
div.p: THE GAS MANAGER AND HIS MEN.

Mr. SaurrtEwotrru asked Mr. Carr what his reasons were for dtscharging so many old hands from the Gas and Water Works.—Mr. Ceuu : Do you simply refer to the men at Netherley works, or to an individual man or the whole of the men discharged aince I came here ?—Mr. STUITTLRWORTH said he was speaking generally.—Mr. CARR : There is a reason in every instance, and I could give you each one. It would be much better if you would take an individual.—Mr. SHUTTLEWORTH : There are two men now under notice at Netherley.—Mr. FORSTER thought it most unreasonable to press this question. If they appointed a manager they must let him have the management and not interfere with him in his duty. Mr. Carr had a perfect right to conduct the business in the way he thought fit, and if the Board was not satisfied let him leave their employ. The question now asked was a most absurd one.—Mr. SIIIITTLEWORTH said it was stated that Mr. Carr was discharging old men, and put- ting in their places men from his native town. He did not think this fair unless he had good reasons for the course he pursued.—Mr. CARR said with regard to such an imputation he had simply nothing to say. It was not true. He had got one man who came from South Shields working as a trenchman, filling the place of a man who left. That was the only man he had brought over here. There had been another man in the position of a stoker, but he had re- ceived an appointment in the north of England, and he had since left. He did not push out any individual. With re- gard to the charge of pushing men out to make way for others from the town where he hal lived, he had nothing to say. He left it to the committee and the Board.—The CHAIRMAN said there had been nothing of that description going on.—Mr. SHurrrLEworcrs observed that it was rumoured so, and he thought it only fair to Mr. Carr that it should be mentioned. He was quite satisfied the rumour had no foundation.—The Board then separated.

div.head: CONSERVATIVE CONGRATIMATIONS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: CONSERVATIVE CONGRATIMATIONS AT RUNCORN.

The Conservative victory in Mid-Cheshire a few weeks ago has had a suprising effect upon the Tory party. Into their dry hopes it has infused an unwonted life, and for the first time for a very great number of years they have had the temerity to attempt to organise a demonstration when the town was not excited by a contest. It trek the good old form of a tea party, and was held in the Public Hall, on Tuesday evening. The attractions of the aromatic tea, however, did not appear to be very strong. Only about 300 persons were present, but it is fair to say that their wants were well aVended to. The crockery and tables removed, then commenced the flow of Tory oratory. Its influence, strange to say, seemed to be as weak as the tea ; no increase in the number of persons present was perceptible; and there was plenty of breathing space in the dingy looking building, whose appearance had been slightly changed by the placing of flags on the front of the gallery. About a third of the audience was composed of the fair sex, to whom the speakers were careful to address no little por- tion of their speeches. div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.

The anticipated result of this contest proved the true one. The five gentlemen nominated by the rival associations suc- ceeded in obtaining the vacant seats, while Mr. Hargreaves, the independent candidate, found hitnselt at the bottom of the poll. But this conclusion did not seem likely at one period of the work of counting the votes, which took place at the Local Board Offices, Alforde Chambers, on Satur- day. Mr. F. S. Gossage was the presiding officer. A return published at half-past eleven showed that. Mr. Hargreaves was third on the list with 300 voles, Mr. B. Dutton being the lowest with 228. Mr. D. Forster stood highest with 399 votes, while Mr. J. Houghton had polled 326, Mr. Pank- burst 28(, and Dr. O'Keeffa 261. The upholders of inde- pendent action could not conceal their elation; Mr. Har- greaves blandly smiled, and it was predicted that "Har- greaves is going to win." The upholders of what Dr. O'Keeffe styled " the compact" were despondent in an equal degree, and for the first time during the contest felt a little less confident of success. But the next return issued dashed Mr. Har- greaves bright hopes to the ground. His star had fallen. Instead of ascending, he had descended, and his name now occupied the last place on the list, with 600 votes The other members were :—Forster, 1,064, Houghton, 064, Parkhurst, 903, O'Keeffe, 844,, Dutton, 774 Shortly before four o'clock, the clerks finished their task, and the final re- turn was :—David Forster, 1,616 ; J. Houghton, 1,540 ;F. H. Parkhuist. 1,362 ; Barnett Dutton, 1,249 ; Dr. O'Keeffe, 1,218 ;W. J. Hargreaves, 932. It will thus be seen that the five candidates supported by the two associations were elected, Mr. Hargreaves being 300 votes behind the lowest successful candidate. When the reault was made known a , considerable number of gentlemen were present, including the successful candidates. Mr. D. Forster remarked that as he .had been returned at the head of the poll he had to perform the pleasing duty of moving a vote of thanks to the returning officer for the able manner in which he had conducted the business of the election. (Applause.)--Mr. MACBETH seconded the motion with pleasxre, and it was carried with acclamation. —Mr. GOSSAGE, who was most cordially greeted, expressed his gratification that the work had been got through so quickly, and in such an amicable manner. He thought the ratepayers of the district had perfect confidence in their representatives there that day. (Hear, bear.) It was not for him to comment upon the result of the election, but he thanked them for their attendance and for the manner in which they had stuck to the work until it was completed. He assured them that when he could render a service to Widnes he was always at their call. (Applause.)—The proceedings then terminated.—The counting of the votes was conducted by Mr. J. F. Allen and the clerks of the Local Bo Ird. On behalf of the Owners' and Occupiers' Association, Mr. William Crabtree and Mr. T. P. Whiteside acted as scrutineers, Mr. S. Owens, Mr. J. Beech, and Mr. j Thomas Sadler performing a similar duty for the Ratepayers' And Property Owners' Association. Mr. Hargreaves was represented by Mr. E. Atherton and Mr. Macbeth. Mr. C. H. Lewin, Mr. H. B. Shores, and Mr. J. Goff also assisted in the work, which was completed with expedition.

div.head: PROSECUTION OF PUBLICANS AT RUNCORN.'
div.p: PROSECUTION OF PUBLICANS AT RUNCORN.'

ijefore Mr. Wm. Bankea and Captain C. W. Hazlehurst, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Thomas Hodgson, landlord of the Feathers Inn, Church-street, was charged with havingon the 19th March, knowingly permitted his louse to be tilt habitual resort of disorderly characters.— lie defended by Mr. Lake.—lt was alleged by P.S. Walley and P.C. Noden that on the night mentioned the defena.ant allowed a number of women of ill-fame, who were accompanied by sailors, to remain in his house for a con- siderable period.—P.S. McMichael stated that he had seen women and sailors dancing in the house, and he bad fre- quently cautioned the defendant. As it was the defendant's first offence the Bench intimated that they would deal leniently with him, and not endorse his license, but be was ordered to pay a fine of 40s. and costs.--Mr. Lake also defended Thonaas Finegan, the landlord of the Rose and Shamrock beerhouse, in Mersey-street, who was charged with unlawfully permitting drunkenness on his premises.—ln- spector Hollingworth and P.S. McMichael gavo evidence to the effect that on the 2nd April they visited defendant's house. In a room behind the vault they found several women, one of whom, named Eliza Clayey, was very drunk. This woman was leaning on the table in a vain endeavour to sing a song, whilst upon the same piece of furniture were a half gallon jug three-parts full of beer, and three glasses containing a similar liquor, In the kitchen was a man,.whom the landlord said was a lodger, and he too was helplessly drunk. The landlord denied that Clayey was drurk, and Mrs. Finegan, Mrs. Swann, Ellen Morris, and Eliza Clayey entered the witness box and supported the denial.—Mr. Lake held that under an order from the Home Office it must not only be proved that a person was drunk, but also that he bad been supplied with drink on the premises where he was found. It had not been proved that Clayey was supplied with a drop of liquor while in the house, and it was only when the officers entered that the landlord's attention was drawn to her con- dition.—Mr. Bankes said the Bench was satisfied there was not sufficient evidence to justify a conviction, and the case would be dismissed. The police, under the suspicious cir- cumstances, had done perfectly right in bringing the case before them.—Clavey was then charged with being drunk in the Rose and Shamrock, and on the evidence of Inspector Hollingworth and P.S. McMichael was fined 5s and costs. —Michael Ryan, keeper of the Lancers' Inn, Wellington- street, was charged with permitting drankenness in that beerhouse.—P.S. McMichael, and P.C.'s Finney and Price, deposed that on the night of the 2nd in- stant they found a man named Gallagher in the house. He was very drunk, and thee were several glasses of beer on the table.—A number of witnesses were sworn, and stated that Gallagher was not in the house when the officers called, and that during the few minutes he was in the house lie had nothing to drink.—The Bench said un- fortunately there was not sufficient evidence to convict. The ease was therefore dismissed.—Superintendent William- son remarked that from the nature of the evidence called for the defence, the Bench could not come to any other decision; but he was compelled to say that sooner or later he should have to take from that court to the assizes some cases of wilful perjury. He should be sorry to do so, but that would be the inevitable result. It was becoming a common prac- tice for witnesses to enter the box and say anything that came into their heads.—John Gallagher was new charged with being drunk in the Lancers' Inn. The officers in the last case gave evidence as to the drunken state of the defen- dant when they visited the house at a quarter to nine, on the 2nd inst., and the Bench fined the defendant 5s and costs. —Superintendent Williamson said several witnesses had dis- tinctly sworn that Gallagher was not in the house, and he felt compelled to take proceedings against them. There had been gloss perjury.

POLICEMEN AND PUBLIC-HOUSES.
CURIOUS CASE AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, David Widders, landlord of the Nelson Inn, was charged with supplying intoxicating liquor to P.C. Burkhill without the order of some superior officer.—Mr. Fletcher, of Northwich, de- fended.—Superintendent Williamson said he was proud that it was not often the Bench had to deal with a case of this kind. From what he saw on the night of the 28th March, he questioned Burkhill as to where he had been, and the officer answered that he had been to the defendant's house, where he had bad three glasses of beer. In consequence of that statement the summons was issued. The defendant had had considerable experience as a publican, inasmuch as he had been in the trade for about five years. When the Act under which this prosecution was taken came into force, and on several occasions 'since, notices had been dis- tributed by the police cautioning publicans against serving policemen with liquor under any pretence whatever. It was with great reluctance be brought the case forward, but the men had to be controlled, and if publicans were to be allowed to encourage constables to drink in their houses when they ought to be protecting the ratepayers' property he did not know what the consequences might be. This might not be one of the worst cases, and the police were not wishful to make a scapegoat of the defendant, but to give warning to all the other publicans.— P.C. Burkhill said at a quarter past ten en the 28th March he was on duty in Rutland-street, when he called at the Nelson Inn and asked for a glass of beer. He was served with the beer, for which he paid 2d., and having drunk it, he asked the defendant if he would have a drink. Defen- dant said "Yes," and they had a glass each, witness paying 4d. Witness then had a third glass at the defendant's ex- pense. Defendant asked how Bossons (another constable) was, and witness replied that he was all right for what he knew, but he had not much to do with him. Defendant said Bossans had no need to speak so " snappy " as he could have "reported him many a time if he had liked." Witness i asked him what he would report him for, when the defen- dant said "Shut up. That will do." He than drank up his beer and left the house.—By Superintendent Williamson: I did not tell defendant I was on duty.—By Mr. Fletcher: He had been "on duty ever since," and nothing had been said about his conduct in the matter.—Mr. Fletcher: If nthor penile Ray it wag a quarter peat, taint, wlieu you weut in the house, is that a mistake ?—Witness : Yes sir, it is. —Your head was not yery clear that night? Yes, 'I never tasted drink anywhere else. Witness added that he had his uniform coat on, and when the defendant threatened to report him, he told him his number was 79. He was not a teetotaller, but he never obtained, nor had he heard of anyone obtaining the consent of a superior officer to get a glass of beer. It was not a " blue ribbon" force there, but he could not say whether other members of the force took beer. He had been in the force ten months, but although he had never been told it was necessary to get the licence of the superintendent before entering a publichouse, he had strict orders not to go in.—Mr. Fletcher : What made you tell the superintendent ?—Witness : He said he would report me and I reported him first. (Laughter).—Oh! and if he had said nothing about reporting you, you would not have reported him ?—No, sir.—lt is a miserable busi- ness then. (Laughter.)—P.S. McMichael stated that he was in charge on the night in question. P.C. Burkhill p traded at the police station at 10 o'clock when he was quite sober. He bad his great coat on with a straight collar so that it would be impossible to turn it down to conceal the number. —Mr. Fletcher, in defence, said he could take a technical objection to the case, but after the expression from the superintendent, he preferred to deal with it broadly and ask their worships to act in the way suggested by the superin- tendent, and to say that there should be no conviction, but the case- should be deemed a caution to other licensed vic- tuallers. But he asked which was the more

blameworthy of the two persons brought before them —the officer Burkhill, who had dragged the defendant into the commission of an offence, and who having got a glass of beer, went straight to the police office to report the circum- stances, or the man who was before them on this charge? Burkhill had told them that he was not a teetotaller, and they might fairly assume that he had on many occasions had beer without the authority of his superior officer. The case rested entirely on the evidence of the man who was the chief instigator of the offence, and who was an informer; therefore according to the absolute rule of the law corro- boration was essential. There was, too, nothing to show the defendant that the man was on duty. It was at an hour when a man might suppose he wished to have a glass of beer after his supper, and under the circumstances he did not think there was a licensed victualler in Runcorn who would dare to have refused to serve a policeman with drink, bearing in mind that there had not been a prosecution of that kind in the town before. Sa far as Burkhill was con- cerned the case was a disgraceful one, and that officer'a gross misconduct changed the whole aspect of it. He thought justice would be met by a caution, which would let it go forth to the public that on no pretext whatever had a pub- lican to supply a constable while on duty with drink, and to go a step higher, a sergeant, or even a superior officer. He did not know whether the superintendent would have to apply to the Chief Constable for a dispmsation—(lond laughter)—but that was the real interpretation of the law. —Mr. Bankes said the Bench hail decided not to convict, hut they trusted the defendant would take it as a warning that in future he was not to supply any officer with beer while on duty.—The defendant agreed to pay the costs, ay To QO

DENTAL APPOINTMENT.-Mr. C. A. Crreenhalgb, L.D.S. (Royal College of Surgeons, Ireland), who, in conjunction with Mr. Parkinson, practices dental surgery with much success in St. Helens, has been appointed honorary dental surgeon to St. Anne's Retreat, Sutton.

STEALING BRASS AT ST. HELENS. An Old MR named Thomas Greener was charged at the St. Helens Police Court with having stolen about 101bs. of brass, valued at 55., the property of Mr. Varley, of the Waterloo Foundry.— P. C. Cottam spoke to having visited the house of the pri- soner on the 6th inst., and there finding the brass which was preduced.—Prisoner said he had picked the brass out of a waste heap. He was, however, committed to gaol for Six weeks. There had been 36 convictions previously recorded against the prisoner. POLICE INSPECTION AT PRESCOT.—The Prescot division of police were inspected on Tuesday by Captain Legge, Government Inspector, who was accompanied by Captain Allison, deputy chief constable of the county. The parade took place in Knowsley Park, the personnel consisting of three inspectors, 11 sergeants, and 79 c,mstables, with Superintendent Barker as chief, the remainder of the force being on duty. The inspection of the men and the subse- quent examination of the books and offices afforded Captain Legge complete satisfaction.

RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS.— At a duly convened meeting of the Runcorn Improve- ment Commissioners, held on Wednesday, the 4th day of April, at half-past three o'clock in the afternoon, at the Boardroom, Bridge-street, Runcorn, it was unanimously resolved :—" That the Commissioners present a petition in Parliament against the Manchester Ship Canal Bill, through the Law Clerk, and that a committee consisting of Messrs. Fisher, Lightburn, Pritchard, Norman, and McDougall, be and are hereby ap- pointed to confer with him during the progress of the petition; and that the costs of, and consequent upon, such petition be charged upon the general district rate."—MAT. STEELE, Chairman of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners.
